GB's Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold on home track

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 20:04:08 GMT

This video can not be played

Hudson-Smith wins gold on home turf in 400m

Great Britain's Matthew Hudson-Smith wrote his name in history as the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships by claiming a dominant 400m gold on his childhood track in Birmingham.

Storming down the home straight to rapturous cheers inside the stadium where he trained as a junior, and which now has a stand bearing his name, Hudson-Smith raced clear to complete a golden treble in the event following success in 2018 and 2022.

Crossing the line in 44.17 seconds, the 31-year-old secured his eighth podium at the championships to equal French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally.

Handling the weight of expectation on his shoulders, the local lad-turned-global star walked up into the north stand to place a hand on the banner displaying his name after delivering for his home crowd - more than two decades after he joined local club Birchfield Harriers at the age of nine.

"Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," Hudson-Smith told BBC Sport.

"Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home.

"I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!

"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."

The team behind Hodgkinson's golden rise and the hunt for a world record

GB's Glave and Azu claim European 100m one-two

European Athletics Championships medal table

It is 12 years since Hudson-Smith won the first of his European Championship medals, claiming 400m silver on his debut in 2014.

Since then he has dealt only in golds in his individual event at this level, alongside two 4x400m relay titles.

With this latest triumph, Hudson-Smith joined British greats Mo Farah and Roger Black on five golds, while matching Dina Asher-Smith as the most decorated British athlete in the history of the championships.

It was Great Britain's third gold of the championships, while Emily Newnham added the hosts' sixth medal overall with silver in the women's 400m hurdles final shortly after Hudson-Smith's victory.

The hosts have further gold medal hopes on Thursday, after newly-crowned 100m champion Amy Hunt and Dina Asher-Smith both qualified for the women's 200m final by winning their heats, while Max Burgin and Ben Pattison will contest the men's 800m final and Elise Thorner will bid for steeplechase glory.

Born in Wolverhampton, Hudson-Smith said before the championships that it would "mean the world" to land gold not only home soil, but inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.

With the illustrious career he has gone on to achieve since those early training sessions - recognised by the renaming of a stand in his honour - he would not be denied in his pursuit of history.

But Hudson-Smith did not make it easy for himself.

Entering the championships as the fastest European this year, the Briton admitted he "misjudged" his semi-final after fading to second place in his heat - an error which meant he had to pursue gold from the outside lane.

Unable to monitor the early progress of his rivals, Hudson-Smith went out hard and had established enough of a gap entering the home straight to reassure the home fans that all was under control.

The European record holder over 400m, and the sixth-fastest man of all time in the one-lap event, missed out on successive global titles by mere fractions of a second at both the World Championships in 2023 and Paris 2024 Olympics.

Those stunning silvers followed the toughest period of his life, but he put three years of "absolute hell" behind him to win world bronze in 2022 as he re-established himself among the world's best.

On the European stage, there has been no shortage of golden moments - but none will come close to this emotional full-circle moment.

Speaking on BBC TV, three-time world heptathlon champion Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill said: "What a moment. This will stay with Matthew Hudson-Smith forever.

"It means so much and the pressure was piled on him. Anything but a gold medal here for him would have been a disappointment."

Hudson-Smith's celebrations had not long concluded when the 22-year-old Newnham achieved her latest international medal of a sensational season.

Delivering from lane nine, just as Hudson-Smith had done just 20 minutes earlier, she produced a personal best of 53.33 seconds to take silver behind Slovakia's Emma Zapletalova, who won in 52.91.

In a breakthrough 2025, Newnham won two relay medals as part of the British team at the European Indoor Championships, and double gold - including individual success - at the European Under-23 Championships.

Building on that progress, she lowered both her 400m hurdles and 400m flat personal bests this summer before clinching her first individual senior international medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow 12 days ago.

This latest glimpse of her exciting potential took her closer still to 1992 Olympic champion Sally Gunnell's British record of 52.74, which has stood for 33 years.

Students wait for A-level, T-level and BTec results

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 19:26:55 GMT

Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive A-level, T-level and BTec results on Thursday morning.

Another record number of students are expected to find out they have secured a place at their first choice of university.

The cost of going to university has been in the spotlight this year, with mounting pressure on the government to reform student loan repayments and a renewed focus on technical education under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

But the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents more than 140 vice-chancellors, urged students to not "let politicians make your decision for you".

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer.

Around 250,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications are also expected to be released to students in England, including BTec National, Cambridge Technical, Cambridge Advanced National and T-level results.

AS-levels, which will count towards students' final A-level results next summer in Wales and Northern Ireland, will also be released.

This year, the pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board.

And last year, the proportion of students getting top A-level results reached a record high, with 28.3% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland marked at A* or A.

Around 41% of UK 18-year-olds had applied to university by the end of June this year.

That is a similar proportion to last year, despite increased scrutiny of the long-term cost of university and a renewed focus on technical education.

Vivienne Stern, chief executive of Universities UK, said she was concerned that "people talking [university] down" could "put off" potential students from the least-advantaged backgrounds.

She urged students to "make the right decision for you", adding: "Don't let politicians make your decision for you."

Jo Saxton, chief executive of Ucas, said on Tuesday that she found "kicking higher education incredibly frustrating".

"It's right that the prime minister and secretary of state [in England] are committed to parity [between academic and technical education] but I still think that there are lots and lots and lots of young people the best place for whom would be in a university," she said.

Their comments follow criticism of the student loan repayment system this year - especially Plan 2 loans, which used to be issued in England and are still issued in Wales.

They also come after Burnham announced that pupils in England will be able to study technical subjects in addition to core academic learning from Year 10.

His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, announced that new V-level qualifications would be an additional vocational option for students from 2027.

Meanwhile, universities continue to struggle with their finances after a long-term freeze in domestic tuition fees and a fall in international student numbers.

Undergraduate tuition fees in England and Wales are rising for a second year running for students starting university in September, reaching £9,790 a year.

But four in ten universities in England are still expected to report a deficit for the 2025-26 financial year.

Most students getting their grades this year were in Year 7 and Year 8 in 2020 and 2021, during the Covid pandemic.

Both years saw spikes in pass rates at GCSE and top grades at A-level, after exams were cancelled and results were based on teachers' assessments, and were followed by a phased effort to bring grades back in line with pre-pandemic levels.

This summer England's exams regulator, Ofqual, said it was "closely monitoring" the marking of an A-level maths paper which students and parents claimed was significantly more challenging than in previous years.

GB's Evans wins European gold in 100m breaststroke

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 19:23:41 GMT

This video can not be played

Evans wins breaststroke gold in British record time

Great Britain's Angharad Evans won her first European Championship gold in the 100m breaststroke final in Paris.

The 23-year-old comfortably finished first in a championship record time of one minute and 4.87 seconds, which was also a lifetime best and British record.

Having also broken the championship record in the semi-final, Evans claimed gold ahead of Ireland's Mona McSharry in second, while Italy's Benedetta Pilato took bronze.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki, who made history for Jersey by claiming gold in the 200m breaststroke at the Commonwealth Games last month in Glasgow, was the fastest qualifier in the semi-final of the same event at the European Aquatics Championships.

The 18-year-old's time of 2:08.60 held off GB team-mate Greg Butler in the first semi-final, with the 25-year-old also progressing to the final.

GB's Amalie Smith picked up a silver medal in the 400m individual medley final, finishing 0.7secs behind Ireland's Ellen Walshe, with Poland's Justina Kozan claiming bronze.

The 16-year-old Smith, who won gold on Monday in the 4x200m freestyle relay, was also part of the part of the 4x100m freestyle relay team that finished fifth.

Another teenager, Italian Sara Curtis, also shone as she broke the women's 50m backstroke world record with a time of 26.63 seconds.

The 19-year-old bettered the world record set by Australia's Kaylee McKeown three years ago by 0.23secs in her semi-final.

Burnham urges shops not to sell disposable BBQs over wildfire risks

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 19:05:38 GMT

Andy Burnham has urged shops to stop selling disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister said he was urging "all retailers big and small" to adhere to voluntary guidance to suspend sales during extreme heat.

He added that in the "longer term" the government would look at potentially banning the single-use grills during summer months.

It comes after a potential ban was discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures.

A number of large retailers and supermarkets have voluntarily stopped selling the devices under a framework agreed in 2023 between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

This says that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.

Earlier, Burnham told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

After the Cobra meeting, Burnham said: "We would say to retailers do not put disposable barbecues on sale at this moment in time."

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

A Labour MP wrote to large retailers last week in a bid to stop them selling disposable barbecues for the rest of the summer, whilst a number of Lib Dem MPs have also backed restrictions.

The National Farmers Union has also called on local councils to issue public space protection orders to restrict their use in public areas.

Authorities including Brighton & Hove and Fylde, in Lancashire, are among councils to have used these orders to ban single-use grills in recent years.

Those who defy such orders can currently be fined up to £100, a limit that is set to rise to £500 in future.

Councils intending to issue the orders are required to consult residents beforehand, and gather evidence of an ongoing risk to quality of life in a particular area.

The Cobra meeting was attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.

There has already been one Cobra meeting on heatwaves this year chaired by officials, but this was the first such emergency session chaired by Burnham.

In June, the government under previous prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced that specialist firefighters would be positioned in key locations across England in response to wildfire risks, with forces encouraged to use a government fund to upgrade equipment.

Burnham had faced calls from the Green Party to chair a Cobra meeting on the heatwaves, with leader Zack Polanksi accusing the prime minister of inaction amid threats to public health and food supplies.

Speaking on Wednesday, Polanski welcomed the meeting but said it was "not enough just to discuss" the threats from heat.

He added that recent temperatures showed the need to offer workers flexible hours to allow them to avoid the hottest part of the day, and for a legally-enforced maximum temperature for workplaces.

The party has previously called for more publicly accessible "cool spaces" for vulnerable groups and financial support to help households heatproof their homes.

Fire chiefs have said that wildfires are becoming a "recurring and growing feature of the risks facing our communities" amid a changing climate.

Crews responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record.

New Forest wildfire continues as temperatures rise

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 17:53:31 GMT

Firefighters on the fourth day of battling a wildfire in the New Forest are facing "challenging" weather conditions with temperatures set to rise again

The blaze began on Sunday 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31, with 23 drivers abandoning their vehicles as the fire took hold.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews had implemented fire breaks and had a 'good hold' of the perimeter of the fire, while changing wind conditions were proving challenging.

National Highways said repairs to the A31 were not expected to be begin until Friday 14 August at the earliest.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire & Rescue Service has issued a new statement, in which it said firefighters had a "good hold of the perimeter of the fire" with "progress being made to implement fire breaks".

But it said changing wind conditions were proving "challenging" and nearby residents are advised to close doors and windows due to the smoke.

The fire service has deployed a heavy volume pump at Hightown Lake in Ringwood "in order to deliver a sufficient water supply to the incident ground".

"We understand this affects local residents, with a hose laid across pavements and driveways, and apologise for the frustration this causes," it said.

"We are working with residents to minimise disruption, and appreciate their understanding as this equipment provides our teams with the supply needed to continue tackling this significant fire effectively and help resolve the incident."

National Highways said: "Significant repairs are needed to the road surface, safety barrier, bridge parapets and boundary fencing.

"Repairs can only begin once Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service confirms it's safe to access the road. This is not expected to be the case until Friday at the earliest.

"Smoke, heat, ash and the fire's ongoing movement mean safe access isn't yet possible.

"We have crews on standby ready for when access is granted, and we will be working round the clock to fully open the road as soon as possible."

The New Forest wildfire is one of several to have ignited across the UK amid continuing heatwave conditions.

The Fire Brigades Union say there have been difficulties recruiting on-call firefighters, and a steep fall in overall firefighter numbers.

This has led to fewer available fire engines and appliances, increasing pressure on services.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, which is responsible for fire services, says it will ensure fire services have the resources they need.

A spokesperson said: "This includes making almost £1.95bn available for fire services in England, and investing nearly £100m in the biggest upgrade to national resilience in almost 20 years."

England and Wales have seen as many wildfires in 2026 so far as there were in the whole of last year, new figures have revealed, as the Prime Minister is set to convene an emergency meeting about the extreme weather facing the country.

Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), the same as last year's record-breaking total.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the New Forest fire is a "great concern".

"There is obviously a significant problem of wildfires in the South," he said.

Burnham confirmed that he is considering a ban on disposable BBQs after the wildfire prompted further warnings about using them in high risk areas.

HIWFRS said: "It only takes one careless action to start a wildfire.

"A single discarded cigarette, campfire or barbecue can rapidly escalate into a serious wildfire, causing widespread damage to wildlife and the countryside, endangering firefighters and putting additional pressure on already stretched emergency resources."

People are advised to take home litter, avoid smoking and using barbecues, and not to light campfires or bonfires.

The fire service also warned drivers not to park on dry grass as the underside of vehicles can reach over 400C.

Major Russian grain export terminals hit in Ukraine Black Sea port attack

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 17:47:01 GMT

A "massive" Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Russia's port of Novorossiysk has damaged two major grain export terminals and hit the last big Russian naval base on the Black Sea, reports say.

Three people, including an eight-year-old child, were killed and another 24 injured in the overnight attack, local officials said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had launched rockets, jet and naval drones in a "unique operation" to strike the Russian base, although he did not mention grain terminals being hit.

Ukraine's military later said four Russian warships, including two frigates, were hit. Russia has not commented on the issue.

"The occupying fleet and all the infrastructure that supports it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues," Zelensky said in a post on social media.

Most of Russia's Black Sea fleet is docked in Novorossiysk - one of the largest ports in Russia - after it was forced to vacate its former home base of Sevastopol, in the Russia-occupied Crimean peninsula, which was too exposed to Ukrainian attacks.

A major grain trading company confirmed to Russia's TASS news agency that its terminal had been hit, while another told Reuters and Russian outlet RBK the same.

The Russian agriculture ministry announced on Wednesday that it was working to redirect cargo flows to ports in the Baltic and Caspian Seas as well as land routes. It did not make any reference to Ukraine's attacks but said it was "taking into account current logistical constraints".

Repeated explosions reportedly rang out over Novorossiysk throughout the night as air defences shot down aerial objects.

An emergency situation was declared in the city on Wednesday, after the barrage of drones struck areas around the port and damaged pipelines, suspending water supply for the city.

Elsewhere in the region a man was killed by drone debris, regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said. Several locations in the surrounding Krasnodar region were also struck by "several hundred drones" overnight, Kondratyev added, with dozens of buildings damaged, including homes.

For its part, Moscow launched aerial overnight strikes which killed at least 11 civilians in Ukraine between Tuesday and Wednesday.

The majority were killed when Russia hit the southern city of Zaporizhzhia with ballistic missiles and glide bombs.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

After a period of relative calm in the Black Sea, over the course of this summer Kyiv and Moscow resumed striking one another's ports and shipping.

The last remaining sea route out of Ukraine has been badly affected by several deadly Russian strikes on cargo ships and the port of Odesa, through which Moscow seeks to put off foreign companies from trading with Ukraine. In July, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) reported a 23% decrease in exports.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown increasingly adept at carrying out long-range strikes on Russian territory. Its recent attacks on vessels in the eastern Black Sea have disrupted Russia's grain shipments, too.

Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter - but according to a Moscow-based analytics company, exports for August could fall by more than half compared to the same month over the last five years due to the disruption in the Black and Azov seas.

On Wednesday, Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of carrying out strikes on Russian grain and agricultural infrastructure, resulting in a hike in global food prices and growing grain shortages.

But Zakharova also said that Russia would continue striking "facilities that [Ukraine's armed forces] use on the Black Sea to destabilise the navigation situation" until "the full elimination of threats to security projected to the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea".

Concerns over how the war in Ukraine would affect global food supplies have been persistent since the start of Russia's invasion in 2022.

Together, Russia and Ukraine account for a significant share of global grain trade, particularly for buyers in North Africa, the Middle East and parts of Asia.

The 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports, did not last after Moscow resumed attacks on vessels using the maritime corridors to Odesa the following year.

Ann Widdecombe's loved ones gather for her funeral

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:31:07 GMT

About 100 family, friends and colleagues have attended the funeral of former Tory minister Ann Widdecombe.

Mourners gathered at Buckfast Abbey in Devon, a Catholic abbey at which she regularly worshipped and called her "safe haven".

Widdecombe died on 8 July aged 78 and was found with serious head injuries at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor.

Those attending could be seen wearing black as they arrived at the Requiem Mass for the former MP, who later became a Reform UK spokeswoman.

Police officers and sniffer dogs were in the grounds of the abbey ahead of the service, which lasted about 90 minutes.

The private requiem mass included a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, Abbot of Buckfast.

He said: "In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this Abbey Church which Ann called her safe haven."

A statement from the Abbey Church earlier said Widdecombe would be "missed and fondly remembered" and "many in our worshipping community knew her as a kind and warm character".

"Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics," it said.

It added: "Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant."

The order of service also included tributes paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe's nephew, and Sir Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

A public memorial for Widdecombe is due to be held later this year.

Donations made in her memory are due to be divided between the Leprosy Mission and Abound, supporting the projects of the Christian Endeavour Hostel (CEH) in India.

Widdecombe's career in politics spanned decades.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

She later represented South West England as a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for the Brexit Party and in 2023 she joined Reform UK as a party spokeswoman.

Joshua Kerry, a 28-year-old man from South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder in July following an investigation led by counter-terrorism detectives.

A provisional trial date has been listed for June 2027.

Israeli settlers besieging Palestinian families in West Bank village

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:14:08 GMT

Israeli settlers have been besieging two Palestinian families in their homes in the occupied West Bank since Sunday, with the families saying their supplies were running out and rights groups urging the authorities to step in.

On Wednesday Israeli security forces were reported to have withdrawn from the Jewish settler outpost in the village of Qusra near Nablus, following clashes with a crowd of extremist settlers. About a dozen settlers are said to remain at the site.

After the Palestinian homeowners made their initial report to the Israeli army, the first soldiers who arrived at the scene were filmed praying with the settlers.

The Abu Ridi and Hassan families have been posting on social media appealing for help after their water and power supplies were cut off and their food stocks ran low.

It is not clear exactly what the settlers in Qusra want. In the past, settlers have forced Palestinians out of their homes and seized their properties.

The stated aim of the settlers is to empty the area of its Palestinian residents.

The latest developments come as a top UN official told the Security Council in New York on Tuesday that "the West Bank is at breaking point".

All settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts are set up without official Israeli authorisation.

Palestinian security camera footage shows settlers tearing down a wall outside the Abu Ridi family's home on Sunday evening and using the stones to block the road.

This left seven people - including two young girls – unable to leave their homes while other Palestinians could not reach them. They live in what is known as Area B, part of the West Bank under Palestinian administrative control and Israeli security control.

Posting on Facebook, Qusay Abu Ridi said the situation was critical, "especially as we are completely isolated".

He wrote: "We are living in our own home, on our own land, and we are asking for nothing more than the right to live safely and with dignity."

Aysha Hassan told Reuters the settlers had "tried to break the gate" to the house and "started throwing stones at us, cursing and insulting us".

She said her family was "dying of fear, extremely terrified".

On Monday, Israeli settlers blocked Israeli journalists from the left-leaning Haaretz newspaper from trying to reach the Palestinian properties. The reporters said Israeli soldiers at the scene refused to help them when their car was blocked for two hours. They were told the area was a closed military zone, however the order was not enforced on the settlers.

A day later the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din urgently appealed to the head of the Israeli military's Central Command for the army to protect the besieged residents, evacuate the settlers' outpost and hold the settlers accountable.

Late on Tuesday, a Palestinian ambulance was finally allowed to reach the families, delivering food and taking one child away for medical treatment.

At about the same time, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) put out a statement condemning the establishment of the new outpost. It said that entering and seizing Palestinian homes was "illegal, reprehensible, and unacceptable activity".

When the head of its Central Command, Maj Gen Avi Bluth and other senior officers arrived at the scene early on Wednesday they are said to have met residents and voiced their "grave concern".

Afterwards, Palestinian security camera video shared with the BBC showed confrontations between Israeli soldiers and border police and a large crowd of settlers. The security forces used tear gas and stun grenades.

In other footage, the Israeli forces appear to have confiscated the canopy under which the settlers were sheltering, while leaving their other equipment.

"Border Police forces evacuated the tent and are working to evacuate the civilians who were staying there. The incident is still ongoing," the IDF stated.

It said it was decided that "disciplinary action would be taken against the security personnel involved, who were documented at the site several days ago".

The Palestinian village mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, told the BBC that local residents had seen "a clear and sustained pattern of targeting Qusra". Last month a newly completed mosque was set on fire with graffiti in Hebrew sprayed nearby.

That settler attack was one of many that followed on from an incident in the Palestinian village of Tal. After Israeli settlers attacked Tal, it triggered an escalation in which six people were killed - four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers – one of whom acted as a security coordinator for a nearby Israeli settlement.

In July, settlers also surrounded a Palestinian home in the village of Jalud, near Qusra, for more than two weeks. Afterwards, the owners fled and settlers took over the property where they remain until now.

"Settler violence has reached unprecedented levels," the UN's Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, told the Security Council in a briefing on Tuesday.

He gave what he described as "the sobering human toll" and mentioned that the Nablus Governorate in particular had been hit hard recently by violence.

According to the UN's figures, 76 Palestinians – including 18 children - have been killed in the West Bank this year, by Israeli forces or settlers. At the same time, three Israelis – including one civilian – were killed in confrontations with Palestinians and in an alleged ramming attack by a Palestinian in the West Bank.

Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities in the West Bank have experienced full or partial displacement, including 47 that have been entirely displaced, affecting more than 6,390 Palestinians, the UN says.

It has registered that in 2026, about 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, have been displaced due to settler violence, demolitions and evictions.

Speaking at the UN meeting, Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon dismissed the idea that settlements were an obstacle to peace. He said that they would remain and continue to grow as his country had biblical, historic and legal rights to the land.

He said that the Security Council "must understand a simple truth: we are not going anywhere".

LA Lakers to be sold in record $12.5bn deal

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:11:04 GMT

Luka Doncic is one of the star players with the LA Lakers

The Los Angeles Lakers are to be sold for a reported record-breaking $12.5bn, external (£9.3bn) - less than a year after Mark Walter took a majority stake in the NBA franchise.

Josh Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, and former Disney chief executive Bob Iger are buying the controlling interest in one of the world's most iconic sports teams.

Walter bought his share, reportedly worth an estimated $10bn (£7.45bn) - a previous record - from the Buss family in a deal that was unanimously approved by the NBA Board of Governors in October 2025.

Kushner and Iger said in a statement: "As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honoured for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world.

"We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss.

"Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles."

Jerry Buss bought the Lakers in a $67.5m deal (£50m) in 1979 that included the Los Angeles Kings hockey team and a Los Angeles arena, known as the Kia Forum.

After he died in 2013, ownership was passed to his six children in a Trust before a deal was completed with Walter, who also owns a stake in the LA Dodgers with Todd Boehly.

"Owning the Los Angeles Lakers has been one of the great honors of my life," said Walter.

"It has been an extraordinary investment, but what I will carry with me is the community, the fans, and a city that treats this team as family.

"I am grateful to Jeanie Buss, the Buss family, the players, and the staff for welcoming me into this chapter. The Lakers belong to Los Angeles, and I have every confidence the best is still ahead."

The LA Lakers have 17 NBA titles - one less than the record of 18 held by the Boston Celtics.

The deal involving Kushner comes after he was part of the recent controversy surrounding Fifa president Gianni Infantino and an aborted plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors.

Thrive Eternal, an American venture capital firm founded by Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group for the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

The Lakers lost LeBron James, the highest points scorer in the history of the NBA, in the summer as the 41-year-old joined the Philadelphia 76ers.

That left Luka Doncic, who arrived from the Dallas Mavericks in February 2025, as the team's main star and he welcomed the takeover.

"Being a Laker means everything to me, and I'm excited to get back on the court and bring a championship to LA," he said in a message on social media., external

"I've gotten used to big changes over these last few years, but I know that no matter what, there is no limit to the potential of this iconic franchise.

"I look forward to meeting Josh and Bob so we can get to work building something special in LA together."

Eurovision Song Contest changes rules for countries at war

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:49:37 GMT

Organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year.

The amendment was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026 in Vienna.

It states that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

The update will be interpreted as a reaction to Israel's continued presence at the contest, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain and Ireland.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

Following their victory, Eurovision organisers undertook a "full assessment and feasibility study" to decide whether the 2023 contest could proceed in Kyiv.

They ultimately decided the security risks were too great, and the UK stepped in to host the competition in Liverpool.

The new rules formalise that process, stating that "where deemed necessary" the EBU, which organises Eurovision, "may commission an independent security assessment of the winner's region".

"Following that assessment, the EBU will consult the Reference Group to determine whether the winning member is able to safely host the Contest."

If the winning country is deemed unable to host, the EBU will select an alternative broadcaster to run the show.

Significantly, they "will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member". (In 2023, the BBC worked in conjunction with its Ukrainian counterpart to reflect the country's heritage in the contest).

Other rules announced on Tuesday raised the minimum age for participation in Eurovision from 16 to 18; and clarified regulations on the use of backing tracks.

Since 1999, live instruments have effectively been banned, with only the lead vocalist performing live.

From next year's contest, the backing track may not "unduly assist" the singer or singers on stage, for example by including a pre-recorded voice singing the main melody to thicken or support the live performance.

"The clarification is intended to protect the integrity of each performance and to ensure the audience always hears the lead vocals on each song performed live," said the EBU.

Commenting on the updated rules, Eurovision director Martin Green said: "These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the Contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special."

Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria, after their entrant Dara won the 2026 edition with her club anthem Bangaranga.

Last month, it was announced that Canada would enter the contest for the first time.

How do I apply for an apprenticeship and what will I get paid?

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:42:49 GMT

Apprenticeships offer an route into work and further qualifications for people who want to learn while earning.

But what is an apprenticeship, how much do apprentices get paid and what careers can they lead to?

An apprenticeship combines paid work with study towards a recognised qualification.

Apprentices usually spend most of their time working and part of their time completing training with an employer, college, university or online provider.

People often choose apprenticeships because they know the career they want to pursue, or because they want to gain new skills without studying full-time.

Any employer can hire apprentices. They are responsible for ensuring apprentices work with experienced staff and receive time away from their job to complete their studying.

Apprenticeships are available across a wide range of industries, including business, engineering, construction, healthcare, digital, hospitality and creative sectors.

You get paid for the time you spend working.

If you are under 19, or if you are 19 or older but in the first year of your apprenticeship, you will be paid at least the apprentice rate of £8 per hour.

Those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate minimum wage for their age:

These rates apply across the UK but employers can choose to pay more than the legal minimum.

Some apprenticeships can also lead to higher salaries after completion.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the different levels of apprenticeship are:

In Scotland, the different levels are:

Advanced apprenticeships - A-level standard - are the most popular, and the number of people doing higher apprenticeships has been rising.

Hundreds of thousands of people are on apprenticeships in England each year.

Apprenticeships are available for school leavers, young people and adults looking to develop new skills or change careers.

The government has introduced a number of measures aimed at increasing apprenticeship opportunities and helping more young people access training.

There have also been concerns about the decline in the number of young people starting apprenticeships in recent years, as well as whether opportunities are equally accessible to people from different backgrounds.

If you know where you want to work, you can head straight to the employer's website and apply.

You can search for apprenticeship opportunities through different official websites in England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.

The Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) website also lets you search for apprenticeship vacancies.

You will be interviewed for the apprenticeship before you start, and will need to pass an assessment showing what you have learned before you can finish.

Think hard about what the apprenticeship offers. Can you picture yourself in a job in the industry? Will the qualification help you in the career? What opportunities exist at the organisation itself?

Make sure you understand what training you will receive, how much you will get paid, and how long the placement will last.

You can also read reviews of apprenticeships on sites such as RateMyApprenticeship. co. uk.

Some apprentices do not complete their training.

Reasons for leaving early can include personal circumstances, changing career plans, problems with the quality of training or not receiving enough time to study.

The government has introduced changes to apprenticeship rules in England, including reforms to course requirements, as it tries to increase the number of opportunities available.

How to get the most out of university clearing on results day

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:42:28 GMT

Have you changed your mind about the university course you want to start after getting your results?

Maybe you did not apply to university originally but now want to go, or you might not end up getting the grades you need to make it into your firm choice.

If that is you, the clearing process will have you covered.

While students in Scotland received their results last week, young people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will find out how they did in their exams on Thursday 13 August.

Here is everything you need to know about clearing.

Clearing is how universities and colleges fill any places that they still have on their courses and how students can change their course or place of study.

This year, clearing runs from 2 July to 19 October.

Prospective students can use clearing if:

Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing.

She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes.

For example, depending on available places:

If you are doing BTecs, T-levels or other qualifications, you can work out how many Ucas points your results are worth using the calculator tool on their website.

The Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.

For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher.

She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.

She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.

Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people.

At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades".

On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history.

"The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says.

"That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.

For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day.

That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade.

"You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says.

"Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."

Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact.

"Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says.

"With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."

For those awaiting results, Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your grades.

But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website.

"I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."

Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand.

On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it.

"It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford.

"All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."

Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available.

"Work up a priority list," he says.

"For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."

Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person.

She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities.

"I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says.

"You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."

Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.

Bradford says many students "can't afford" to spend days ruminating on their offer as popular courses do get filled quickly, but it is important to not agree to one straight away.

"Spend a small amount of time thinking, what do I really want from my experience? Don't panic buy and accept the first offer that comes along."

Wade says students need to ask their preferred university how much time they have to accept the offer on results day as every university is different.

"The more super-selective the university, the less time they will have," she says.

"Generally, I would always say sleep on it. Most universities will give students some time, but ask that question on the phone."

Everything you need to know about university costs

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:42:11 GMT

Graduates in England leave university with more than £47,500 in student debt, according to the latest statistics.

Figures from the 2025-26 financial year suggest that the amount borrowers owe when they first become eligible to repay has, on average, fallen compared to the year before.

Many students getting their A-level and other Level 3 results might still be unsure about whether to pursue a university degree - so is it worth it?

Can graduates still expect to earn sufficiently more than those without a degree to cover the cost of going in the first place?

Last August, the annual cost of an undergraduate degree in England and Wales went up to £9,535 a year. It is set to rise again to £9,790 in 2026.

The increases came after universities expressed growing concerns about funding pressures in recent years, pointing out that tuition fees had been frozen at £9,250 since 2017.

They argued that inflation meant those fees were worth less in real terms and there had been fewer international students to help make up the financial shortfall.

In October 2025, the government said that university tuition fees in England would go up every year in line with inflation from 2026.

They are expected to increase every year by an inflation measure called the Retail Price Index minus mortgage payment interest, or RPIx.

UK nations set their own fees.

In Northern Ireland, the maximum annual cost of an undergraduate degree is £4,855 for Northern Irish students or £9,535 for other UK students. That will rise to £4,985 and £9,790 respectively in 2026-27.

In Scotland, undergraduate tuition is free for the majority of Scottish students and £9,535 for other UK students - rising to £9,790 in 2026-27.

Student loans are made up of two components:

Most people are entitled to the tuition fee element, which is equal to the annual cost of their course.

Maintenance loans are means-tested, so how much you can borrow depends on your family's income, and may not cover your actual bills.

The maximum maintenance loan for students in England is also set to increase by inflation every year from 2026.

For example, the maximum maintenance loan for students from England who live away from their parents outside London will increase to £10,830 for 2026-27, up from £10,544 the year before.

You are charged interest on your total loan from the day you take it out, but do not have to start paying it back until your annual income reaches a certain level.

Once you reach that level, you make a regular payment which covers both your tuition fees and maintenance loans.

Repayment rules are also different across the UK. They changed in England in 2023, meaning current and future students are likely to pay back more, over a longer period of time, than those who went to university earlier.

Money saving expert Martin Lewis said the extended repayment period would increase "costs by thousands" for lower and mid-earners.

Graduates in England who became liable to pay back their loans in April 2026 had an average debt of £47,730, according to the Student Loans Company - down from £53,000 the year before.

That's partly because this was the first year that any students who took out Plan 5 loans – introduced in England in 2023 – became eligible to repay, and their loans accrue less interest than earlier Plan 2 loans.

Plan 5 borrowers accounted for more than 10% of the total number of borrowers in the 2025-26 financial year.

Student rents have risen sharply in recent years, alongside other living costs.

The Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi) says average weekly costs for a first-year student in 2023-24 were £260 without rent, or £418 when rent is included.

Average annual rent across 10 university towns and cities - excluding London and Edinburgh - rose from £6,520 in 2021-22 to £7,475 in 2023-24.

Separate figures for London found that the average rent for purpose-built student accommodation in the capital was £13,595 in 2024-25.

Hepi said last year that students needed £61,000 over the course of a three-year degree in order to have a "minimum socially acceptable standard of living" - and that's excluding tuition fees. In London, that figure is £77,000.

The think tank's 2026 student survey found the percentage of full-time undergraduates in paid employment during term time was 65% - a slight fall from the previous year, but much higher than the 45% in 2022.

Eligible students in Wales and Northern Ireland can claim maintenance grants which do not have to be repaid.

Full-time undergraduates normally resident in Wales are entitled to at least £1,000, rising to £1,020 in 2026-27. Students from the poorest backgrounds who choose to study in London can get up to £10,124, which will rise to £10,325.

In Northern Ireland the maximum grant is £3,475, rising to £3,569 in 2026-27.

The government in England is bringing back maintenance grants of up to £1,000 per year for students from lower income households on courses that support its Industrial Strategy. They will be available from 2028 and the government is still drawing up a list of eligible courses.

The Scottish government offers financial support to certain categories of students, such as those with dependants.

Across the UK, students in financial difficulty can apply for hardship funding and they may also be entitled to financial assistance from charities.

Recent research from Hepi and AdvanceHE suggests that 45% of undergraduate students think the value for money of their course is "good" or "very good", up from 37% last year and the highest proportion recorded in more than ten years.

Whether or not university can be considered "worth it" will vary from person to person, depending on what they want to get out of it.

When thinking about the financial cost, it's important to consider that, once graduates earn a certain amount, they are required to pay back student loans over a period of up to 40 years. MPs launched an inquiry into student loans in England this year amid "widespread dissatisfaction" over repayment terms.

In general, graduates can expect to earn more than non-graduates, according to government statistics from 2024.

Median pay for working-age graduates rose to £42,000 in 2024, ahead of the £30,500 earned by non-graduates - though this data does not account for external factors, like prior academic attainment.

However, the Higher Education Statistics Agency (HESA) has said that when taking account of inflation, graduate wages have declined in real terms - and the level of the decline varies depending on which job you're in.

When measured against prices in 2015, graduates surveyed in 2022 were earning £448 per year less on average than their counterparts who graduated three years earlier.

Earnings also depend on the subject studied and university attended.

Research published in 2020 by the IFS think tank in England suggests that, on average, women who study creative arts and languages degrees earn the same amount in their lifetime as if they had not gone to university.

In contrast, women who study law, economics or medicine earn over £250,000 more during their career than if they did not have a degree.

Men who studied creative arts on average earn less across their lifetimes than if they had not attended university. Male medicine or economics graduates earn £500,000 more.

Attending university can help students from poorer backgrounds earn more than their parents might have done, according to 2021 research by education charity the Sutton Trust in England.

But it found that only a fifth of graduates who were eligible for free school meals went on to be in the top 20% of earners - compared to almost half of graduates who attended private schools.

The Sutton Trust says attending a selective university - such as those in the Russell Group of leading universities - gives young people the "best chance of being socially mobile".

Results, appeals and resits - what to do if your A-levels don't go to plan

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:40:41 GMT

Hundreds of thousands of A-level students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland are waiting for their results.

They will be released at 08:00 BST on Thursday 13 August.

Those who have applied to university should be able to see whether they have been successful then too, as the Ucas Hub updates at the same time.

Here is everything you need to know about results, appeals and resits.

Each exam is graded on a scale from A* to E.

Grade boundaries show the minimum number of marks you need for each grade.

They are decided by assessment specialists at each exam board every year and are only published on results day.

Some exam boards, like AQA, have their old grade boundaries for previous years' exams published on their website.

If you do not think your grade is right, you should first talk to your school or college.

It will contact the exam board on your behalf and ask for your marks to be reviewed.

If you still think you have been unfairly graded after a review, you can ask your school or college to appeal.

The exam board will consider whether a correction is needed.

If you are still not satisfied, you can request a review from the exams regulator Ofqual.

First things first, don't worry. Life is about reacting to challenges.

Take a deep breath. Exhale. You're going to be ok.

So what do you want to do next?

Just because you didn't get the results you expected doesn't mean your education is over. Or maybe you want to try something different?

Great, you've got a couple of options here.

You can apply for university with your current grades and see what places are available (called "clearing") or you can re-sit your exams.

Traditional university degrees are far from being the only option for learning after A-levels, BTecs, T-levels, or whatever Level 3 qualifications you’ve just got results for. And, in fact, there are certain courses designed with a job in mind.

If you’re keen to get hands-on experience and earn some money, there are lots of different ways you can start working.

This includes getting a job or combining working with further training. 

Starting work doesn’t mean your education or training comes to an end.

Depending on what you feel ready for, there are pathways to train for specific jobs or careers, such as school leaver programmes, or ways to train as you go, such as apprenticeships.  

Now you’ve finished college, the world opens up. You might have dreams of changing it, or just seeing it. Or maybe you want to start a business or make art. All of that is possible.

Sometimes a bit more life experience can help bring the future into focus. That might mean taking a job straight away, or taking a gap year (or more) between school and your next step in education.

If you only just miss out on the grades you need to get on to a university or college course, the admissions office might accept you anyway or offer you a place on a different course.

You could also try applying for a different place through the clearing process - see more details below.

It may also be possible to resit some or all of your exams. Talk to your school or college if you want to explore this route.

Resits will take place in May or June 2027.

The Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) runs a clearing process matching students with university and college courses which still have spaces.

Students can use it if they:

Clearing opened on 2 July and closes on 19 October.

Universities make an offer to a student to join a course based on qualifications and grades or the Ucas tariff points system.

Each A-level grade is worth a certain number of Ucas points. For example, an A* is worth 56 points and a D is worth 24 points.

Many students decide not to go to university and start an apprenticeship or go straight into work.

Others take a gap year so they have more time to decide what to do next.

Scotland has a different qualification system. Students take Highers instead of A-levels.

Results day in Scotland this year was on Tuesday 4 August.

Your heatwave tips on how to cope in extreme temperatures

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:30:28 GMT

As the UK faces its fifth heatwave of the year, we're getting used to the drill.

When temperatures soared and records were broken at the end of June as the UK faced its second heatwave of the summer, BBC News spoke to readers to get their top tips for keeping cool in the heat.

Some were using tried-and-tested methods such as putting bedding in the freezer and keeping blackout curtains shut all day, while others turned to slightly more unorthodox methods.

Here are your best DIY hacks for coping in a heatwave.

Bethan Earley, from Rugby, told us she kept her home cool by putting foil blankets on the outside of her windows before closing them. "The house does still get warm," she told BBC Your Voice, "but it takes much longer to warm up."

In a more unusual move, Emma Kent, 42, painted yoghurt on her windows to keep her house cool, inspired by an experiment by building science researchers at Loughborough University.

On one particularly hot day in June, she used a paint roller to spread a kilogram of yoghurt on the outside of the windows of her house in Hitchin.

It took her around 10 minutes and the difference in temperature inside was noticeable, Emma said.

John Turbefield, 38, from Chichester, placed white bed sheets on the outside of the windows in some of the hottest rooms in his house. He also bought a pack of survival blankets - often used to help athletes regulate their body temperature - and places them on the remaining windows.

"They're designed to reflect heat and they are large, so they're ideal for taping to the window frame to reflect most of the light back out," he added.

As well as trying to block heat coming in through the windows, John also stocked his freezer with two-litre plastic bottles of water, which he put in front of and behind the five fans he dotted around his house. However, anyone who wants to copy him will need patience: large bottles may take a couple of days to freeze, he added.

The UK Health Security Agency advises people to only open their windows when the air feels cooler outside than inside, and to turn off non-essential electronics that can generate heat, such as TVs, laptops and chargers.

Some councils have published lists of "cool spaces", including churches, libraries and museums, where people can take refuge from the sun. Some have air con, toilets and water fountains.

But when Alice Jenner, 31, couldn't find any dedicated cool spaces near where she lives on the south coast, she decided to instead ask workers at her local M&S if she could sit in their air-conditioned store for a bit. Her medication makes it harder for her to regulate her body temperature, she says.

"The staff at M&S were very kind and let me sit with my book by the fitting rooms for about an hour and a half that day, which definitely saved me," she said.

For Stephanie Reed, 39, from Chorley, it was especially important for her to stay cool during June's heatwave, as extreme heat triggers her epilepsy.

When it gets hot at night, she wet a hand towel and laid it across the end of her bed. She then slept with her feet and ankles on it. "It helps to regulate body temperature and it does stay cool all night," she said.

Stephanie also started sprinkling her seven-year-old daughter's bed sheet with water and putting it in the freezer for about half an hour before bedtime - long enough for it to be cool for falling asleep on, but not long enough for it to actually freeze.

Gordon Cooper, 73, from High Wycombe, told BBC Your Voice that he hung a wet bath towel in his bedroom and places his fan nearby to help cool down the room, while Jacqueline Pearce, from Lancashire, filled her hot water bottle with cold water from the fridge and placed it in bed with her.

Others changed where they slept to escape the stifling heat.

During May's heatwave, Anabelle Holschuh, found it so hard to sleep in her attic bedroom that she picked up a blanket and cushion and slept on the floor in the hallway.

When temperatures soared again the next month, the 30-year-old, who lives in London, slept on the sofa in her living room, with an electric fan switched on. The room is north-facing and has tall ceilings.

"I slept fairly well on the sofa, so no need to wander further downstairs to the hallway," she said.

For Clare McDermott, 52, getting out of the house was essential. After setting a gazebo up in her garden in West Sussex, she decided to spend two nights in June sleeping under it on a rattan sofa with a blanket. "It was so much cooler and I slept really well."

Tahlia David, 28, took it even further. She and her partner drove their campervan to a wild camping spot by a lake near where they live in Carmarthenshire, Wales. They read books, played with their dog and then slept on a mattress in the van.

"We were comfortable with blankets on too, which would be unthinkable at home," Tahlia said. "It was a lovely break from the heat of the house."

Some people told BBC News they had rearranged their remote work set-up during the heatwave, by moving their desk to the coolest room of the house.

Teresa Curran, 44, from Warwickshire, said she filled her bath with cold water when the heat of her house gets too much. "I get in and wade around between meetings and it really does give instant relief," she said.

For Aimie Ludgate, 29, from Bradford, using an oven or hob during a heatwave is a no-go. Instead, she made as many meals as possible using her air fryer, even boiling eggs and cooking steak in it.

She also froze a big bottle of water overnight that she took to work the next day.

Dietitian Kate Hilton says that during heatwaves she drinks more iced water and eats cool, hydrating foods like cucumber, tomatoes, melon and frozen smoothies. Other fruits that can help hydrate you are berries, peaches and citrus fruits, she says. For kids who are fussy eaters, freezing fruit juice or smoothies into ice pops can be a good way to help keep them cool.

She says both caffeine and especially alcohol can have dehydrating effects, and recommends drinking alcohol in moderation during hot weather and alternating it with non-alcoholic drinks.

"Water is generally the best thing to drink, but remember that all fluids, other than alcohol, are considered hydrating, so if you prefer sugar-free squash or other flavourings, this does still count towards hydration," she says.

Jess Jepson, 31, who lives in Manchester, said she dresses for the weather by wearing loose-fitting, light and airy clothes and opting for paler colours. She wore black one day and "really regretted it," she said.

When it's hot, she keeps her hair off her face and neck by wearing it up in a claw clip.

"It's a challenge to keep cool whilst still feeling put together," Jess added.

Stylist Chantelle Znideric advises people to opt for natural fibres such as cotton and linen, which she says are "highly breathable and disperse moisture across the fabric rather than trapping it against your skin", whereas silky, synthetic fabrics will make you sweaty.

When it comes to accessories, basketball caps will shade your eyes when it's sunny, but will leave your ears and neck completely exposed. Instead, Chantelle recommends choosing a wide-brimmed fedora or bucket hat to get full coverage.

Some people switched up their daily routines to beat the summer heat.

Annie Smith, 27, from St Albans, said she and her husband walked their two dachshunds in the morning and did enrichment activities with them in the house to keep them occupied "since it's too hot to walk them after 8am or 9am".

They've bought cooling vests for their dogs and kept wet dog food in the fridge.

Annie said she and her partner also tried to get their house chores done before about 10:00 "so I can sit still and stay cool the rest of the day".

Helena Kandzialka, 55, said she had avoided car journeys when possible, and chose to sit outside in the shade because the breeze made it cooler than in the house.

Additional reporting by Alex Akhurst, Alex Emery, Mary Litchfield and Rozina Sini

Double murderer and rapist told to 'rot in prison' by relatives of victims and survivor

BBC News Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:46:38 GMT

Relatives of victims and a survivor of double murderer and serial sex offender Simon Levy have branded him a "parasite" who deserves to die behind bars.

Levy, 49, was jailed for life on Wednesday after murdering two women and raping another, all while he was on bail for a series of other sex assaults.

On Wednesday families of the two women he murdered faced him in court, as a survivor of one the attacks told him he was "not worthy" of any more of her "words or time".

The sister of murdered mother-of-four Sheryl Wilkins was in tears as she remembered a "beautiful soul who you cruelly took away in an evil act of crime".

Lindsey Hicks told the Old Bailey hearing: "There will never be enough words to express how I feel since losing my big sister Sheryl.

"You, Simon Levy, have destroyed our lives and we will never get over this."

"We should have been growing old together like sisters do and be there to support each other. Instead, I'm having to realise that one day in the near future I will be older than my big sister.

"We hope you spend the rest of your miserable life behind bars and we get justice for Sheryl. This last year has been the worst year of our lives; the pain you have put us through has been unbearable. Sheryl's life was taken unlawfully and violently."

Addressing Levy directly, as he sat wearing sunglasses for an eye condition in the dock, she added: "Know this, you lose. We get to leave here today knowing we will keep Sheryl alive by sharing memories about her and living for her.

"We will continue to live as a loving family through our loss, supporting each other. You don't get to take that away. I hope you rot in prison for the rest of your life."

Sheryl's mother Mary Wilkins said she believed her daughter's murder in August 2025 had meant Levy was finally brought to justice, saving the lives of other potential victims.

In a statement read by junior prosecutor Kerry Broome, she added: "Our Sheryl has ended your chances of hurting anyone else, she lost her life to do this but we truly believe Sheryl has saved countless women.

"You took away our beautiful daughter Sheryl. She was a mother, a sister, a daughter, a friend and a beloved family member. She had four beautiful children.

"Sheryl was taken from us one day before her 40th birthday, she had so many hopes and dreams. She should've celebrated her 40th birthday, she should've grown old with us, instead all of that was taken away."

"Sheryl's children had been robbed not only of their mother but their future with her. This was the destruction of a life, a family and a future.

"Sheryl's life mattered, Simon you have changed our lives forever but you cannot take away our love for Sheryl.

"We will continue to talk about her, we will continue to remember her."

Levy killed grandmother Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025. Her daughter Nazly Johana Fuenmayor Valencia said in court her mother had come to the UK to give her family a better life.

"There's an emptiness that can't be filled. I have been ripped apart… we will never be the same again," she said,

"She was a truly special person who gave so much love to others. Her kindness, her smile and the love she shared so freely will stay with us forever.

"We have been living a nightmare we cannot wake up from. We don't know why she was taken from us. The rest of our lives will never be the same.

"My mum came to this country to give her children a better life and for safety. Instead her life was taken so cruelly."

A woman who survived Levy after he raped her in January 2025 said she could not forget his smell as he attacked her.

In a statement read by a prosecutor she said: "He took away my soul that night and he took away my dignity. He took my soul like a parasite.

"I feel like people have taken advantage of me all my life. I can't forget the smell of his sweaty hands on my mouth. I thought I would die.

"It's taken me a long time to trust people, I can trust a small number of friends.

"I want to try to forget this monster. This man is a parasite not worthy of any more of my words or time."

Both of Levy's murders were sexually motivated. Valencia-Trujillo, who was found in a largely abandoned block of flats on the Aylesbury estate in south-east London, had been suffocated.

He had done the same to Wilkins before she was found behind a car park wall near Tottenham High Road, north London.

His rape attack had happened in the same car park, but despite the victim telling police where he lived he was not interviewed until after his two murders.

His case has posed serious questions for the authorities over why he was repeatedly set free on bail - despite increasing attacks on women.

Judge Mark Lucraft KC, the Recorder of London, sentenced Levy to a whole life prison term.

He told him: "You are clearly someone who ruthlessly exploits others for your own personal sexual satisfaction.

"You are someone who appears to have a morbid fascination with sex, rape and crime."
