What is the optimal way to ice a cocktail?

New Scientist August 12, 2026

What is the optimal way to ice a cocktail: fewer big cubes or lots of small ones?

Hillary ShawNewport, Shropshire, UK

How fast the ice melts is by far the biggest influence on the temperature of your cocktail. It takes 334 joules of energy to melt 1 gram of ice, which is about 80 times the energy to raise 1 g of water by 1°C. There is negligible heat energy available in the surrounding air, whatever the ambient temperature, to warm the cocktail, as the specific heat capacity of air is even less that of water. Therefore, the ambient air temperature is irrelevant, as is your hand size, temperature and the dimensions of the glass. The melt speed of the ice is determined by its surface area. A 2 × 2 × 2 centimetre cube of ice has a surface area of 24 cm2, but the same ice in eight 1 cm cubes has a surface area of 48 cm2.

Advertisement

So, if you drink the cocktail fast, you want smaller pieces; bigger, if you want a longer-lasting cooling effect. With too large pieces, some ice will still be unmelted when you have finished; too small and it all melts before you have finished. It also dilutes the cocktail a bit if it all melts (some may prefer that).

There is a downside – the smaller your ice cubes, the faster they melt and the faster your drink gets watered down

So it depends on your taste and speed of drinking. I am hereby volunteering to act as a guinea pig to drink lots of cocktails with different-sized pieces of ice to determine the ideal drinking speed and ice cube size.

Ron DippoldSan Diego, California, US

That depends what you’re looking for – there is a trade-off. If you want to make your plonk as cold as possible as fast as possible, then you want your ice to be as small as you can get it. This means more ice is in contact with the liquid. The ultimate form of that is shaved ice, or ice slurry as in some margaritas, which will make your drink cold instantly. But there is a downside – the smaller your ice cubes, the faster they melt and the faster your drink gets watered down. With something as overwhelmingly sweet and flavourful as most commercial margaritas, that isn’t a problem, perhaps even a blessing. But it is a problem if you are looking to unwind with something fancy that was properly made in the first place.

Most spirits will benefit from a drop or two of water. Many aromatic compounds bind tightly to the alcohol, and water cuts those bonds and sets them free so you can smell them. Scottish whisky fans call this “unleashing the serpent”. Similarly, it can precipitate solids out of liqueurs and push them to the surface, again giving you more flavour and nose. You can actually see it if you add a little water to anise liqueurs like Pernod and watch the tiny clouds form in the drink. So, in my opinion, you don’t want to drink most things totally neat (no ice) unless your goal is just getting sloshed as fast as possible. Even good vodka benefits from it!

However, you need very little water for this – just the melt from the ice, especially if shaken or stirred, is plenty. Shaking will melt the ice more than stirring, so James Bond preferred his drinks effectively watered down a bit. I don’t think you want a good martini, paper plane or vesper to be watered down much, so use ice that will keep it cool but not melt. And the best way to do that is with large, air-free, spherical ice.

A sphere is, by definition, the shape with the most volume for the least possible surface area – less surface area means it melts slower, and it has no sharp corners like cubical ice that will melt faster. As a bonus, many spherical ice-makers are designed to remove as much air from the ice as possible, freezing them from the bottom and pushing the air upwards. This makes them perfectly clear, which looks nice, but it also makes them denser. And without the tiny air pockets, it will melt much more slowly.

Of course, while large spherical ice goes well in a tumbler, you won’t get one in a traditional v-shaped martini glass without it looking ridiculous and making it hard to drink. In that case, the most British of drink columnists, Kingsley Amis, suggested filling the glass about a third of the way with water and then sticking it in the freezer. This effectively turns the entire bottom of the glass into an ice cube. He had many opinions, many of which I don’t agree with, but I have to say that does the job.

The risks and what is being done to prepare for a strong El Niño this summer

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

With El Niño being officially declared, agencies across New Zealand are preparing for potentially severe weather.

The weather phenomenon will bring dry and windy conditions for most areas, while the western and lower South Island will get more rainfall.

In dry areas, the wildfire risk is likely to be elevated while a lack of rain will put pressure on people’s water tanks as well as the agricultural sector, Earth Sciences New Zealand (ESNZ) chief weather scientist Chris Brandolino said.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand is concerned about the conditions increasing the fire risk.

High winds could spread fires, which will start more easily because of the dehydrated landscapes, making them harder to contain, wildfire manager Tim Mitchell said.

“When you’ve got wind, that really pushes any fires along but also further enhances, I guess, that dryness of those fuels and availability of fuels to burn.”

Mitchell told the Herald that 98% of wildfires in New Zealand were started by people.

It is possible to have minimal fires during high-risk conditions but people must take the necessary precautions, he said.

People are “strongly encouraged” to clear their properties of vegetation, make sure fires are properly extinguished with water and always check the fire risk.

“Don’t leave those fires to smoulder for days after the main burn as you perhaps have always done.

“You might have got away with it last few seasons; you may not get away with it, or you’re unlikely to get away with it this season.”

People should also make sure their properties are accessible by fire truck, make water supplies accessible and have a plan in case a fire happens.

“There is a potential that we may have to evacuate more people this season.”

He said preparation is important because “once the smoke’s in the air it’s too late”.

Crews have been checking equipment and have increased foam and retardant stocks by 20,000 litres to carry 120,000 litres to brace for the possibility of more fires.

Fire and Emergency has also been in contact with the Department of Conservation, Forestry and the Defence Force on how they could co-ordinate their efforts.

The National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) hosted a forum last week where agencies discussed what they were expecting and how they would deal with the upcoming phenomenon.

ESNZ is expecting this El Niño, first declared in July, to be the “strongest in recorded history”, Brandolino said.

Although it has around 25% influence on the weather in New Zealand, its impacts can be significant.

It is caused when warmer-than-normal water temperatures slow down trade winds in the eastern Pacific that would typically carry moisture to New Zealand and Australia.

Because of New Zealand’s position, it means most areas, particularly the east and northeast, become drier while the southwest of the South Island is wetter.

Temperatures could also vary, occasionally spiking “unusually high” for a few days at a time, Brandolino said.

Parts of the country could also reach 30C earlier in the spring, and some places could reach high temperatures not felt in “several years”, he said.

A “Super El Niño”, which this is likely to be, lasts longer and increases the odds for outcomes such as high temperatures, floods, heat, humidity and fires.

El Niño typically comes around every 10-15 years, while New Zealand has had five Super El El Niños since the early 1970s.

The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) is encouraging farmers and growers to have a plan, national response manager Andrew Curtis said.

“It’s important farmers make decisions early, including identifying feed deficits and assessing the potential for summer feed crops.

“It could also mean prioritising livestock for destocking early and feeding the remainder as well as possible.”

El Niño can bring increased risk of drought and water scarcity, wildfires, heat-related human and animal health concerns, as well as flooding, he said.

The ministry is working with sector groups to support farmers and growers to prepare, Curtis said.

Resources through levy organisations, talking to experts who have been through El Niño before, and information on the MPI website are tools farms and growers can use, he said.

Bridges not up to scratch, roads to be returned to gravel - South Island counts cost of under investment

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

A new report revealed the south accounts for 40% of international visitor spending, but receives only 11% of transport spending. Photo / 123rf

By Tim Brown of RNZ

Only $1 of every $9 of Government roading funds gets spent in the South Island, a new report obtained by RNZ reveals.

The south accounts for almost a quarter of the country’s population, 22% of GDP, a third of export goods and 40% of international visitor spending, but receives only 11% of transport spending.

Local political and business leaders say the lack of investment is disappointing.

Southland mayor Rob Scott has told RNZ that trucks are unnecessarily driving an extra 3.5 million kilometres in his district every year because bridges are not up to scratch and the council will soon have to weigh up reverting sealed roads to gravel.

But South Island Minister James Meager says the Government has made a huge investment in the South Island’s roads and other infrastructure, as well as simplifying and speeding up consent processes and cutting red tape.

It was “simplistic” to suggest the Government was not listening to the South Island’s leaders and delivering on their priorities, Meager said.

The report, released on Thursday and commissioned by the South Island Regional Transport Committee Chairs Group, highlighted the disparity between the south’s contribution to the economy and what was being delivered by the National Land Transport Fund.

If National Land Transport Fund expenditure matched the population in the South Island it would have resulted in an extra $1.2 billion in spending in the past year alone – about the cost of the currently unfunded Woodend Bypass or the Hope Bypass.

“That’s a fair point,” Meager said.

“I guess my response would be is that it’s a little more complex than just looking at the population makeup. It’s actually part of my job, and part of my colleagues’ jobs, to make sure that we raise these issues with decision makers, with cabinet, and making sure that we’ve got the investment in the right place.

“The key thing is we need to not necessarily look at writing checks based on what the population is here or there. What we need to do ... is to identify the infrastructure constraints that we have in the South Island that actually are holding back growth.

“And we have got a lot of stuff underway. We can’t underestimate all the work that actually is happening. You’ve got Ashburton Bridge. The Woodend Bypass is proceeding – just got consenting, just got fast-track consent. In the budget there was $400 million for roading infrastructure resilience and $140 million of that went to the South Island. So there is a lot happening.”

Canterbury Regional Transport Committee chair Deon Swiggs said the report highlighted what many in the South Island had been feeling for some time.

“When I look at the numbers it’s disappointing ... and resilience is the big piece that we are fighting for in the South Island.

“We’ve got storm events that are happening, we’ve got ageing infrastructure. So, yes, the South Island is definitely punching above its weight from an economic activity point of view and the money generated here is going towards New Zealand at large, but the South Island needs this investment.

“We’ve been saying this for quite some time that the numbers do not stack up ... and investment in the South Island needs to improve. We do not want to see the degradation of our existing corridors. We all know that when you don’t maintain what you’ve got, it costs a lot more to then fix it.”

Rob Scott said Southland was at a tipping point.

“I’ve seen the great work that our staff have been doing and I’m seeing the stress coming through now and it’s keeping us awake at night as a council, knowing that once we get over that tipping point we’re not going to be able to recover as a Southland region and also as a country. It’s going to be a lot more expensive to fix the roads up later on ... rather than just actually keeping on top and maintaining our network properly.

“If you look at the length of road per capita that people are looking after, in Auckland a resident is looking after four metres worth of road. Wellington, 1.6 metres. And if we come to the South Island and we’ve got our fastest growing district in the country at the moment, Selwyn, someone’s looking after 30 metres. What do you reckon Southland’s number is? It’s 151 metres.

“We are subsidising Auckland, which I don’t mind, but it’s actually coming at the expense of our roads. All of the road user charges that we generate on our roads, only half of that is coming back for that road maintenance.”

It led him to write a letter to Transport Agency chair Simon Bridges calling for a new way of allocating road funding as Southland was tens of millions of dollars short of just maintaining the status quo.

Meanwhile, central government was pushing ahead with further expressways and highways that would put even more pressure on maintenance spending, Scott said.

“If the heartbeat of New Zealand’s export market loses the routes to get that produce to market, we’re going to be in trouble as a country,” he said.

“We’re not actually asking for much. I scratch my head when I see all of this money – that $55 million going on to that Harbour Bridge Extension paperwork, the $250 million going on a [Queenstown] roundabout, the new 26 kilometres worth of expressway in the North Island – we just need a drop in the bucket from all of those projects just to be able to maintain our roads.”

Swiggs said politics was at play.

“What we’re seeing here is that there is a weighting of North Island politicians and less South Island politicians and especially in Cabinet. I think we have two politicians in Cabinet from the South Island.

“We need to have a better mix of proportionality around the politicians that are decision makers at Cabinet. But we also need a more transparent process about how the money has been apportioned and where these big projects are.”

Local councils had to be far more transparent in how they decided to spend money compared to central government, Swiggs said.

Business Canterbury chief executive Leeann Watson agreed South Island representation was lacking among senior politicians.

“We are underrepresented, absolutely. We have two cabinet ministers in the whole of the South Island and I believe Auckland has 16. So that in itself speaks some volume,” she said.

Despite that, Business Canterbury had regular contact with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour and Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Watson said.

Willis claimed after this year’s Budget she had not “had a request for a major headline project in Canterbury”.

Luxon offered a similar view last year and called for Canterbury’s leaders to get their priorities straight.

Watson said the remarks were frustrating.

“There is no doubt that we have asked for some investment.”

Swiggs said there was “no shortage of projects that we could do tomorrow to make the South Island a better place”.

“I’m going to pick on one, which is the long-touted mass rapid transit for Christchurch. Mass rapid transit is an end goal.

“To get to the mass rapid transit system we need to do the investment in our existing public transport. We’ve put through business cases to NZTA. This council appropriated the money through our long-term plan. We went through consultation. We had it on our budgets and then the [Government Policy Statement] comes out and cut the funding.

“That has a flow-on effect to us not being able to deliver the improvements to our public transport that we wanted and then that has an impact on the mass rapid transit down the line. When the Government puts a cap on what the region wants or the city wants it has flow-on effects.

“That was there and that could be delivered relatively quickly if there was a will from the Government and ... they have that information. So that’s just one example. They could invest in that with us, with the region, with the city, but they’ve chosen not to.”

Meager said the Government was committed to delivering the Woodend Bypass.

“We’re not short on ambition. What we are short on is, quite frankly, the revenue needed to get these projects across the line.

“Now part of that is to do with the growth we need to generate revenue, whether that’s through fuel excise and road users which help fund the land transport fund or general growth.

“So we need more revenue coming in. We also need to make these projects a lot more affordable and a lot cheaper and so that’s why we’ve done things like Fast-track and reforming the RMA system so that when these large-scale projects are actually underway, we can make them more affordable.”

There was a significant amount taking place in and around Canterbury, including the recently opened Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch, flood protection improvement and spending in health, education and transport, Meager said.

The report laid bare what has been described as New Zealand’s “two-speed” economy.

“The South Island is outperforming the North Island with GDP growing by 1.2% in the March 2026 year compared with 0.2% in the North Island,” the report said.

“This outperformance has persisted, with South Island GDP growth averaging 0.6 percentage points above the North Island over the five years to 2025.

“South Island employment rose by 0.4%, while North Island employment fell by 1.2%. Southland, the West Coast, Canterbury and Otago recorded growth. The South Island’s unemployment rate is 4.1%, below the North Island’s 5.7%.”

The South Island was making an outsized contribution to the country’s economy but further investment was important to maintain it, the report said.

The roading network was vital to connect people and businesses with supply chains and markets and for tourism.

The South Island accounted for 43% of the country’s roading network and 45% of the State Highway network.

“The South Island’s share of roading expenditure appears disproportionately low relative to its contribution and level of road use. In 2025 the South Island received 11% of NLTF roading expenditure despite generating 27% of national vehicle kilometres travelled, 22% of GDP, one third of goods exports, and 40% of international visitor spending,” the report said.

“This imbalance is evident across South Island regions, where shares of population, GDP, exports, visitor spending and road use generally exceed each region’s share of NLTF roading investment. Ensuring that South Island transport infrastructure is adequately maintained and invested in is therefore important not only for the South Island but for New Zealand’s overall economic performance.”

The report also underscored the importance of the Cook Strait ferries to the South Island’s economy.

“The Cook Strait ferries provide a ‘sea bridge’ connection between the South Island and the North Island. The transportation infrastructure provided by the ferries is a critically important economic enabler for the South Island economy and its broader contribution to New Zealand.

“An estimated 3.5 million tonnes of annual freight are carried on ferries.”

More than $10 billion crossed the strait last year with 71% southbound and 29% northbound.

About $1.8 billion of South Island international spending came from visitors who took the ferry.

“This is equivalent to about 23% of the total international visitor spending that occurred in the South Island over the past year, which highlights the critical importance of the ferries as an enabler of international tourism earnings. Transport connectivity is fundamental to sustaining this contribution.”

Watson said the Government needed to be investing more in the South Island’s infrastructure for the good of the country’s economy.

“We can have the best innovation, we can have the best quality products, but if we haven’t got the infrastructure to support the imported components coming in to make those manufactured goods or the right roads to get our exports to Lyttelton Port or to Christchurch Airport or not sufficient freight capacity then ... we can’t actually realise the full potential of those exports to this country.

“Infrastructure is vital, just like energy is. It underpins everything that we do from moving our people, moving our freight and just having connectivity across the South Island.

“Our message to political parties is really simple – if New Zealand wants stronger productivity and higher incomes and greater resilience then backing the South Island right now is exactly what they should be doing because we can provide all that with the right settings.”

The Government could not afford to not invest in the south, Watson said.

“We often talk about what the costs are of delivering projects but we don’t talk about the cost of delaying and deferring.

“First of all, I think we’ve got to do a better job of actually costing up the project. Secondly, I think we need to look at those alternative procurement and funding and financing models because we know if we continue to use the same funding and financing and the same procurement models that we’ve always used, we’ll get what we’ve always got.

“Right now we’ve got a country that has definitely got some resilience issues in terms of some of its core infrastructure. We’ve got a whole lot of maintenance that we need to do and so we’ve got to make sure that we also look at those alternative ways of doing things.”

Watson and Swiggs emphasised that funding infrastructure in the South Island was an investment.

Swiggs said money spent in the South Island benefited the whole country.

“This is definitely not a handout. We have shown where the money has been generated, we’ve shown the economic activity is happening here,” Swiggs said.

Watson said Business Canterbury was working on a project called Canterbury Ambition that set out the region’s vision for improving growth, innovation and quality of life.

She said that, alongside government investment, could unlock the private sector.

“In some cases it’s actually about getting the government out of the way.

“The piece of work around Canterbury Ambition is actually about not waiting for government to tell us what we should be as a region or what we should do. It’s about us shaping our own future. So the private sector is in the driving seat of that and actually pushing ahead and what we’ve heard from this Government is that they actually want to partner with business.

“Our businesses don’t want to hand out. Our businesses want to shape their own future.”

Thousands sell houses for less than they paid

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

Across the country, 13.1% of the properties sold in the second quarter were at a loss, the highest number since 2012. Photo / 123RF

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

Just over 13% of all properties sold in the second quarter of this year changed hands for less than the seller paid for them, and the number tops 20% in Auckland.

Cotality has released its latest “pain and gain” report, which tracks how many sellers are taking a loss. It will understate the true number because it does not include the costs of sale, such as real estate agent commissions.

Across the country, 13.1% of the properties sold in the second quarter were at a loss, the highest number since 2012. In Auckland, the proportion was 20.9% and in Wellington, it was 18.4%.

The median amount lost was $60,000, for a total loss of $159 million. The median gross profit was $280,000, down from $440,000 at the housing peak.

People who made money on their properties had held them for a record length of time – 10.4 years. People who sold had only held for a median 4.3 years.

Cotality chief economist Kelvin Davidson said that could indicate that people were choosing to hold for longer than previously to wait for a market recovery or because selling was more difficult than usual.

Apartments were much more likely to be sold for a loss, at 45.4%.

It was the weakest resale performance for apartments since 2010.

Davidson said apartments had fallen in value by 6% on average in the past 12 months compared to 2% for townhouses and little movement for standalone dwellings.

He said apartments tend to be more likely to resell at a loss because they did not have as much capital growth over time, even in an upswing. “They’re a bit more vulnerable to being sold at a loss simply because they haven’t made as much capital gain through the cycle so that’s part of it.”

Some parts of the country had very small percentages selling for a loss such as Timaru and Gore, where 1.8% of sales lost money.

Davidson said the pattern was consistent with lower house prices.

“It’s been a pretty sluggish housing market for a number of years so no surprise that resellers are not faring as well as they have done in the past.

“The 13% of resales in the second quarter sold for a loss is the highest figure we’ve seen for 11 or 12 years but it’s been more of a slow grind downwards, it hasn’t been the sharp adjustment we saw in the global financial crisis.

“Back then, the share of properties being sold for a loss rose from nothing to about 20% in a year or two. This time it’s risen from nothing to around 13% in four or five years so it’s been an adjustment but it’s been a bit slower than what we’ve seen in the past. It’s consistent with the servicing testing that we’ve got within the banks now.

“People who might have run into problems and had to sell sooner than what they thought, perhaps haven’t even got the mortgage in the first place.

“And also employment has stayed up, people have stayed in work. So that’s helped sellers in terms of they can hold on a little bit longer if they need to. They don’t necessarily have to sell at a loss.”

He said the four-year median hold period for losses went back to the start of the housing market slowdown.

“We’ve seen regionally Auckland’s still a little bit weaker, Wellington’s a little bit weaker. There’s perhaps no great surprises there.”

He said he did not expect things to turn around any time soon.

“We’ve still got economic uncertainty. If anything, mortgage rates are sneaking higher. There are still a lot of listings out there. It’s a buyer’s market.

“So I just think house prices might not necessarily fall too much further because affordability has been restored quite a lot, but they may not necessarily rise any time soon either.

“And with that pricing power probably resting with buyers, it’s going to be just a little bit challenging for sellers or property resellers for the next little while.”

Police apologise for spreading incorrect information about Rakesh Naidoo party candidacy

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

Superintendent Rakesh Naidoo has received an apology from police. Photo / Supplied

Assistant Police Commissioner Tim Anderson is apologising for allowing incorrect information to be publicised about when Superintendent Rakesh Naidoo first disclosed he was considering becoming a Labour Party candidate.

Naidoo, police’s former ethnic, iwi and communities national partnerships manager, was revealed as a Labour candidate on June 8, ranked 13th on the party’s list.

The revelation prompted criticism from Police Commissioner Richard Chambers, who said he only learned Naidoo was considering standing as a candidate days earlier on June 4.

In addition to criticism from Police Minister Mark Mitchell, Chambers said Naidoo should have disclosed his considerations to either him or Anderson as his superior much earlier.

Naidoo has since lost his police powers, the ability to wear his uniform and is transitioning out of police after Chambers said it would be untenable for him to remain in his role. Naidoo is also under investigation after Mitchell and Chambers expressed concerns about sensitive information Naidoo might have shared during the period he was being courted by Labour.

Police have not provided updates about the investigation. Naidoo is expected to leave police this month.

The Herald earlier this month revealed an open letter, written to Mitchell, from a close associate of Naidoo who claimed Naidoo had disclosed his considerations to Anderson earlier than had been made public and claimed Naidoo had not been told his position was untenable.

Police have not responded to the letter.

Correspondence released under the Official Information Act to the Herald yesterday proved Naidoo had first discussed the matter with Anderson in the week commencing May 25.

“Superintendent Naidoo verbally advised AC Anderson he was considering standing as a candidate for the New Zealand Labour Party, although, at that stage, he had not decided to do so,” the document read.

On June 4, Naidoo told Anderson in person he would put his name forward for Labour’s list and would be attending a party meeting on June 6.

“Assistant Commissioner Anderson verbally briefed this information up to Commissioner Chambers by telephone at 3.21pm the same day.

“In a further verbal communication after his call to the Commissioner, AC Anderson spoke again briefly with Superintendent Naidoo.”

On June 7, Naidoo confirmed to Anderson he had been selected as a list candidate and later that day affirmed he would be accepting it.

In a statement this morning, Anderson confirmed Naidoo had spoken to him a week before Anderson told Chambers, admitting that that led to “incorrect information” being given to media.

“At the time Superintendent Naidoo had not reached a decision on whether to stand and I therefore treated our conversation as a confidential discussion and did not inform the Commissioner of this conversation.

“In hindsight, it would have been helpful for me to have advised the Commissioner of Superintendent Naidoo’s first approach.

“I have apologised to both Superintendent Naidoo and Commissioner Chambers for the confusion, which has resulted in incorrect information being provided to media.”

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

The Opportunity Party would be “very open” to a confidence-and-supply agreement with the next government, rather than a formal coalition, “if it means we can stay true to who we are”, leader Qiulae Wong says.

And Act Party leader David Seymour is not ruling out working with Opportunity – if they give up key “radical left-wing” policies including a land tax.

It comes after Opportunity – formerly TOP – surged to 8% in the latest 1News-Verian poll, potentially meaning it could act as kingmaker post-November 7.

Wong told Herald NOW’S Ryan Bridge Today that Opportunity wouldn’t reveal its bottom lines for another month or so, as it wanted to see what other parties were putting on the table.

“That will influence ultimately where we think we can work with them, where we could push them harder on different issues, and so that’s ultimately why we want to do it closer to the election,” she said.

Asked if a land tax was foundational to its policy plan, Wong said she had been clear that Opportunity did not expect tax reform to happen overnight.

“We’ve got strong policies around innovation, competition, our energy market – these are things that are going to affect the cost of living for New Zealanders and they don’t require a change in our tax system to happen.”

Opportunity had not held any formal discussions with other party leaders about coalition arrangements, she said.

The poll was carried out from August 8 to 11, before Wednesday’s attempted National leadership spill.

It put Labour on 30%, National on 29%, Act on 9%, New Zealand First on 8%, the Greens on 12% and Te Pāti Māori on 1%.

Those numbers would see Labour able to form a government with the Greens, Opportunity and at least one other partner. National, Act and NZ First would have a combined 57 seats and no clear way to power, with Christopher Luxon having ruled out working with Opportunity due to its tax policy.

However, Seymour confirmed to Ryan Bridge Today that Act was open to an arrangement with Opportunity, while saying a land tax and universal basic income were “not happening”.

Asked if it was “not a no”, he said “no” - adding “let’s see if they get there, first of all. I mean, there’s lots of hype right now, but let’s see”.

Taxing every piece of land in New Zealand was “a policy that we just can’t abide”, while the UBI plans were “extraordinary”, he told Newstalk ZB’s Ryan Bridge Early Edition earlier this morning.

But pushed repeatedly on whether his party could be in a governing coalition with Opportunity, Seymour said he was focusing on policy and it appeared the party was happy to give those two policies up.

“[It] makes you wonder if they’re really the Opportunity Party or the Opportunist Party.”

Child sex abuse victim says family punished her for speaking out

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

Colin Davis Smith stands in the dock at his sentencing in the Wellington District Court for child sex offending, March 2023. Photo / Melissa Nightingale

The victim of a now-elderly child sex offender who finally got justice as an adult feels she’s still being punished years on for speaking out about what happened to her.

The woman, who has permanent name suppression, said almost her entire family turned on her despite the offender, Colin Davis Smith, admitting what he had done to her.

She has even had to take out a restraining order against a man close to Smith due to ongoing harassment – an order the man has now been convicted of breaching.

Smith, 85, was sentenced in 2023 to community detention and supervision for indecency with a girl under 12, having earlier pleaded guilty to the historical offending.

According to the summary of facts, the offending happened in the Hutt Valley in the late 1970s.

She was asleep in Smith’s home when he crept into the room and lifted the bed covers, using a torch to illuminate her body.

He touched the top of her underwear, which woke the girl, who fled. She spent the rest of the night in someone else’s bed.

Smith had previous convictions for similar offending between 1959 and 1984.

Speaking to the Herald three years on from the sentencing, the victim said she has been treated as a “villain” by much of her family ever since.

“It took several years of counselling and healing to come to terms with what they had done to me,” she said, adding it had confused her that they had turned on her even though they knew she was telling the truth.

“The grief of losing contact with family members who you once loved and thought they loved you was excruciating.”

She said the pain was “unbearable for years” and caused her mental and physical illness.

She felt in particular the family wanted to protect Smith’s wife, who fought strongly for Smith to receive name suppression, arguing at the time she would leave her husband if he were to be publicly named as she did not want to be judged by her friends for staying with a sex offender.

“I guess they didn’t want to embarrass her or perhaps they thought his behaviour reflected on them,” the victim said. “Whatever the reason, it didn’t make sense.”

Despite a widely read Herald article confirming Smith had pleaded guilty to the offending, the victim’s relatives have “kept their distance”.

The woman said it was “really hard” to cope initially when the relatives turned on her.

“I now realise that I am better off not having people like them in my life. They are not supportive. In fact they are destructive, because who does that to victims of child sexual abuse? In fact, who does that to any victim?”

She felt such fallout was a large reason why some victims chose not to come forward about their own abuse.

“It actually perpetuates the offending and gives confidence to offenders to continue their abuse,” she said.

“I believe that if victims are challenged as I have been challenged, then sexual or violent abuse will always be in our communities.”

After she laid her police complaint against Smith, a man known to him began to harass and abuse her “over several years”, until she successfully fought in court for a restraining order against him.

At first she felt protected by the order, and thought she could go about her life “in peace”, but the man has since been convicted of breaching the order, which remains in place for one more year.

“It’s like he’s trying to have the power over me by still punishing me for speaking out,” she said.

“I am completely confused as to why he cannot let me live in peace. All I want is to live a quiet life.”

The Herald is not reporting the nature of the breach in order to comply with suppressions. The man pleaded guilty and was convicted and discharged at his first appearance on the matter.

Smith and his wife initially fought for him to receive permanent name suppression, with his wife saying she would end the marriage if his name were published.

“I really feel I could not go on with our relationship, if [his] name enters into the media, because my friends would see it,” she wrote in an affidavit.

“I could not cope with what people would think of me, if I were to stay in a relationship with someone convicted of child sex offending.”

She also said that, if his name was published, she would lose a close friend who had confided in her about one of her family members being “interfered with”.

But Judge Tompkins said allowing suppression on that basis “would see the court condone [her] retaining a friendship on the basis of a lie”.

Colin Smith also swore an affidavit, saying every so often he would “start howling”. He said if his relationship were to end it would put him under extreme hardship due to psychological harm.

“She has always stuck by me since she found out about my history of peeping in 1984,” he said.

The application for suppression was declined, as was a High Court appeal a few months later.

Melissa Nightingale is a Wellington-based reporter who covers crime, justice and news in the capital. She joined the Herald in 2016 and has worked as a journalist for 10 years.

How AI is an ‘exaggerator’ for the reach and impact of domestic and global threats to NZ

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

Generative artificial intelligence is amplifying an increasingly volatile threat environment for our national security, according to a new NZ Security Intelligence Service (NZSIS) report.

The threat level remains “possible”, where it has been since November 2022, meaning there is a 25% to 50% chance of a terrorist attack.

“Within that band we’re moving up, particularly as a result of the deteriorating global environment,” Andrew Hampton, NZSIS director-general, told the Herald.

The annual Security Threat Environment Report, released today, identified five areas creating risk: geopolitical uncertainty, rapid advances in technology, foreign interference including by states or their proxies, offshore conflicts, and an increasingly contested Pacific region.

Hampton said there was increasing volatility in those areas, none of which look to be quietening down.

“When you put them together cumulatively, the impact is a significant one, and in terms of the long-term trajectory, a lot of those themes are probably here to stay for some time.

“Our message is that New Zealand shouldn’t be trying to disconnect from the rest of the world. We can’t. But we need to be increasingly aware of the impact of those trends on our national security, both from a risk perspective but also in terms of how we can take steps to make us more resilient.”

He specified Generative AI (GenAI) as a “multiplier or an exaggerator” for malicious actors to increase reach and capability.

“It can be used to identify vulnerable people and radicalise them, where they may think they’re engaging with a person but they’re actually engaging with a bot of some sort.”

GenAI is being used to enhance radicalisation methods by making individually tailored propaganda at scale.

Islamic State supporters are using it to generate ideological content in multiple languages to appeal to a global audience; for example, white-identity violent extremists have used it to translate Adolf Hitler recordings for a modern audience.

“And it can be used to enhance development of weapons,” Hampton said.

“We have seen in New Zealand people using GenAI to find out how to make IEDs [improvised explosive devices] or 3D weapons, or to assist with attack planning.”

These are not new threats, but GenAI shortens the potential journey from a curious and vulnerable young person to a radicalised one capable of acts of violence.

“On the flip side though, rapid technology change has huge benefits for New Zealand,” Hampton added.

“We need to engage with it. Similarly, it has significant benefits for agencies such as ours to counter those threats.”

He said New Zealanders and New Zealand companies need to be aware of and resilient to the malicious uses of AI, while the NZSIS needed to help support them doing so.

The report is silent on the threat of AI acting on its own, rather than as someone’s tool. Models created by Anthropic and OpenAI recently went rogue, with the former trying to trick developers into accepting malicious code and the latter hacking a tech company.

This issue is likely to be addressed in the cyber threat report from the Government Communications Security Bureau in October.

The most likely terror event, which transpired in Christchurch in 2019, remains a lone wolf using easily accessible weapons in a crowded place.

Identity-based and faith-based extremism are the two dominant motivations, Hampton said.

Others included nihilism (advocating for change through violence without moral and legal restrictions) and misogyny.

“It’s increasingly complex, particularly when we are talking about individuals who are radicalised online and are not part of any formal network,” he said.

A contributing factor is increasing polarisation and the mainstreaming of “more extreme, more grievance-based language”, which makes the space where radicalisation can foster much noisier.

“It does increase the risk that someone may be radicalised to undertake an act of violent extremism, for example someone who starts engaging with anti-Semitic or Islamophobic narratives online. They could only be a couple of clicks away from someone who is advocating for violence,” Hampton said.

“It also becomes even more difficult to identify the small number of individuals who actually have the intent and capability to undertake an act of violent extremism, amongst all of that noise.”

He made these comments after being asked, in the context of white identity motivated groups, about NZ First leader and Foreign Minister Winston Peters’ comments to Green Party MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to “go back to your own country”.

Hampton replied that the NZSIS was focused on violent extremism.

“We have not seen or heard any elected representative in New Zealand engaging in violent extremist language. But the point we make in our report is, both internationally but also in New Zealand, that there has been a mainstreaming of more extremist language.”

There are hundreds of leads that the NZSIS follows each year, but he said the number of active investigations is in the low 10s.

“We are not all-seeing and all-knowing.

“That’s why it is really important we share as much information as we can with the public around the indicators of someone who may be on that pathway to radicalisation, and encourage them to share that information with us or the police.”

The NZSIS report is peppered with recent cases of how national security has come under threat:

In each of these cases, the NZSIS intervened to mitigate risk.

The wider threat context includes the global conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine, military activity closer to home – including China testing a nuclear-capable missile in the Pacific and conducting live-fire exercises in the Tasman Sea – and New Zealand’s proximity to important geographical assets such as Antarctica.

“This makes New Zealand not only geopolitically relevant, but attractive to threat actors who are unsentimental in their pursuit of our information and their influence over us,” Hampton said.

“We are seeing state actors targeting both Government but also private sector organisations to get access to critical information, including technological innovation.

“And we have seen an intensification of foreign interference focusing on diaspora communities, including examples of foreign states seeking to exercise a degree of control over people in New Zealand in ways inconsistent with our democratic values.”

The report highlights collective responsibility, where threats can be mitigated by improved cyber security and AI literacy, due diligence on foreign partnerships and investments, and more support for vulnerable diaspora communities.

Policies that build trust and counter the fragmenting of communities would also help mitigate risks.

“We’re not trying to be alarmist or cause fear,” Hampton said.

“It’s about being as open as NZSIS can on what we see so that sectors, communities and individuals have the information they need to keep themselves and New Zealand safe.”

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

A popular Nelson running event has given participants another reason to lace up and hit the pavement.

The Spectacle is an independent, New Zealand-owned international running event held in December.

This year, organisers have integrated online fundraising platform Grassrootz into the registration system, meaning runners can pick a local charity to race for.

Runners can set up a page through Grassrootz’s digital platform, pick a participating charity and share their efforts with friends and family.

Spectacle co-founder Julian Matthews said as the event expanded, it was a “no-brainer” to rally around local charities.

“This means every runner who registers for The Spectacle – in any event – can turn their entry into something bigger that gives back to the community,” said Matthews.

“The Spectacle wouldn’t be the wonderful event it is without Nelson Tasman.

“As the event continues to grow and attract people to our beautiful region, it was a no-brainer for the team to make the event into something everyone can rally around, whether you’re running or cheering someone on.”

Email us

Matthews said it also gave runners “that extra bit of motivation”.

“It doesn’t matter how fast you are – knowing each training session and footstep translates to donations to a charity you’re passionate about is that extra bit of motivation – whether you’re running 5km through the heart of the city or 100km through the backcountry.”

The Spectacle’s 2026 partner charities include: 261 Fearless; Big Brothers, Big Sisters Nelson Tasman; Bone Marrow Cancer Trust/Rānui House; Brook Waimārama Sanctuary; Kai Rescue; Nelson Marlborough Rescue Helicopter Trust; Nelson Tasman Hospice; NZ Transplant Games Association; Speed Freaks Charitable Trust; RISE; and Whakatū Riding for the Disabled.

Matthews encouraged every runner to add a Grassrootz commitment to their race on December 4 and 5.

PM Christopher Luxon sacks Chris Penk from Cabinet, strips portfolios after leadership challenge

New Zealand Herald August 12, 2026

Sacked minister Chris Penk won’t seek re-election after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon stripped him of all of his portfolios on Wednesday afternoon.

Luxon outed Penk as the person who launched a challenge for the National leadership.

Luxon publicly announced the emergency caucus meeting on X just hours before it was due to take place after the Herald story reported on discontent within the party and a potential Bishop or Stanford challenge for the leadership.

The ordeal came after a series of gaffes by Luxon: the leader caught his MPs off-guard when he revealed plans for an MMP referendum if National won the election and he insulted the small business community in Rotorua with comments he later apologised for.

Parliament is currently in recess, meaning most will not be back this week.

As the emergency caucus meeting continued in Wellington, former National leader Sir John Key spoke at Financial Services Council New Zealand conference in Auckland, where he reiterated his support for Luxon, whom he described as a “very capable person with the best intentions”.

“I’ve supported Christopher, and I continue to do that because I believe in him. But I believe in that team, a team full of incredibly good people, and they are starting to shine.”

Mark Mitchell, the Police Minister and one of Luxon’s most senior MPs, dampened at least his involvement in the brewing speculation on Wednesday morning when he told Newstalk ZB he had sat with the Prime Minister until late the previous night to ensure he was in the “strongest possible position today and supported for the caucus meeting”.

Speaking to reporters at Parliament, he acknowledged the last-minute caucus meeting was not a good look for National, saying “it’s not flash – we’ve got to get this done today and then move on”.

“I’m supporting our leader. My hope is that he has got support inside the caucus today and that he emerges as our leader.”

Some MPs were confused (Mt Roskill MP Carlos Cheung asked the media what was happening) and others frustrated, saying they would rather spend their recess from Parliament in their electorates.

The spectrum of support shown by Luxon’s MPs ranged from silence – or refusing to answer questions on whether Luxon had their confidence – to declarations they backed Luxon “100%”.

“We are 100% behind our Prime Minister, and that’s the wonderful thing, because when I go door-knocking in Takanini, they’re not worried about this stuff,” Takanini MP Rima Nakhle said.

Tim Costley, the MP for Ōtaki, said he “always backs our Prime Minister” but when asked specifically about Christopher Luxon, Costley told reporters he would speak with them after caucus.

Mark Mitchell says Chris Penk's leadership challenge fell apart overnight because "there was just never the support there for it".

Speaking on Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking Breakfast, Mitchell said the contest was "an unnecessary distraction" but stressed it had finally been dealt with.

"We've re-emerged united behind the leader and this is not going to happen again."

Asked how much certainty he could give to that, Mitchell replied: "110%."

Mitchell didn't believe Penk served as a stalking house, saying he considered him a friend and a "very good" person.

"It was completely, totally out of character.

"I haven't had the chance to sit down and talk with him and find out actually what was going on.

"He's announced he's leaving the party. I just want to acknowledge his service. I mean, I backed him to become Defence Minister in Cabinet."

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little appeared alongside Bishop for a housing announcement in the capital this morning.

Asked whether he had any advice for the National Party, Little, who resigned the Labour Party leadership seven weeks out from the 2017 election, said parties in Parliament need to move away from “distractions” and “circus elements”, and focus on the “serious issues the country is facing”.

“Different circumstances, different conditions, different time, different people, the only message I would have for this Chris and every Chris in Parliament is this is a really important election and actually this is a country that is in desperate need of good, sound leadership,” Little said.

“We’re a country that is struggling with infrastructure, struggling with response to climate change, struggling with wealth creation, struggling with fair distribution. And that’s what I think people want to hear about.”

Bishop rejected suggestions that Chris Penk was doing the numbers for him, claiming talk that Bishop was a leadership contender is “completely unfounded”.

“We’ve had two goes at this in April and August, The matter has been put to bed,” he said.

“We’re united behind Chris Luxon as Prime Minister and leader of the National Party, we’ve got an election to fight in 87 days and I intend to fight as hard as humanly possible to make sure we win that election.”

Thomas Coughlan, the Herald's political editor, says some National MPs will likely be in two minds over the outcome of yesterday's crisis caucus meeting, given Christopher Luxon still holds the top job while Defence Minister Chris Penk has been booted from Cabinet.

Despite public assurances from several MPs that Christopher Luxon maintains full confidence as leader, Coughlan said there were whispers of a potential coup within the National ranks that he began to piece together over the weekend.

"As soon as the Herald rumbled the coup on Monday evening - I think the plotters probably wanted it to stay below the surface for a bit longer - but as soon as we rumbled them, [Luxon] basically got his people together before about midday the next day.

"So within 12 hours basically, he'd launched his counterattack, and that counterattack was clearly successful."

Despite the apparent blindside, Luxon emerged from yesterday's closed-door meeting unscathed and safe for the time being.

"If the polls crash after this coup, then who knows, we might be here again in a few weeks' time," Coughlan said.

"But it would be pretty embarrassing if you were one of the plotters, and you win on your third shot.

"It doesn't give you a massive mandate, I would think."

While National MPs have stressed Christopher Luxon maintains full caucus support, and that Penk was acting alone instead of for someone else, Coughlan said he was still hearing otherwise.

"I think, at this point ... clearly some people are not telling the truth, because everyone is saying that they support the Prime Minister and that everything is fine, and clearly it is not."

A Labour Government wouldn't support the tax proposals of other parties, leader Chris Hipkins told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

“Labour's campaigning on one tax policy, which is the introduction of a simple targeted capital gains tax. We won't support the other taxes the parties are proposing like a wealth tax or a land tax.”

Asked if he’d resign if a Labour Government did introduce anything other than a capital gains tax, Hipkins said: “I'll stake my own reputation on it, absolutely, because we're not going to sign up to things after the election that we've said that we won't support before the election.”

It was up to other political parties whether other taxes were a bottom line for them in coalition negotiations.

“That's the way MMP works … one of our bottom lines is that we won't support the introduction of significant new taxes like a land tax or a wealth tax. We won't breach that.”

Asked if any of his MPs was “doing the numbers on you”, after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon saw off another leadership challenge from National MPs yesterday, Hipkins said “absolutely not”.

“I don’t need to [ask if they are]. I know my team are 100% behind me.”

Senior National Party minister Chris Bishop says the crisis caucus meeting over a leadership challenge was a “surprise” and is denying he had a hand in any aspect of the failed bid.

This morning Bishop told TVNZ’s Breakfast the move by now-demoted Chris Penk came as a surprise to many and that the Prime Minister took the right actions yesterday.

He said it was frustrating to hold the emergency crisis vote over a leadership vote. He described the challenge from Penk as having fizzled.

"Chris Penk mounted a leadership challenge or spill and that came as a surprise to many people I think and the Prime Minister did the right thing."

Bishop refused to discuss conversations that might have taken place around the leadership spill before yesterday's meeting.

And he dismissed speculation of playing a hand, along with Education Minister Erica Stanford, in the failed attempt to oust Luxon.

”There’s all sorts of media speculation around that sort of stuff. I’m not particularly fixated on that at all to be honest.

“What I’m focused on is my portfolios of which they are very important to the country’s future.”

Bishop described Penk's challenge as an isolated case and didn’t believe others would lose roles as a consequence.

Peter Dunne, United future leader and Ōhāriu MP from 1984 to 2017, says National Party MPs must now prove to voters they are truly united behind Christopher Luxon after he emerged unscathed from yesterday's leadership challenge.

Speaking on Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking Breakfast, Dunne agreed Luxon should be commended for surviving his second leadership challenge in four months but thinks "three times is probably a stretch too far".

"This has got to be the end of it through to the election," he said.

"All the sentiments yesterday about, 'We're 100% united', have now got to be demonstrated in fact if National's to come through this unscathed."

Dunne was sceptical of the idea that Penk had launched the challenge to put himself forward for the job, saying he felt it was "a bit far-fetched" and that Penk was more likely testing the waters for others, namely Chris Bishop and Erica Stanford.

"I don't think he necessarily was actively working with Bishop and Stanford, although he was clearly touting their cases," Dunne said.

"[Luxon] can't really run a credible government without those two, so they have to be there, they have to be [kept] in senior roles, and they have to be seen to be treated as senior ministers."

Mark Mitchell says Chris Penk's leadership challenge fell apart overnight because "there was just never the support there for it".

Speaking on Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking Breakfast, Mitchell said the contest was "an unnecessary distraction" but stressed it had finally been dealt with.

"We've re-emerged united behind the leader and this is not going to happen again."

Asked how much certainty he could give to that, Mitchell replied: "110%."

Mitchell didn't believe Penk served as a stalking house, saying he considered him a friend and a "very good" person.

"It was completely, totally out of character.

"I haven't had the chance to sit down and talk with him and find out actually what was going on.

"He's announced he's leaving the party. I just want to acknowledge his service. I mean, I backed him to become Defence Minister in Cabinet."

Opportunity would be very open to a confidence-and-supply agreement with the next government, rather than a formal coalition, “if it means we can stay true to who we are”, the party’s leader Qiulae Wong says.

“I guess it depends how the votes fall and how much they need us in there, what policies we might be able to get across the line and therefore you know how we'll work with a government,” Wong told Herald NOW’s Ryan Bridge Today.

Opportunity would wait another month or so before releasing its bottom lines, so it could see what other parties were putting on the table.

“That will influence ultimately where we think we can work with them, where we could push them harder on different issues, and so that’s ultimately why we want to do it closer to the election,” she said.

Asked if a land tax was foundational to its policy plan, Wong said she had been clear Opportunity did not expect tax reform to happen overnight.

“We’ve got strong policies around innovation, competition, our energy market - these are things that are going to affect the cost of living for New Zealanders and they don't require a change in our tax system to happen.”

The party had not held any formal discussions with other leaders about coalition arrangements, she said.

Quilae Wong has reiterated she won't have NZ First's Winston Peters as Foreign Minister in a potential coalition government with the Opportunity Party but refuses to rule out whether he could adopt other ministerial portfolios instead.

Speaking on TVNZ Breakfast, the Opportunity leader was hesitant to draw bottom lines with potential coalition partners as it was "just playing into the tribal politics", noting that while Opportunity diverged with Act and NZ First on some issues, there were others they agreed on.

"Look, I don't think it's useful to play this ruling in and out game," Wong told Tova O'Brien.

"We have to sit around the table and try to make things work. Because if we continue playing tribal politics, New Zealand will just go backwards."

Asked for her thoughts on National's caucus crisis meeting, Wong said it wouldn't be appropriate for her "to comment on the leadership of any parties" but said it was clear voters were feeling disillusioned by both Labour and National.

"I think we will bring that stability," Wong said.

"We've made it clear we will use our leverage as a kingmaker to bring the parties together. So it's not just about working with National or Labour as the governing party, but about finding that common ground across Parliament."

Act Party leader David Seymour isn’t ruling out working with the Opportunity Party, despite saying Act “can’t abide” one of their biggest policies.

It comes after a 1News-Verian poll, conducted from August 8-11, put Opportunity on 8%. That would give the party nine seats and potentially make it a power broker in forming the next Government.

Seymour told Newstalk ZB’s Ryan Bridge Early Edition that Opportunity’s plans for a land tax and universal basic income (UBI) were “radical left wing” policy.

Taxing every piece of land in New Zealand was “a policy that we just can’t abide”, Seymour said, while the the UBI plans were “extraordinary”.

But pushed repeatedly on whether his party could be in a governing coalition with Opportunity, Seymour said he was focusing on policy.

“They say that actually those policies aren’t that important to them and maybe they could give them up,” he said. “[It] makes you wonder if they’re really the Opportunity Party or the Opportunist Party.”

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has already ruled out National working with Opportunity.

Sacked minister Chris Penk won’t seek re-election after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon stripped him of all of his portfolios on Wednesday afternoon, outing him as the person who launched a challenge for the National leadership.

Luxon has confirmed Penk’s challenge prompted Wednesday’s confidence vote in Luxon’s leadership, which Luxon won.

“This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios,” Luxon said.

Penk, who has been in Cabinet since April, lost his Defence, Veterans, Space, GCSB and NZSIS portfolios. These will be taken over by Paul Goldsmith, who also holds major portfolios like justice.

Climate Change Minister Simon Watts will take over Penk’s Building and Construction portfolio.

After being dumped from Cabinet, Penk, the MP for Auckland’s Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate, announced that he will not seek re-election in November.

“It has been a privilege to serve my community of Kaipara ki Mahurangi for the last nine years, and I am proud of the progress I have contributed to as a Minister this term,” Penk said in a statement last night.

“However, I have decided it is the time for me to seek other opportunities to serve New Zealand.”

The challenge comes after Penk publicly declared his support for Luxon while batting off rumours he was shoring up a leadership challenge behind the scenes, potentially acting as a stalking horse for the campaigns of Erica Stanford or Chris Bishop, both of whom were touted as likely challengers. Speaking on his way to a pre-arranged speech on Wednesday night, Bishop said it was “utterly incorrect” that Penk was working on his behalf.

A National Party-linked source told the Herald Penk had been involved in a possible leadership challenge on behalf of senior MP Erica Stanford by doing her numbers ahead of the caucus meeting. Penk denied this when asked by reporters on Wednesday morning.

“I think everyone else needs to get their story straight, because I’m hearing multiple different versions,” Penk said.

“None of them are true, and as I said, I’m not going to be able to disclose private conversations, except only to say I have confidence in Christopher Luxon.”

After the vote, Penk refused to say whether he had voted for Luxon to remain as National Party leader. He denied plotting against Luxon – and said he was pleased the confidence vote had delivered “clarity and certainty”.

“We don’t talk about what happens in caucus, but I’m really pleased with the result.”

The saga follows a frantic 24 hours for National MPs who scrambled from their electorates across the country to get to Wellington for the urgent, last-minute caucus meeting with their leader.

Luxon publicly announced the emergency caucus meeting on X (formerly Twitter) just hours before it was due to take place after the Herald story reported on discontent within the party and a potential Bishop or Stanford challenge for the leadership.

As the MPs flooded into Wellington in the hours before the caucus meeting, speculation over Luxon’s future grew while the MPs’ jobs – and the jobs of their staff – hung in the balance. The ordeal came after a series of gaffes by Luxon: the leader caught his MPs off-guard when he revealed plans for an MMP referendum if National won the election and he insulted the small business community in Rotorua with comments he later apologised for.

In a pledge of support for Luxon, Minister for Women Nicola Grigg said while walking through Wellington Airport that Stanford – her “very good friend” – was “not a Prime Minister”.

Mark Mitchell, the Police Minister and one of Luxon’s most senior MPs, dampened at least his involvement in the brewing speculation on Wednesday morning when he told Newstalk ZB he had sat with the Prime Minister until late the previous night to ensure he was in the “strongest possible position today and supported for the caucus meeting”.

Speaking to reporters at Parliament, he acknowledged the last-minute caucus meeting was not a good look for National, saying “it’s not flash – we’ve got to get this done today and then move on”.

“I’m supporting our leader. My hope is that he has got support inside the caucus today and that he emerges as our leader.”

Some MPs were confused (Mt Roskill MP Carlos Cheung asked the media what was happening) and others frustrated, saying they would rather spend their recess from Parliament in their electorates.

The spectrum of support shown by Luxon’s MPs ranged from silence – or refusing to answer questions on whether Luxon had their confidence – to declarations they backed Luxon “100%”.

“We are 100% behind our Prime Minister, and that’s the wonderful thing, because when I go door-knocking in Takanini, they’re not worried about this stuff,” Takanini MP Rima Nakhle said.

Tim Costley, the MP for Ōtaki, said he “always backs our Prime Minister” but when asked specifically about Christopher Luxon, Costley told reporters he would speak with them after caucus.

Consumer Affairs Minister and Upper Harbour MP Cameron Brewer refused to answer questions about his confidence in Christopher Luxon – but insisted National would emerge from the saga “united” to go on to “win the election”.

As the emergency caucus meeting continued in Wellington, former National leader Sir John Key spoke at Financial Services Council New Zealand conference in Auckland, where he reiterated his support for Luxon, whom he described as a “very capable person with the best intentions”.

“I’ve supported Christopher, and I continue to do that because I believe in him. But I believe in that team, a team full of incredibly good people, and they are starting to shine.”

MPs were leaving Wellington on Wednesday evening. Parliament is currently in recess, meaning most will not be back this week.

A billionaire secretly anointed his youngest son as successor. His other children were blindsided

Sydney Morning Herald August 13, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Two months before his death in Greece, billionaire Nick Andrianakos met his youngest son for lunch at upmarket Glen Iris restaurant Grazia, where he anointed him successor to the family’s petrol and property empire.

The ailing founder of Milemaker Group told Theo Andrianakos he would have full control of the family’s multibillion-dollar businesses, and that his vast portfolio of assets in Australia and Greece would also be passed on to Theo and his two sons.

Theo also learned at the meeting in January 2025 that his father intended to bequeath €5 million ($8.17 million) to his substantially younger partner Hatouna Sakvarelintze, an architect the ailing businessman had met a couple of years earlier on a hotel redevelopment project.

However, there was a sticking point in the patriarch’s grand succession plan – Andrianakos’ three other children, who would later claim in the Supreme Court of Victoria that the revised “family agreement” had not been relayed to them, nor formalised in a signed will.

The death of the 81-year-old patriarch on March 17 last year – just days before he was due to sign the will and the family agreement – sparked a toxic legal battle between the siblings over control of their late father’s assets and extensive business interests.

The case was set to proceed to trial last month, with siblings Kristina and Paul Andrianakos and Vicky Papamarkou relying on the original documents, signed by their father in 2018 and 2019, which gave the sisters a greater slice of their father’s $183 million estate, and the siblings shared control over Milemaker Group.

Under the signed will, Andrianakos wanted to give his sons the bulk of his inheritance – allocating them $83 million each, and his daughters $24 million respectively.

However, the siblings reached an eleventh-hour agreement that avoided a trial and ultimately allowed Justice Peter Gray to grant probate of the unsigned will.

The settlement, on July 17, handed Theo and his sons all of Andrianakos’ estate, which included CBD penthouses, beachfront homes on the Mornington Peninsula, and properties in Greece, along with a $200,000 black Bentley and a tractor.

Theo received the lion’s share of the estate, reducing his brother’s inheritance and seeing his sisters receive substantially less than the $24 million they were originally entitled.

The court dispute also laid bare the tensions between the family and Andrianakos senior’s partner, Sakvarelintze.

The daughters claimed in respective affidavits that during the months that the drastic changes to their father’s estate were drafted, he had been frail and could no longer understand English.

Papamarkou warned her father that his Greek girlfriend was “probably only after his money” a year before he made changes to bequeath her millions, she claimed in her sworn statement.

“I warned him that it was strange to see a woman so young be romantically interested in someone around 80 years of age,” she said in an affidavit.

“I told my father to be careful because she was probably only after his money. My father responded by saying words to the following effect: ‘There is no way Hatouna is getting any of my money or property. I am leaving all my property to my children’.”

The late billionaire’s wealth planner Peter Pagonis claimed the revised, unsigned will represented the lawful and legitimate plan for his inheritance.

Pagonis, who consults to more than 450 ultra-high-net-worth families, said in an affidavit that the family patriarch first ordered him to draft the changes in November 2024 after expressing concerns the three siblings would seize control of Milemaker Group.

“The deceased said word to the effect that he was concerned that Vicky, Paul and Kristina would ‘gang up’ on Theo, who was CEO of Milemaker Group, and who was instrumental in operating and growing the Milemaker Group business with [Andrianakos],” he said.

“He was concerned his children Vicky, Paul and Kristina will disrupt the family legacy and seek to break up the family assets and the business that he had grown over time.”

Pagonis said that Andrianakos told him in November 2024: “I want to make sure that Theo has full control of the business going forward.”

The order came only a few months after the tense exchange between Papamarkou and her father over his romance, which had strained their relationship.

She said after that confrontation in July 2023, the pair did not speak for some time until finally reconciling in August 2024.

Andrianakos’ instructions in November 2024 led to significant changes to the family agreement, the formal succession document which includes clauses of the family values (among them: family is first, business for future generations, integrity, and no drugs).

The succession plans were later thrashed out over a series of meetings – including several lunches at Grazia and secret meetings at Andrianakos’ CBD penthouse – during what would be his last visit to Melbourne.

The businessman jetted into town on Christmas Eve 2024 with Sakvarelintze, in time for the family’s Christmas lunch, held at Nobu in Crown Casino.

Paul, Vicky and Kristina did not attend any of the estate discussions, with Papamarkou noting she didn’t discuss it with her father over Christmas lunch.

“When the family met on Christmas day, my father appeared frail and unwell. Because the Christmas lunch was very busy, I did not get to spend any one-on-one time with my father that day,” she said.

Papamarkou said when she did later catch up with her father, he was unwell and had difficulty getting up off the couch.

Before returning to Greece in January 2025, Andrianakos visited Kristina’s home, where she claims he reassured her about his estate: “My father brought up his will again and told me that Vicky and I would be included and get a share of everything.”

“My father assured me Hatouna would not have any lasting control over his estate,” she said.

The siblings, except Theo, received an email in March 2025 from Pagonis that outlined their father’s plans to downgrade Milemaker Group’s Family Board from a “decision-making authority” to one that “only had a right to be advised of changes from time to time”.

The new will, now granted probate, gives Theo total control of the company’s assets, including a property portfolio that spans Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide. It acquired its crown jewel in 2025 with a $385 million half-stake in Melbourne’s Northland shopping centre.

His sons, Nicholas and Giorgio, were the other beneficiaries of the property assets. The eldest, Nick, has been chosen as the successor of Milemaker after Theo, and he received the family’s $2.9 million sprawling Greenvale mansion.

Giorgio inherited a $1.95 million private penthouse on Collins Street.

None of the siblings was present at the Supreme Court of Victoria on July 15, on what was supposed to be the first day of the trial. Instead, the court heard the parties had reached a last-minute, closed-door agreement to enforce their father’s unsigned will.

Sakvarelintze, who had flown from Greece for the trial, and Pagonis did appear, sitting among a retinue of silks involved in the case.

The Georgian-born architect rubbed the hands of an interpreter who accompanied Sakvarelintze as Justice Peter Gray ordered the probate that ensured her $8 million windfall.
