How a lost bag in an Uber spawned one of the best shows of the year

Sydney Morning Herald August 13, 2026

Had Jude Troy taken her bag with her when she got out at Tullamarine, The Airport Chaplain might never have existed.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Inspiration comes from the strangest of places. In the case of the brilliant new SBS series The Airport Chaplain, it arrived in the back seat of an Uber. Or, to be precise, it departed, taking Jude Troy’s most vital belongings with it.

It was August 2023 and Troy – the Irish-born producer whose company Wooden Horse (co-founded with Richard Finlayson, former head of television at the ABC) has made The Other Guy, Stuff the British Stole and The Clearing – was heading back to Sydney after the first public screening of her show Mother and Son at Melbourne’s ACMI.

“I was really desperate to get home, distracted, running late as always for a plane,” she says. “I jumped out of the Uber, turned around, and the car disappeared into the late afternoon sun, taking my bag, my laptop, my phone, everything.”

She stood on the footpath for a couple of minutes waiting for it to turn around “but it never came back”. Growing increasingly frantic, she tried to get assistance from Uber’s offshore “help” line using phones borrowed from strangers, and realised how few phone numbers we commit to memory these days.

Finally, a federal police officer, about to race off to collect her kids after school, came to the rescue. “She said, ‘I’m going to introduce you to a gentleman called Martin, and he’ll look after you.’”

Martyn Scrimshaw, the chaplain at Melbourne Airport, did exactly that. But first, he led Troy on what she calls a “two-hour, 25,000-step adventure deep into the bowels of the airport, through security, into the upper echelons of what is a class system in the airport”.

He told her stories “of people dying on aeroplanes, which happens every week; of the woman who comes to the airport every day and thinks she’s being watched by MI5; the young girl who’s camping on the roof of the airport because she’s been abused; the Russian who arrived with an empty suitcase and has literally no idea where to go. Story after story – the absurd, the ridiculous the emotional – and this man, Martyn Scrimshaw, is there to support those people and the workers in the canteens, in security, in the taxi ranks, the terminal manager and the check-in staff. So many people seek his counsel, it’s quite extraordinary.”

By 9pm, Troy was on a flight home, her retrieved bag beside her, in the business class seat for which Scrimshaw contrived an upgrade. “And next morning, I rang my co-pilot [writer Elise McCredie] and told her this story, and she was like, ‘We’re making a TV show.’”

Troy tells me all this in an excited jumble – I suspect frantic is, in fact, her default mode – while we sit at a plastic table beneath a temporary marquee in a carpark at Flemington Racecourse.

We’re not here for the horses. We’re here for the hustle and bustle of Melbourne International Airport, re-created with cunning sleight-of-hand in the Members Stand. (For obvious reasons, filming the series at the airport was impractical.)

Watching Hugo Weaving as the fictional Tobias Wallace, it’s easy to see why McCredie was as inspired by the promise as Troy. It’s fast-paced, dynamic, full of drama and comedy and generosity and tension, and all neatly resolved (more or less) within a half-hour (SBS has commissioned eight episodes in this first season; the show’s creators hope there will be many more to come).

McCredie met the real-life airport chaplain, too, spending several days following him around the airport, also wearing a hi-vis vest emblazoned with the words “Airport chaplain”. This functions – at least when accompanied by the man himself – as a kind of access-all-areas pass.

“He told me it’s the best job in the world because every day he doesn’t know what’s going to happen,” she says. “He meets different people. He’s a problem solver, he gets to laugh and be joyful, but then he also helps people in really dark places. And so for a series, it just had everything for me as a writer.”

The rollcall of characters and micro-dramas provides endless short-term storylines, but a series needs a continuing narrative to make it more than just a collection of vignettes. This is where Shabana Azeez lands.

The 28-year-old from Adelaide, who had plugged away in indie fare for seven years before The Pitt catapulted her to fame last year, plays new terminal manager Mira Ansari-Cole, an MBA-toting corporate drone whose only loyalty is to the bottom line. Virtually her first interaction with Tobias is to offer him a redundancy. Things only get worse from there.

Mira – a single mother, an outsider (she’s come to Australia via the UK and Hong Kong), and not especially gifted with interpersonal skills – is at first glance the polar opposite of Tobias. Not just a formidable foe, she’s also someone fighting her own battle for acceptance in a corporate structure that regards people as headcounts on a spreadsheet.

“This show starts with Tobias’ perspective and it slowly shifts to a more holistic view of the airport,” says Azeez. The challenge is to make Mira, a “complicated” character, relatable despite the lack of obvious likeability.

“There’s something about how women in positions of power gain power, how they keep power, and how hard it is for women to be likeable when they have power,” says Azeez, adding “we’re really happy to build women up to tear them down”.

Mira has been brought into “an impossible position”, she says. “Her predecessor has made some choices that have left the airport compromised, and she’s coming into a shitshow, frankly, tasked with fixing it.

“And nobody likes her because she’s not trading on likeability or beauty or any of these things that historically have been the ways women get power. She’s trading on competence, and a lot of people are getting in the way of her doing her job. So that raises a lot of tension and drama in the workplace.”

Azeez is “very, very excited by the idea of playing young women who are complicated. I really want my career to be me going into bat for young women – until I’m not a young woman any more; you know, there’s a real timeline on that – so I’m grateful to have this opportunity now. I think it’s a really political show, a socially aware show, and it’s very complex and layered.”

Azeez’s sister, two years older, works in management, and she tapped her for insights. “She’s also a psychologist, so she’s very useful for every role, ever.” She also tapped friends with kids for insights into juggling work and parenting. And she drew on her own experience of being a child of migrants – her parents were born and raised in Fiji – for that aspect of Mira’s backstory.

“For me, acting is the perfect job in terms of the work of it,” Azeez says. “I love to research, I love to interview people, I love to read. I’m quite obsessive, and I can get hyper-fixated on things. The research is my favourite, and then flow state – performance is flow state when it’s going well.”

Azeez never studied drama, not at school – “I did maths” – or university. “My parents were like, ‘Absolutely over our dead bodies.’ Lawyer, doctor, accountant: those were the options.”

They consented to her trying for one drama school, though, on the basis that if she didn’t get in they would never have to hear about this ridiculous acting thing again. “And I crashed my car on the way to the audition – it was horrible – and I just fumbled the whole thing.”

She did an arts degree, with the aim of doing something acting-adjacent, and landed a job in arts administration. Her boss could tell her heart wasn’t in it though, and when Azeez confessed all she really wanted to do was act, the boss took action.

“Within an hour, she got me an audition, and I booked it, and that tape got sent around to a bunch of directors, because it’s Adelaide,” she says. Soon, she was cast in indie shorts, and eventually features. “Adelaide being Adelaide is why I have a career,” she says. “Just, like, seven people being really nice to me.”

Talent and brains may have something to do with it – and ambition, too. Azeez has no shortage of that.

“I shadow every director on The Pitt, I shadow pre-production on The Pitt, I’m going to shadow post-production on season three,” she says. “I want to make my own stuff, but because I didn’t train, I want to know my business before I get into that. I think it’s important not to squander opportunities by not knowing.”

Little chance of that, you suspect. With The Airport Chaplain adding to her rapidly growing resume, Shabana Azeez is well and truly flying.

The Airport Chaplain (episodes 1-3) premieres at MIFF this weekend; details: miff. com. au. The series premieres at 8.30pm on Wednesday, August 26, on SBS and SBS On Demand.

The email many authors dream of getting – and why it’s a trap

Sydney Morning Herald August 13, 2026

Every author wants to hear “we love your book”. Increasingly, those words are coming from scammers.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Less than two weeks after her debut novel Touch Grass was published in June, Mary Colussi received a dream email for many young Australian authors: a message from the head of prestigious UK publishing house Granta, Bella Lacey, raving about her novel’s “originality, intelligence, and distinctive narrative voice” and asking to discuss future projects. The email was detailed and effusive – the kind of praise that “as a writer, you want to believe”, Colussi says. Except it wasn’t from Bella Lacey or anyone from Granta – and the person who sent it almost certainly had not read Colussi’s novel.

One of the red flags, Colussi says, was that “everything that they were praising is something that you can find in the synopsis, and in one paragraph they actually quoted directly from the synopsis”. The definitive giveaway was the email address, which ended with @aol. com. A quick check of the Granta website confirmed her suspicions: a warning note from the publisher about fraudulent emails being sent from scammers impersonating staff and offering publishing deals in exchange for money.

Colussi’s experience is increasingly common, thanks to a new wave of AI-generated scam emails targeting authors internationally, offering publishing or promotional opportunities in exchange for money. In the past year, the Australian Society of Authors (ASA) has been inundated with messages from writers seeking advice and sharing their experiences, some of them receiving multiple scam emails a day.

Email scams targeting authors have existed almost as long as email itself, but they have been turbocharged by AI. The latest wave of scams is “far more sophisticated”, says ASA chief executive Lucy Hayward. “It’s not just that they might be impersonating people from the book industry, it’s that they’re able to provide detail and give the impression that they have read an author’s work, which makes the email convincing. And they can do that because the author’s work has either already been ingested [by AI companies], or it can be ingested by these AI tools and then summarised.”

Kelly Gardiner, an established author and member of the ASA board who receives these kinds of AI-generated emails daily, says “authors have been getting unsolicited approaches from PR ‘experts’ for a while, but the sudden expansion of AI has turned it into a flood”.

Most authors have a story – or several. Veteran author and academic Dennis Altman has written about receiving effusive, detailed emails about his books from individuals purporting to be acclaimed authors Annie Ernaux and Patrick Süskind; Walter Marsh described being “flooded” by emails offering paid reviews and promotion after the publication of his second novel (ironically, a novel about theft and fraud) late last year; and Jane Sullivan detailed a “highly convincing” email ostensibly from the (real) Melbourne-based Classic Book Club, offering to promote her 2024 crime novel.

While authors are the primary targets, respected editors, literary agents and media figures are caught on the other side of the sting. Scammers steal their names and professional authority to trick writers into fake pitch offers, promotional junkets or film deals. Such was the case with a recent scam email purporting to be from ABC Radio National presenter Sally Sara, offering an author a guest appearance on her show. By leveraging the cachet of a major public broadcaster, the scammers created an offer that felt almost too prestigious for a writer to turn down (the ABC was contacted for comment).

Some of the initial emails mention money, but most don’t. Instead, they lead with flattery and promises, waiting to hook the author before they raise the issue of fees. These kinds of scams are sometimes referred to as “pig butchering” operations, a term that originated with romance scams and graphically evokes the process of fattening up a prospective victim with flattery before draining them financially.

Like romance scams, author scams target vulnerability and play on emotions. “They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted,” Hayward says.

The tactic has proved remarkably lucrative for its perpetrators. In a recent case, the US government determined that just one of these publishing scam operations, based in the Philippines, defrauded nearly 800 writers of more than $48 million over six years.

US author Victoria Strauss, who has covered author scams since 1998 via the website Writer Beware, says they have proliferated over the past decade, fuelled by outfits based in the Philippines, Pakistan and India. The more recent AI-driven scams come from a different location, however.

“I’ve gotten hundreds of reports of these AI scams, and I traced a lot of them back to the payment information, and everything that I can collect and deduce indicates that they primarily come from Nigeria,” says Strauss. “I see them as kind of a descendant of the ‘Nigerian prince’ scams of old.”

Authors who have been inundated with these kinds of emails have become far more adept at identifying them. “The AI-generated copy is its own genre now and you can spot it once you’ve seen a few,” says Gardiner. The emails also have telling similarities: “same terms, same logic, same sentence structures”.

They’re also often about older books. Gardiner says most of the scam emails she receives “are about two young adult books I published years ago. Perhaps it’s something to do with how often they were ingested in a pirate database used to train AI. No real publicist would want to talk to me about them, although sometimes local schools or readers do, so I always have to check.”

Hayward says sifting the real emails from the fake has become a problem in itself. “[At this point] it’s not so much that authors are falling for these scams and handing out money, it’s the volume of the emails that they are receiving. It becomes very difficult to determine what might be a legitimate offer and what is a scam.” One of the key ways to check is looking at the email address, she says, “but for Australia, we have a smaller market, and where book clubs and podcasts are concerned, you might not have someone with a professional email address”.

“You waste time trying to sift the real from the fake,” Gardiner says. “No doubt some genuine approaches have not got through, too, which means writers and readers miss out on real opportunities to engage.”

How are scammers continuing to thrive, if authors are getting wise? Strauss says the dozen or so emails she receives each week about people who have lost money to these scams involve non-professional and first-time authors.

“There are a lot of people who just want to write one book; they want to write a memoir, or they want to write about their cancer journey or something they feel is meaningful and will help people. There are a lot of older people who retire and write children’s stories, or a memoir,” she says.

These people are vulnerable to scammers in more than one way: not only are they unaware of how the publishing industry works and outside professional support networks and communities, but the personal nature of their material can make them particularly susceptible to emotional manipulation.

“I sometimes hear from the relatives of older people, often on fixed incomes, who’ve lost enormous amounts of money – tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars – and cannot be convinced that they’re being scammed because the scammers are using psychological manipulation to establish personal relationships,” Strauss says.

As she embarks on her career, Colussi can well understand how people are taken in. “Writing a book is such a dream for so many people. They are waiting for that one ‘yes’, and pretending that you are that one ‘yes’ is unfortunately an easy way to take advantage of someone.”

This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s

Sydney Morning Herald August 13, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In the new Australian hospital drama The F Ward, there’s a lot of talk about mistakes and second chances. A group of embattled medical interns is given a last chance when they’re sent to a teaching hospital on Sydney’s northern beaches. Each has previously stuffed up in ways that could be career-ending. Now, under all manner of pressure, from power cuts and problematic patients to a no-nonsense supervisor, they have the chance to prove themselves.

This idea of characters messing up and struggling, often-clumsily, to get their lives back on track is common in a show from John Edwards. One of Australia’s most successful and significant creative forces, this prolific writer and producer has been steadily making TV about the messiness and complexity of human relations since the mid-’80s.

From The Secret Life of Us to Love My Way to Offspring to Bump, his series often focus on people’s fallibility and fragility; their impulsive or destructive decisions; the liberating though possibly damaging rebellions; the heady but possibly reckless affairs. And, alongside that, sits the possibility of redemption, as identifiable almost 40 years ago in Police Rescue as it is today in The F Ward.

Over the decades, Edwards has been involved in productions on four of the five free-TV networks (Seven, Nine, Ten and the ABC) and a number of subscription services (Foxtel, Stan, Paramount+). His CV, too extensive to cover comprehensively here, includes the cops ‘n’ docs staples of police and medical shows, as well as period pieces and series focusing on sport, politics, media and family life.

A cursory scan of his credits reveals some standouts: the propulsive police series Rush (2008-11); the dramatisation of the great cricket schism in Howzat! Kerry Packer’s War (2012); the evocative revisiting of the ’70s in Paper Giants: The Birth of Cleo (2012); the irresistible antics of the Proudmans in Offspring (2010-17). And a couple of less prominent but audacious efforts: reworking Anna Karenina in The Beautiful Lie (2015) and the gritty hospital drama, The Surgeon (2005).

Amid the host of productions that bear Edwards’ name as a producer or executive producer, there’s a particularly consequential string of loosely connected series – almost a spine through the body of work. It’s a choice selection of shows that resists neat generic categorisation and that portrays the challenges of life over generations. It begins with the spirited twenty-somethings of The Secret Life of Us (2001-04), moves on to the troubled thirty-somethings of Love My Way (2004-07), and then to the fraught forty-somethings of Tangle (2009-12). This trio will soon become a quartet with the arrival of Dalliance on Paramount+, which turns its attention to life, love, regret and death among sixtysomethings and features a cast including Heather Mitchell, Hugo Weaving, Georgie Parker and David Wenham.

These are original drama series created for TV, but if the impressive adaptation of Kathy Lette’s Puberty Blues (2012-14), dealing with teenagers and their troubled parents, is added to the list, Edwards’ shows span an even broader spectrum of life, from tentative adolescent romances and early sexual experiences, through pregnancy and parenthood, to grandparenting and memorial services.

All of these series showcase vibrant ensembles, memorable collections of artfully drawn and cleverly cast characters. They’re also notable for displaying Edwards’ “old head, young head” philosophy, on-screen and behind the scenes. He’s long believed that pairing experienced writers and actors with gifted newcomers creates the ideal combination, and the rewards of that approach have been abundant.

The pairing of Edwards’ longtime collaborator, actor, writer and producer Claudia Karvan with novice screenwriter Kelsey Munro to create and develop Bump (2012-24) delivered one of the country’s best local productions (if you skip the regrettable telemovie tacked on at end). The series also gave us newcomers Nathalie Morris, Carlos Sanson Jr and Ioane Sa’ula in key roles, convincingly moving from high-school kids to adult parents negotiating family life and careers. They’re cast alongside proven players including Karvan, Angus Sampson and Anita Hegh, creating an ensemble alive with zesty energy.

But the practice reaches further back, reaping rewards on a host of series and revealing Edwards’ keen eye for emerging talent. Asher Keddie, Joel Edgerton, Samuel Johnson and Michael Dorman in Secret Life; Ashley Zukerman and Nicole Da Silva in Rush. Celia Pacquola displaying her range beyond comedy in Offspring and Beautiful Lie. Lincoln Younes perfectly cast as Ben Mendelsohn and Justine Clarke’s son in Tangle.

These then-rising stars have shared the screen with some of the most accomplished actors in the country, Edwards’ frequent flyers including Susie Porter, Catherine McClements, Dan Wyllie and Rodger Corser.

The credit roll behind the scenes presents a similar picture. Fledgling writers Judi McCrossin and Jacquelin Perske on Secret Life and Love My Way respectively; emerging producer Imogen Banks on Tangle and Offspring; rookie director Emma Freeman on Rush. And Dalliance features writer Christopher Lee, whose association with Edwards stretches back to Police Rescue. So as fresh talent is tapped, trusted colleagues continue their collaborations.

Erudite, energetic and not one to hold back on his opinions, Edwards is not the kind of producer who restricts his role to simply that of a money man: he’s intimately involved in the creation and development of his shows. And with more than 40 TV productions to his credit, he’s had an indelible impact on the local industry.

Now, his screen work comes through Roadshow Rough Diamond, the company he set up in 2016 with his son, Dan, co-creator of The F Ward. It’s an additional manifestation of the “old head, young head” strategy, as well, perhaps, as an indication of a generational passing-of-the-baton. Yet the indications are that Edwards Sr’s output, thoughtfully and compassionately exploring people struggling, stumbling, surviving and sometimes succeeding, is happily showing no signs of slowing down.

The F Ward is streaming on Stan now. Dalliance premieres on Paramount+ August 27.

Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary, Trump says

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 21:36:21 GMT

US president announced departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving to ‘spend more time’ with family

US politics – live updates

Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced.

The US president revealed her departure on social media, saying Leavitt was leaving “so she can spend more time” with her family. The 28-year-old gave birth to a daughter, Viviana, in May, and returned from maternity leave last month.

The departure of Trump’s most prominent spokesperson comes with his approval rating at a historic low as voters express discontent over rising prices and a war in Iran that has no end in sight.

Trump said Leavitt, who became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary on his return to office in January 2025, “will now be one of my top outside advisors” in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Leavitt wrote on X: “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary – and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.”

Leavitt served Trump as a press aide during his first term in the White House. She ran for Congress in 2022 as the Republican nominee for New Hampshire’s first congressional district but lost the race.

She joined Trump’s 2024 ​campaign ​and was transition ​spokeswoman before Trump selected ​her to ‌be White House ​press ​secretary. At 27 she was younger than Ronald Ziegler, who was 29 when he was Richard Nixon’s spokesperson.

A devout Christian, Leavitt, wearing a cross necklace, and her team would hold a short group prayer before she walked into the briefing room to face reporters. The briefings rarely strayed off message or made headlines but did keep factcheckers occupied. For example, her claim that “tariffs are a tax cut for the American people,” was rated false by Politifact.

In a smooth delivery with few verbal stumbles, Leavitt zealously defended the president while berating Democrats and the “fake news” media. In her first appearance on the podium, she described Trump as “the hardest-working man in politics” with “wildly popular” policies responsible for a new “golden age”.

Leavitt was cordial with reporters behind the scenes but could be combative in front of the camera. In January this year, when a journalist raised the killing of Renee Good by an ICE agent in Minneapolis, Leavitt demanded to know why Good had been killed. The reporter answered: “Because an ICE agent acted recklessly and killed her unjustifiably.” Leavitt, jabbing her finger, snapped: “You’re a leftwing hack. You’re not a reporter. You’re posing in the room as a journalist … You shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.”

Trump often praised Leavitt as an effective communicator and drawing attention to her appearance. He once told the Newsmax network: “She’s become a star. It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.”

On Wednesday the president’s allies joined the acclaim. Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, tweeted: “Karoline Leavitt has served President Trump and the American people with courage and conviction. She’s a great colleague, a fearless voice for the President’s agenda and a true professional.”

Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, added: “Karoline Leavitt has been the most successful Press Secretary in history. Always strong, clear and right to the point … We are all Karoline Leavitt fans!”

Democrats, however, took a different view. Adam Schiff, a senator for California, posted: “Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House to spend a little more time … with the truth.”

Trump did not outline plans for who might succeed her. He had four press secretaries during his first term. Sean Spicer is now a political commentator and podcaster; Sarah Huckabee Sanders is now the governor of Arkansas; Stephanie Grisham is now a fierce critic of Trump who spoke at the 2024 Democratic national convention; Kayleigh McEnany is a host on Fox News.

Israeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 21:29:10 GMT

Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror

Israeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in the West Bank village of Qusra through a campaign of terror.

A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters.

The Israeli men gathered just metres away from the spot where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh was killed by a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault.

“Every night, the settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. We are living in a state of terror,” Hassan said. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off.

Settlers used the same tactics to steal another Palestinian home in neighbouring Jalud village, driving the al Tubasi family out in July after a months-long siege.

They cut off water and electricity to the homes, although a solar panel allows Hassan to keep some devices charged in Qusra. They have also blocked medical care.

When his younger daughter, a two-year-old, fell ill with vomiting and a high fever on Monday, settlers blocked an ambulance from reaching the house. The girls and their mother were eventually evacuated on Tuesday.

They are short on food and are drinking water and juice delivered by the ambulance that came to collect his daughter. “The situation is extremely dire,” Hassan said.

On Wednesday morning, the commander of Israeli forces in the region, Gen Avi Bluth, visited the families and promised to lift the siege, an Israeli military spokesperson said. Hassan confirmed the visit.

“Today, the area commander came and spoke with us and assured us that he would evacuate the settlers. For the first time, I feel that there is some seriousness on the part of the army in dealing with the settlers,” Hassan said, but added that it had not yet produced tangible results.

Soldiers took the tent but not bedding and other possessions and, after brief clashes with the settlers, withdrew. “The settlers are still there in front of the house, and we are still unable to leave.”

An Israeli military spokesperson said commanders were “gravely concerned” about the settlers’ actions and that soldiers who supported them would face disciplinary action, but declined to give a timeline for lifting the siege.

On Wednesday evening, chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Eyal Zamir, met other senior commanders to discuss the situation in Qusra. He ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank.

“The battalion, which is currently undergoing a period of refreshment and training, will be deployed to the sector in order to strengthen operational control. Furthermore, additional soldiers will remain on standby for deployment as necessary,” a military spokesperson said.

The military is working with the police to bring “those responsible for the disturbances to justice”, the spokesperson added.

Israeli militants target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only one indictment over those deaths.

Violence is deployed as part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes.

“What is happening in Qusra is not an isolated incident,” said B’Tselem’s executive director, Yuli Novak.

“Settler militias, backed by the Israeli military, are expanding their attacks into Palestinian villages and towns – seizing land, attacking homes and forcing families out. Israel’s ethnic cleansing of the West Bank is accelerating and expanding in plain sight.”

Dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite have threatened legal action against their government over its failure to tackle “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank.

As the occupying power in the West Bank, Israel is responsible under international law for ensuring the safety of Palestinian civilians and meeting their basic needs.

The Israeli military has declared the area a closed military zone and blocked journalists from approaching the Palestinian homes. Israeli settlers are subject to the same orders but have not been removed.

Sufian Taha contributed reporting

Hudson-Smith dazzles home fans as he surges to golden European 400m hat-trick

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 21:07:48 GMT

Becomes first man to win three European 400m titles

Hudson-Smith: ‘Nobody is going to beat me on this track’

Stand … and deliver. On a balmy night in Birmingham, Matt Hudson-Smith powered past the stand bearing his name at the Alexander Stadium and into history by becoming the first man to win three European Championship 400m titles.

And afterwards, as the adrenaline flooded his body and he posed wearing a crown in front of the Matthew Hudson-Smith Stand, the 31-year-old made it clear just how much it meant. “Nobody is going to beat me on this track,” he said. “This is my home. I have been here since I was nine. I know this track like the back of my hand.”

Born in Wolverhampton. Made in Birmingham. Forged in the fire of competition. But this wasn’t the easiest of wins given that Hudson-Smith started in lane nine, which meant he was blind to the challengers inside him.

No wonder that when the starting gun went off he went off like a man sprinting for the last bus of the night. And while he began to tie up in the final 70 metres, he easily had enough to win in 44.17sec.

“I knew it would take one hell of an effort to get past me,” said Hudson-Smith. “Every time someone beats me, I kind of end their career. I knew that for them to beat me, they would have to have a supernatural moment.”

Muhammad Abdallah Kounta of France took silver in 44.40, while Jonas Phijffers of the Netherlands took bronze, a hundredth of a second further back, in a new national record.

They were happy with their spoils. But no one was more ecstatic as Hudson-Smith, although there was a little sharpness to his celebrations, as he took a dig at the BBC afterwards for suggesting he might be carrying an injury.

“You guys need to come with the facts, man,” he said. “Saying I was injured and everything. The whole point of rounds is to survive and advance. I tried to conserve in the rounds.

“Me and my coach were laughing all the way around. I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that. On paper, I was a second faster than these guys.

My coach said: ‘Once you seal the deal, make sure you do it,’” he added. “This is your home. Defend it.”

The only disappointment was that the stand named after him was not packed to the rafters to celebrate his triumph. There has been a lot of talk about prices being too high. However, it is not as simple as that given that most of the £110 Category A seats in the main stand were sold out.

It has been the cheaper tickets, some of which have been priced as low as £40 and £20, that have struggled to sell out.

There are many reasons for that. The stadium is out of town. It is not easy to park nearby. There is a cost of living crisis. And, in fairness to the organisers, the last four days of competition are said to be sell-outs. Who can blame people for waiting for the end of the week when there are more finals?

European Athletics say 80% of tickets – about 200,000 in total – have now been sold and they are expecting big crowds for the last few days. But there is perhaps another factor for that figure not being higher.

The last four European championships have been staged in Rome, Munich, Berlin and Amsterdam. These are cities where it is easy to combine a city break with sport, art and culture. Birmingham just doesn’t pack that punch. As one press box wag put it, Rome has the Colosseum, Birmingham has the Bullring.

“Naturally, we would love to see a full stadium for every session, because nothing compares with the energy of a packed Alexander Stadium and the support it gives to the athletes,” European Athletics said in a statement. “We are very pleased that demand for tickets to the second half of the championships is strong.”

There was a second British success of the night as Emily Newnham came through with a late charge to take silver in the women’s 400m hurdles.

The favourite, Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia won comfortably in 52.91 sec, but Newnham went from fourth over the final hurdle to second by running a personal best of 53.33. Fatoumata Binta Diallo set a national record for Portugal of 53.55 for bronze.

Afterwards Newnham dedicated her win to her mother, who has been undergoing health issues. “Mum, I love you so much,” she added. “You’re my inspiration this year. Keep fighting – you’ve got this.”

Désiré Doué does the business as PSG edge Aston Villa to lift Super Cup

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 21:07:02 GMT

Uefa Super Cup: Paris Saint-Germain 2-1 Aston Villa

Kvaratskhelia 20, Doué 62; Madjo 45

Luis Enrique says it doesn’t matter what sport he is playing – football, tennis, padel or parchis, a board game – he wants to win every game, all the time. In Paris Saint-Germain, he has built a winning machine, the back-to-back Champions League victors maintaining their habit by conquering Aston Villa in an absorbing Super Cup contest in Salzburg. For PSG, after the joy of Munich and Budapest, three months ago, does a three-peat in Madrid in May beckon? They will surely go close.

Aston Villa more than played their part in an enthralling showpiece, Brian Madjo becoming the competition’s youngest scorer after the 17-year-old cancelled out Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener. Villa had chances to gain the lead but Désiré Doué was the match-winner, the forward picking his spot after beating Villa’s offside trap. The goal was initially disallowed but, after a VAR review, Omar Artan, the Somali referee handed the game by Uefa after being denied entry to the US to officiate at the World Cup, awarded it after replays showed Matty Cash played Doué onside.

Before kick-off, the sights and sounds were in effect an extension of Villa’s victory in Istanbul, a party atmosphere raining down from the 6,000-strong Villa following. There were huge cheers when Unai Emery’s face appeared on the big screens in opposite corners after the teams were read aloud and hearty roars for the £38m arrival João Gomes and Madjo, the hulking forward handed his full Villa debut. Madjo’s inclusion felt particularly ominous for Tammy Abraham, the striker signed seven months ago, his £18.3m permanent arrival yet to pay dividends. A claret and blue mosaic formed behind Marco Bizot’s goal as Jeff Beck blared over the speakers. Villa supporters crooned to Erasure and chanted the name of their superb captain, John McGinn.

“We won’t be in our best moment,” Emery said on the eve of the game but his side were almighty fun; some good, some bad, just as he predicted. Only five players from their memorable victory over Freiburg remained in Villa’s XI, though Emi Martínez, Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins are still on holiday. Boubacar Kamara made his first start since sustaining a serious knee injury against Tottenham in January.

Emery could also finally unleash Madjo in a competitive game for the first time since his £10m arrival from Metz in January, Villa winning an appeal at the court of arbitration (Cas) to register him after Fifa prohibited him from playing. Only João Pedro, for Chelsea, had scored more goals in pre-season than Madjo but his equaliser here was on the grandest stage yet after goals against Walsall, Real Sociedad and Indonesia All Stars. Here was Madjo against Willian Pacho and Marquinhos, the PSG captain and one of the most decorated defenders in the world.

Kamara drilled wide in search of the opener but PSG seized the lead on 20 minutes through Kvaratskhelia, who had the summer off with Georgia failing to reach the World Cup. Madjo’s clunky control allowed Vitinha to take hold of the ball and pass the baton on to Désiré Doué. Then Kvaratskhelia took charge, jinking inside Matty Cash and blasting his shot into the top left-hand corner at Bizot’s near post. Kvaratskhelia blew a kiss down the lens of the nearest television camera. Six minutes later, it should have been 2-0 after more Kvaratskhelia brilliance, but PSG could not apply the finishing touch. Nuno Mendes galloped on to Kvaratskhelia’s flipped pass down the left flank but the Portugal defender’s cutback evaded four red and blue shirts.

A couple of minutes later came the first of Madjo’s hat-trick of chances from McGinn’s cunning crosses before the teenager levelled. Madjo glanced at a replay after misdirecting a free header and then overcooked a shot when looking for the far corner after George Hemmings got the better of Achraf Hakimi. Another flunked header followed when McGinn twirled clear of Kvaratskhelia. With the half-time whistle looming, Madjo made amends, dispatching a left-footed volley into the roof of Matvey Safonov’s goal after meeting another brilliant cross from McGinn. As McGinn’s flighted ball flew towards the back post, Pacho clung to Madjo for dear life, but Madjo kept him at arm’s length to ripple the net.

Ousmane Dembélé replaced Maghnes Akliouche, a £43m buy from Monaco, at half-time, leaving PSG only shy of Fabián Ruiz from the starting lineup that overcame Arsenal in Budapest in May; the Spanish World Cup winner later replaced João Neves. But it was Villa who registered the first chance of the second half, McGinn working Safonov after Madjo cleverly spread play. A few minutes later, Neves released Dembélé but the France forward ran out of road, allowing Bizot to intervene.

PSG would regain the lead just after the hour when another pass from Dembélé unlocked Villa’s defence, exposing an imperfect offside line. Dembélé zipped a pass into the right channel and, while Ian Maatsen and Pau Torres raised their hands and Doué’s goal was initially ruled out, semi-automated offside exposed Cash.

Villa still had chances to level. Warren Zaïre-Emery’s extraordinary block prevented Gomes from a near-certain debut goal. Safonov repelled a Hemmings strike and the substitutes Alysson and Abraham almost combined to devastating effect but Abraham did not gamble in the box, much to Emery’s frustration. Perhaps Villa will, as McGinn suggested, prove everybody wrong – again.

The Spy Next Door review – a wild story … once the endless string of men have stopped talking

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 21:00:39 GMT

The gripping case of Russian spy Anna Chapman somehow becomes quite dull in parts of this very male documentary. Thank goodness for the only woman to speak in it – who livens things up ahead of a thrilling ending

In June 2010, Anna Chapman was arrested in New York City as part of a major FBI operation targeting Russian spies. Members of the “illegals programme” had, for decades, ingratiated themselves into American workplaces and communities, all while working for Russia’s foreign intelligence service (SVR). While Chapman was ostensibly in the US to sell real estate to wealthy Russians, she was something of an outlier among the group. The 28-year-old had been in Manhattan for only a year, having spent much of the previous decade in London. There, she had married (and later separated from) a British citizen, Alex Chapman. It was also where she may or may not have been initially recruited as a Russian state asset. Her connections to Britain would, for a while, make Anna Chapman a tabloid mainstay; here we see her ex, Marcus Read, reading an old interview he did with the Mirror, headlined “My crazy six weeks of passion with Russian spy girl Anna Chapman”.

The working title of this two-part documentary was Red Hot Spy: The Anna Chapman Story. Indeed, much is made of how irresistibly alluring and apparently manipulative Chapman was, and the pull of her flame-coloured locks (tabloid infamy also coincided with a dye job). Read met Chapman in Zimbabwe, and she ended up joining him in Brighton for a time, before ditching him at a techno night to embark on a relationship with Alex Chapman. “Here I am, 20-odd years later , still talking about it,” says Read, perhaps wistful, clearly still incredulous. It is, maybe, the first clue that The Spy Next Door doesn’t contain any big new revelations about Chapman (who has returned to Russia and didn’t want to be involved with the programme), but rather is a slick reworking of old news.

Still, it is rather slick. Former US intelligence staff paint a picture of a slippery young spy who managed to blend in with a crowd of freelancers on laptops at her local Starbucks, all while sending sensitive data dumps to her handlers. We also hear from esteemed figures such as Sir Roderic Lyne, British ambassador to Russia between 2000 and 2004, who outlines the wider political context that made the Chapman case – and the broader FBI operation – so charged. From the early 00s, Tony Blair and George Bush – and later Barack Obama – were adopting a canny keep-your-friends-close-and-Putin’s-inner-circle-closer approach to foreign policy. Lyne says: “[the west] said, we no longer consider ourselves as adversaries.” Cue archive footage of Obama and the then-Russian president Dmitry Medvedev gorging on cheeseburgers and Coca-Cola. How times have changed.

Back to Chapman, then, and this woman with “an air of mystique”, as Read puts it. He knew little about her, except that her father had been in the KGB. Ed Foley, an FBI agent, says that Anna “knew exactly what she was doing” when she was in New York. She didn’t seem to have undergone sophisticated training, but she had a talent for social engineering and, he says, “seduction”.

The Bechdel test was the least of Chapman’s problems, but it is a little tiresome to hear an endless string of men (and it is all men, apart from one) talk about her. Foley says that Chapman was “quite literally in bed with some of the top Wall Street financial people, people who had influence in political circles”, adding “you sleep around with anybody … she could’ve been the first lady of New York City”. But where does sex end and spy craft begin?

There is an interesting documentary somewhere in here, but – ironically – it’s not the parts about Chapman that are the most engrossing. The only woman interviewed here is Marina Litvinenko, widow of Alexander, killed in London in 2006. Russia has never admitted killing Litvinenko with a cup of polonium-laced tea but, in 2021, the European court of human rights ruled that it was responsible. What we hear from Litvinenko is brief but impactful, not least when it comes to her view on how Russia would later use Chapman in its propaganda efforts. And, from Litvinenko to Boris Berezovsky – found dead at his home in Ascot in 2013 – via a string of other suspicious deaths on UK soil, there is another, more intriguing set of threads that is mentioned only briefly here (for more, maybe try Patrick Radden Keefe’s nonfiction book London Falling).

The final sting on Chapman is told in tense, exciting fashion, with asides for all the surreal details of course (her ex-husband being advised by the infamous spin doctor Max Clifford, for one). But ultimately this programme is little more than a salacious look at a footnote in spy history. “Red hot” indeed.

The Spy Next Door: The Anna Chapman Story is on Channel 4

Jack Draper: ‘When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again’

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 20:31:15 GMT

Former world No 4 reflects on emotional reaction in Canada and rebuilding after the most difficult period of his career

Those painful images have relentlessly spread to all corners of the internet. Deep in the final set of the first-round match at the Canadian Open against Térence Atmane just over a week ago, 15 months of pent up emotion erupted. Two games from defeat, Draper spent the entire changeover in tears.

This was a devastating and alarming sight. Injuries had already defined so much of Draper’s career, but the uncertainty of trying to recover from a bone bruise injury to his left arm over the past year has been more challenging than anything he has experienced. All of his efforts since last July have been focused on trying to find a way to compete consistently at the highest level again, to no avail.

It was reasonable to wonder if his tears represented the realisation he may never recover, but the 24-year-old was seen on the practice court the following day in Montreal and his name did not shift from the entry list of the Cincinnati Open, where he is a wildcard recipient.

Ahead of Thursday’s first-round match against Martín Landaluce, Draper speaks with admirable vulnerability and optimism about this most difficult period. “I don’t get emotional often,” he says. “There was once I got emotional in practice in May when I had really bad knee tendinitis and my arm was really sore as well. I was in so much pain. I was running and my knee [hurt] and my hitting the balls and my arm was sore.

“Last week came from a place of, I think I had so much to focus on and manage, so much change going on in my tennis. I got to [No]4 in the world through doing the same things, the consistent work, the differences, and then went through this whole process of a lot of setbacks and a lot of struggle.

“That’s taken a lot out of me. But then at the same time, I’m in a position where I’m having to start again. That reality is difficult sometimes.

“The reason I got emotional was that through all the challenges, you can forget who you are on the court. And last week I felt like I couldn’t give any more. I was emotional because I didn’t recognise the player I was out on the court due to my injuries and due to probably the way I’ve been feeling for a long time.

“When you reach rock bottom like that you can come back up again. Since then I’ve practised really well, I’ve had amazing support from the people around me and you get to a point more and more of acceptance. We’ve definitely reached that acceptance phase now.”

Draper has spent the past year desperately trying to find solutions to this injury. After retreating on some of his earlier changes to his racket strings and technique, his retirement from Wimbledon on the eve of the tournament forced him to make even more extreme changes in his attempts to reduce the strain on his arm.

Not only has he returned to a hybrid gut string setup, he is playing with a completely different, more flexible racket. Draper appears to be using a frame from a company other than his sponsor, Dunlop, which he declined to comment on.

“After this long period, my shift has gone away from performance,” he says. “I’m changing my string. I desperately don’t want to. I desperately know it’s hopefully not something that I’m going to have to do moving forwards, but it’s something I have to do for the nature of my injury. Same with the racket.

“It’s a difficult one because I’m a winner. I’m out there, I want to perform. But I have to accept reality, which is that I have to find a way in very uncomfortable circumstances right now. But if that can get me to the end of the year where I’m feeling really good again and my body’s in a great place and my mind’s in a great place, then that’s only going to help me to move completely past this injury. But there is a way out and I’m seeing that on a day-to-day basis.”

A year ago, Draper stood at a career-high ranking of No 4. Now he is ranked No 143 and the stop-and-start nature of his injury struggles mean he is not eligible for protected ranking. “At the very start of my injury, if I was to say to myself: ‘Right, I’m four in the world now, what’s the worst outcome?’ It would probably be where I’ve got to,” he says, smiling. “But there’s a certain peace in that and acceptance because I have to start again. And what a challenge.”

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 19:56:41 GMT

Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland

It was a moment of awe shared by millions across Europe: an eclipse that blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness in which temperatures dropped and birds suddenly went quiet.

Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north, going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out.

The most sought-after experiences were in Greenland, Iceland and Spain along with a small strip of Portugal. It was in parts of these countries that totality – referring to when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – was on offer, drawing millions of local people and thousands of tourists from across the globe into the path of the eclipse.

“It was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen in my life,” Sara García Alonso, a reserve astronaut for the European Space Agency, told broadcaster RTVE. “It gave me goosebumps.”

Standing next to her, the astronaut Pablo Álvarez Fernández nodded in agreement: “It had been described to me so many times, but it was much more beautiful than what I had expected.”

In Iceland, people flocked by air, land and sea to take in the country’s first total solar eclipse in 72 years. Amid concerns that clouds would block the view, a record 31 cruise ships plied the waters off the western part of the country, hoping to secure a top view for about 53,000 passengers and crew.

The sun during a partial solar eclipse and partially obscured by clouds, the International Space Station silhouetted as it transits at roughly five miles per second. Photograph: Nasa Handout/EPA

The sun during a partial solar eclipse and partially obscured by clouds, the International Space Station silhouetted as it transits at roughly five miles per second. Photograph: Nasa Handout/EPA

Keep scrolling

The eclipse-themed activities included a day-long music festival hosted by the Icelandic artist Björk in Víðistaðatún park, offering a DJ-curated backdrop as people took in the eclipse. The 10-hour set list included two minutes set aside for totality, the artist said on social media, while the festival website noted that every ticket included a pair of approved solar eclipse glasses.

Those watching from Iceland included the US space agency, Nasa, which followed the moon’s shadow using a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft while Nasa-funded teams launched balloons to study the atmospheric impact of the sudden darkness and cooling.

Cary Klemm, sensor equipment operator, and pilot John Gustine of Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre pose in front of a WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

Cary Klemm, sensor equipment operator, and pilot John Gustine of Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre pose in front of a WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

Keep scrolling

In Spain, where some of the best views of the total eclipse were expected, the hours leading up to the celestial alignment were filled with frenzied debate about weather forecasts and where best to watch the phenomenon.

More than 450,000 tourists had arrived in the country from as far as Canada and Australia, crisscrossing Spain by train, bus and caravan to stake out the perfect viewing spot.

People wait for a solar eclipse at the beach in A Coruña, Spain Photograph: Lavandeira/EPA

People wait for a solar eclipse at the beach in A Coruña, Spain Photograph: Lavandeira/EPA

Keep scrolling

“Our car was cancelled,” one woman, who had travelled from Brazil with her sister to take in the eclipse, said on social media. After her appeals to hitch a ride to their chosen site were met with no response, they took matters into their own hands. “So we took a three-hour bus, a 20-minute taxi and two-hour hike. Arrived at the location!”

About 10,000 metres above sea level, the Spanish airline Iberia livestreamed the moment when the sun, moon and Earth aligned from a special charter flight. “Some flights take us to new destinations. Others allow us to see the world from a different perspective,” the airline said as it announced the charter flight.

Spanish officials estimated that as many as 6 million people were expected to flock to the path of the eclipse, which stretched about 124 miles (200km) from A Coruña in Spain’s north-west to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca. On Wednesday, just hours before the eclipse, officials reported traffic jams on the major thoroughfares out of Madrid and Barcelona.

Others took their chances in the cities. In Madrid’s Parque del Oeste, hundreds gathered in hopes of catching a good view of the eclipse, cheering as they watched the moon cover the sun – plunging the park into darkness – and gasping as the outer corona left a glowing halo around the moon. Just over a minute later, when daylight returned to the park, the crowd burst into raucous cheers.

It was, in the words of César González, an astronomer and science communicator at the Madrid Planetarium, “a spectacular experience”. He had left Madrid early in the morning to set himself up in a field in northern Spain to watch the eclipse. “Until one goes and experiences it, there’s no way to explain what it is to see an eclipse.”

The moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Arcos de las Salinas, near Teruel, Spain Photograph: Christian Hartmann/Reuters

The moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Arcos de las Salinas, near Teruel, Spain Photograph: Christian Hartmann/Reuters

Keep scrolling

He was able, however, to explain the impact. “In broad daylight, all of a sudden the light dims to a point where you can see the brightest stars in the sky. When totality starts, the temperature drops several degrees. If you’re in a field and surrounded by animals, their behaviour often changes. The birds stop singing because they think it’s nightfall. And all of this lasts for a few minutes – in this case around 1 minute and 45 seconds.”

In Spain, most eclipse watchers were heading to rural areas, filling often quiet villages and towns clogged with skygazing tourists. The eclipse had helped put some parts of “empty Spain” on the map; this week people linked to Nasa turn up in northern Spain’s Villalibado to set up a live broadcast for millions of people around the world, breathing new life into a municipality whose last two residents left in 1998.

Throughout human history, eclipses have sparked amazement, fear and reverence. In villages and cities across Europe, the eclipse forged ad hoc communities, as people came together to witness one of nature’s great wonders.

In Camberwell, south London, an impromptu crowd of all ages gathered in Brunswick Park to experiment with different methods of seeing the eclipse, which reached 92% totality. Some held up colanders, others a spatula with holes, still others makeshift pinhole cameras made of old candy boxes.

Ludmila, a Ukrainian woman in her 70s, said she had worked at an observatory in Crimea for 30 years. “What a surprise to find an actual refractor,” she said, pointing to a telescope with a solar filter taped on the end brought out by a resident. “It’s like a wonderful gift.”

Later, as the eclipse passed its zenith and the sun began to set for real, dozens of neighbours who had never previously spoken to each other stayed on picnic blankets to drink beer and swap photos.

Double murderer and rapist Simon Levy sentenced to whole-life tariff

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 19:46:32 GMT

Errors by police and prosecutors after first murder had left serial sex offender free to kill again

Simon Levy, the prolific sexual predator left free by police and prosecution errors to murder two women, will never leave prison after being sentenced to a rare whole-life tariff.

Judge Lucraft KC said Levy, 40, “ruthlessly” exploited women for his sexual pleasure, and had a proven history of sexual offending dating back to 2018.

Levy will be one of a group of just 76 people currently confined to jail for the rest of their lives.

Police have admitted that it is likely his second murder victim could have been saved were it not for errors by officers and the prosecution service.

The sentencing was watched by the families of his murder victims, Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, killed in south-east London in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins, murdered five months later in Tottenham, north London. Wilkins was murdered just a day short of her 40th birthday and had 83 marks on her body.

Levy was also convicted of attacking and raping another woman, aged 35, in Tottenham in January 2025, known as “ED” to protect her anonymity. She survived and gave damning testimony of how she was beaten, suffocated and raped.

Levy, from Tottenham in north London, was on bail as a suspect for the first murder when he committed the second, after police said they lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.

Before the killings he already had an extensive history of sexual offending and was on the sex offender register, having been jailed in 2021 for two sexual assaults.

Sentencing Levy at the Old Bailey on Wednesday, the judge told him he was “someone who appears to have a morbid fascination with sex, rape and crime”. Lucraft added: “You will be in prison for life.”

Months before the first killing, British Transport Police arrested Levy for sexual assaulting women on trains but made errors that delayed charging him, leaving him free.

In total he carried out 10 attacks on trains in London, many while on bail for the first set of train attacks. He was convicted of those crimes earlier this year.

The prosecutor, Tom Little KC, said Levy’s offending was so severe it deserved a whole-life tariff, and an aggravating feature was that sexual violence was “inextricably interwoven with the killing” of both victims.

The sentencing heard harrowing testimony from the victims’ loved ones that the women were vulnerable because they were sex workers and used drugs, but that they were much loved and central to the lives of their families.

Wilkins’s mother, Mary, said her daughter was a sacrifice to keep others safe: “You have done this before and wouldn’t have stopped. Our Sheryl has ended your chances of hurting anyone else.

“She lost her life to do this, but we truly believe Sheryl has saved countless women from being subjected to your disgusting and horrendous acts. I hope you never walk the streets again as you are a threat to all women.”

Wilkins’s sister, Lindsey Hicks, said: “You, Simon Levy, have destroyed our lives. Sheryl was a beautiful soul … the pain you have put her through is unbearable. I hope you rot in prison for the rest of your life.”

The woman Levy attacked in January 2025 told the court she was a “mum and a classical pianist” from eastern Europe and had been trafficked into the UK and used drugs to deal with the pain.

She said Levy was a “monster” but said she was stronger now, and had vowed to overcome the “humiliation” he had inflicted on her. He had tried to steal her “soul and dignity” as he set on her, she said, and had left her for dead after raping and strangling her. She vowed: “‘I will play music again and smile.”

The woman said that when she first told officers of the attack they “spoke to me like a child”. This was in January 2025, before the other two murders.

The judge and DCI Neil John, of the Met police, said the woman’s bravery was crucial to ensuring Levy was jailed for life. After all the Met’s failings, its murder team had arrested Levy for Wilkins’s murder, then found Levy’s first victim and got a full statement, and also linked him to the first murder, of Valencia-Trujillo.

John said: “I must also commend the victim-survivor who showed considerable bravery and presented vital evidence in court. Her testimony was crucial.”

The judge said: “It takes considerable courage to come to court and to give evidence … she should be commended for doing so.”

Victims groups have described the litany of failings in the Levy case as staggering. Government sources say they have no plans for an independent inquiry into the errors – but they come after other scandals highlighting catastrophic errors by police that led to women being seriously hurt or murdered.

Police errors were a factor in allowing the black cab rapist John Worboys to drug and rape scores of women.

And the murderer and kidnapper of Sarah Everard, Wayne Couzens, had earlier exposed himself repeatedly, but police had taken no action and left him as a serving police officer.

Another Met officer, David Carrick, was able to use his status to intimidate and sexually assault women, while complaint after complaint against him was ignored.

Harriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said: “The catalogue of combined failures in this case provides terrifying evidence that our criminal justice system is in a state of collapse.

“Given the series of catastrophic failures by the Met police on top of an appalling history of police failures … we must conclude that the Met police are not fit for purpose.”

Next year the official Angiolini inquiry, set up after the Couzens scandal, will report and is considering a finding that police are institutionally misogynist.

Met commissioner Sir Mark Rowley, who said in 2023 his officers would take the “terrorism approach to male predatory violence”, said his force had apologised and blamed errors in the wider criminal justice system, and not just by police: “He was repeatedly by the police put before the courts seeking remanding in custody. The police were saying this guy is too dangerous to be on the streets, and between CPS and the courts, they kept bailing him.”

He added: “We need a justice system that helps us rather than keeps putting dangerous people back on the streets when that’s obviously the wrong answer …”

Two Met officers are under investigation by the police watchdog in relation to the case. Levy’s risk assessment was downgraded by the Met in August 2024 from high to medium, in part because he was blind in one eye, believed by detectives to be a reprisal for the rape of another woman.

British Transport Police moved one officer, blamed for the delay in charging Levy for the train attacks, out of investigations, and verbally told off his supervisor, but have not referred themselves to the police watchdog.

Prosecutors admitted bungling efforts to have Levy remanded in custody after the first murder and after he was charged with the train attacks. They failed to provide three court hearings with key information demonstrating the full extent of the danger he posed to women.

A Crown Prosecution Service source said people have and will continue to be disciplined, but refused to give details.

When first arrested for murder, Levy, who lived with his mother and sister, was wearing children’s pyjamas. He needed an appropriate adult present when detectives interviewed him and had dyslexia, autism and learning difficulties. He is believed to have been long-term unemployed.

The Plot review – exploding myths in an hour of gunpowder and treason

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 19:00:36 GMT

Summerhall, EdinburghSet in purgatory, Emma Howlett’s two-hander rethinks the national intrigue with 5 November

Never play with matches is good advice – especially when gunpowder is involved. That the historical figures of Thomas and Robert Wintour begin this two-hander testing each other’s capacity to endure a naked flame suggests they have a high tolerance for risk. It is not clear if there are still explosives lying around, but they should know better.

Not that it matters any more. These two Catholic brothers have sussed they must be in purgatory, their plot to blow up parliament having been foiled. Their accounts of what happened next are fuzzy, but they both remember being sentenced to death. They are not happy about their fate, but feel even more sympathy for the mercenary stooge known as Guy Fawkes, who has had to carry the can.

Fawkes has become part of England’s self-mythology. That is one of the threads of the gunpowder plot that intrigues writer-director Emma Howlett most: beyond the simplified myth that justifies today’s 5 November fireworks, she finds a slippery pattern of power play, double dealing and political spin that implicates almost everyone except Fawkes himself.

The intrigue spread through society. Alive to a good story and sensitive to the interests of James I, Shakespeare almost certainly channelled the events of 1605 into Macbeth, with its lesson about what happens to those who try to usurp a king.

All these knotty machinations feed into the TheatreGoose production, as Sophie Kean and Abby McCann put on doublet and hose to tell this very male story. They do so with much energy, but are burdened by the formality of Howlett’s vaguely period text. They declaim the dialogue where it calls for subtlety and fail to match the physical invention and lightness of touch of last year’s Aether. There is an engaging drama in here somewhere – but as it is, this feels more of a history lesson.

Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 18:46:30 GMT

Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violence

The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.

Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.

On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.

A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”

Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.

The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.

On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.

But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.

The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.

Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

Organisers says new rule will ensure contest provides ‘safe and welcoming environment’ for participants

Broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the Eurovision song contest if their state is involved in an “armed conflict” or “sensitive geopolitical situation”.

Eurovision is traditionally hosted by the previous year’s winner’s broadcaster, with next year’s show due to take place in Bulgaria after the singer Dara’s victory for the country in May.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises Eurovision, said it had changed the rules after feedback from participating broadcasters. It said the new rules would provide greater clarity for artists and production staff and ensure the contest provided a “safe and welcoming environment”.

Eurovision has faced protests in recent years over the participation of Israel, a competitor since 1973. Five longtime participants – Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia – boycotted this year’s competition in Vienna after organisers declined to exclude Israel over its conduct in the war against Hamas in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.

It is unclear if or when any of the boycotting countries will rejoin the contest. Israel claimed second place in this year’s competition, as it did in 2025.

The Eurovision song contest director, Martin Green, said: “The Eurovision song contest is constantly evolving and our annual review of the rules is an important part of making sure the contest remains fair, transparent and consistent for all those who participate, including the millions who engage with the event globally.

“Guided, as always, by feedback from our members, we have clarified and strengthened several areas for 2027. These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision song contest so special.”

In potentially difficult situations outside armed conflict, the winning country will be assessed by an independent security body to help the EBU determine whether or not it could safely host.

If the winning member is ruled ineligible, the EBU will identify an alternative host broadcaster to “assume all rights, obligations and liabilities associated with hosting the contest”, and it will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member.

The 2023 Eurovision song contest was held in Liverpool after Ukraine’s win the previous year. At the time, the EBU said Russia’s war made it impossible to begin the 12 months of preparation needed to organise the show.

The new rule changes also increase the minimum age for artists from 16 to 18.

According to organisers, the 2026 Eurovision final was watched by 130 million viewers around the world, down from 160 million in 2025.

Despite the blows to Eurovision’s finances and viewership from the boycott, the contest is set for expansion, with a spin-off Eurovision song contest Asia due to take place in Bangkok in November.

Last month it was announced that Canada would ​join the main contest, becoming the first new ⁠participant since Australia in 2015.

Participation is not limited to countries in geographic Europe and instead is open to all members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which Canada recently joined. Australia is an associate member.
