Trump administration pulls support for annual Arctic environmental report

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 18:17:51 GMT

Move by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is latest government rollback of climate science activity

The Trump administration has pulled its support for an annual report on the environmental changes across the Arctic, a region that is already heating up four times faster than the global average due to the climate crisis.

On Tuesday, Kim Doster, the communications director of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), said the federal agency was withdrawing its support for the Arctic Report Card, which has provided environmental updates on the region to scientists and the public since 2006.

Without explaining why the government stopped its support, Doster told the New York Times: “Coordination of the 2026 Arctic Report Card will not be facilitated through NOAA … All data historically contributed by NOAA to the product will continue to be collected and will remain publicly available.”

Doster told the outlet that other Noaa programs would continue to support research in the region that contributes to “national security, weather prediction, safety of navigation and the economic vitality of coastal communities”.

The Guardian has approached Noaa for additional comment.

Over the last 20 years, the peer-reviewed report has tracked crucial changes across the Arctic’s atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere and tundra. The climate crisis has made the Arctic the world’s fastest-warming region. In recent years, the region has experienced severe sea ice decline, carbon sink reversals and ecosystem upheavals.

In the 2025 Arctic Report Card, scientists found that surface temperatures across the Arctic from October 2024 through September 2025 were the warmest recorded since 1900. It also found that in March 2025, Arctic winter sea ice reached the lowest annual maximum extent in the 47-year satellite record.

Meanwhile, on land, the report noted that ongoing glacier loss contributes to steadily rising global sea levels, threatening Arctic communities’ water supplies, driving destructive floods, and increasing landslide and tsunami hazards.

It also found that in more than 200 Arctic Alaska watersheds – large land areas where rain and melted snow drain northward into the Arctic Ocean – iron and other elements released by thawing permafrost have turned rivers and streams orange in the last 10 years. The “rusting rivers” have in turn increased acidity while elevated levels of toxic metals have degraded water quality, in turn affecting aquatic habits, rural drinking water supplies and subsistence fishing.

Rick Thoman, the lead editor for this year’s report, said: “We are scrambling to pull the pieces together. I am optimistic that we can find a path forward for 2027 and beyond. Given the late date, whether we can pull it together for 2026 is an open question, but we’re trying to make it happen.”

Meanwhile, Twila Moon, one of the report’s editors and a scientist at the Colorado-based National Snow and Ice Data Center, said: “The US is an Arctic nation. It’s not just a distant place. It’s also our national place. So many of the changes there have impacts that reach down into our mid-latitudes, even further south.”

Moon added: “Even if we’re able to move the Arctic Report Card forward in a way that brings information to people, there’s still a real loss in this not being a US federal effort. That’s a real stepping back of US leadership in the science arena, in the environmental intelligence arena, and that kind of has a whole other flavor of harm as well.”

Rick Spinrad, the former Noaa administrator under Joe Biden, called the decision “really unconscionable”.

“It provides the baseline of what’s happening in the Arctic,” Spinrad said, referring to the report. “Then in terms of value for future planning, you can imagine anybody who’s dependent on Alaskan infrastructure – for example, like the oil pipeline, or the fishing community, or local communities that are worried about changes in weather conditions that are going to affect frost heaves on their roads,” he added, highlighting municipalities like Anchorage and Fairbanks.

“Now we will not have that tool, and it will be up to them to try to ferret out where the data are, and then to find somebody who can do the analysis to tell them what the trends have been and what they can expect in the future.

“It’s not clear to me why the administration made this decision. I can only infer that it’s tied to their aversion to anything associated with having a better understanding of climate change,” Spinrad added.

The funding cancellation is the Trump administration’s latest move to impede government-led studies on the climate crisis and its global effects.

Since retaking office last January, the Trump administration has stripped away support for scientific research that mentions “climate”, dismantled a key climate research center in Colorado in a move that the governor, Jared Polis, warned would put “public safety at risk”, attempted to scrap a $368m crucial deep-sea observation system, as well as removing key climate change reports from government websites.

Other federally led environmental rollbacks include Noaa’s decision to stop tracking the costs of climate crisis-fueled disasters, as well as the dismissal of all contributors to the US government’s flagship report on climate crisis preparedness.

Myanmar’s ousted ambassador to the UK has gone on trial on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after being unceremoniously locked out of the embassy in 2021.

Shortly after Myanmar’s military seized power in 2021, triggering mass protests that spiralled into a civil war, Kyaw Zwar Minn was locked out of the embassy for declaring his loyalty to the deposed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

On Wednesday he appeared in a London court charged with trespassing at a diplomatic residence between May 2021 and November 2024. Kyaw Zwar Minn, who still lives at the ambassador’s residence in north-west London, has pleaded not guilty.

The former ambassador argues that the current president, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who plunged Myanmar into conflict and economic chaos, is illegitimate and had no power to ask him to leave the property.

Min Aung Hlaing’s pro-military party won a landslide victory in elections earlier this year that have been widely condemned as a sham. Min Aung Hlaing is wanted by the international criminal court for crimes against humanity against the Muslim Rohingya minority.

Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer, David Perry, told the court: “The military authorities could not lawfully terminate his licence at the address. Nor could they legitimately use the property.”

Prosecutors said Myanmar’s authorities instructed the former ambassador to “hand over state-owned properties” in April 2021, and that the Foreign Office also told him to leave the residence, but he did not comply.

They argue that his view of the Myanmar government – which is not formally recognised by most democratic countries, including Britain – does not provide a defence.

“Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed from that position means that he is guilty of the offence of diplomatic trespass,” the prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court.

Kyaw Zwar Minn previously told the Guardian he spent a night in his car outside the embassy in April 2021 after his then deputy, Chit Win, and a military attache, Soe Aung, locked him out of the building on the regime’s orders.

He said at the time that he no longer felt safe at the north London residence and had contacted the police after former staff delivered a letter ordering him to move. Friends and relatives in Myanmar had been forced into hiding fearing reprisals as a result of his stance, he said.

He anticipated in 2021 that the crisis would lead to civil war. “You can see the military government is not going to step back,” he said. “More people will die and the economy is going to collapse. Then anything can happen in our country.”

Greenland authorities have forced a US oil company connected to Donald Trump to postpone drilling wells in the Arctic territory, defying claims by the US president’s envoy that Americans could be extracting crude by next year.

Amid Trump’s imperialist threats, tensions have been rising on Greenland’s eastern coast after the oil company brought drilling equipment ashore in July without permission, drawing a “strong warning” from the government.

Just week before Greenland Energy intended to sink its first wells into the tundra, the government said on Thursday: “The necessary regulatory process cannot be completed, and the necessary approvals cannot therefore be obtained before the planned start of drilling.”

It said that during talks Greenlandic officials had expressed concern that the timetable was too tight to assess the environmental and social impact.

The authorities will have to decide whether to sanction drilling in a protected wetland that is home to rare birds and the muskoxen on which local hunters depend. At the earliest, drilling could now commence in the winter of 2027, the government and the company said.

That is a long way off the prediction made as recently as May by Jeff Landry, the hard-right Louisiana governor whom Trump named as his envoy to Greenland. He said after a visit that oil supposedly lying under Greenland could ease the energy crisis caused by the US attack on Iran.

Landry, whose stated goal is to “make Greenland a part of the US”, said: “We could have those barrels on production within 10 months or so.”

Robert Price, the Greenland Energy chief executive, who maintains that oil worth $1tn could lie under the remote Jameson Land region, said: “Greenland Energy remains committed to advancing its oil exploration programme responsibly and in accordance with Greenland’s regulatory process, and in full compliance with Greenlandic authorities.”

Price added: “We will use this time to refine our plans and deepen relationships with local communities, strategic partners and relevant authorities.”

Since a rich friend put the idea of acquiring Greenland in Trump’s head during his first term, the president has threatened to do so by buying it from Denmark, seizing it with military force or cutting a deal.

Shareholders in Greenland Energy had been hoping for a “Trump pump”, a presidential endorsement that could send the New York-listed stock rocketing. But on Wednesday the price fell by more than a third after the drilling delay was announced.

Price had said a ship bringing 300 containers of drilling kit would set sail from Canada for Greenland in September, with a first well to be sunk the following month. He told a community meeting – falsely – that Greenland had granted permission for the company to start landing equipment.

Greenland Energy’s British partner 80 Mile said in an update for investors on Wednesday that the delay was due to the need to “complete the permitting and regulatory approval process”.

80 Mile holds exploration licences granted before Greenland stopped issuing them in 2021, citing the climate crisis.

Greenland Energy, formed last year, has announced plans to spend $60m (£44m) raised from investors to fund drilling in exchange for a majority stake in the project.

Its representatives have said its oil venture is “not related to American annexation”, yet the company has established multiple connections to the Trump administration.

Phil McGraw, better known as the chatshow host Dr Phil, has a deal with Greenland Energy to “capture the mission of these modern-day wildcatters” for a documentary series to be broadcast on television and social media. He recently appeared in the Oval Office alongside Trump, having served on the president’s religious freedom commission.

A US navy veteran who is working on Golden Dome, the missile defence plan for which Trump says controlling Greenland is “vital”, sits on Greenland Energy’s board. And Kenneth Griffin, a Wall Street billionaire who gave $1m towards Trump’s second inauguration, bought 9% of Greenland Energy’s shares in April.

Rod McIllree, 80 Mile’s boss, said: “While we are disappointed that the timing of the Jameson drilling programme has been impacted, the company remains fully committed to advancing this highly prospective project.”

The Guardian view on early prisoner release: don’t lose sight of systemic reform

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 17:40:24 GMT

Empathy is a strength in a prime minister but there is a risk of letting emotional urgency obscure the strategic view in policymaking

There are no votes in leniency for criminals, which is why oppositions demand harsher penalties and ministers acquiesce. It is a policy ratchet that can keep turning as long as there are enough cells to accommodate those who are jailed.

But spending on new prisons, or for that matter improving conditions in the dilapidated, overcrowded ones already in use, is also not a vote-winner. Most people can think of more deserving beneficiaries of public money than prisoners.

There is an argument that everyone in society benefits when incarcerated citizens are humanely treated, more likely to be rehabilitated and less likely to reoffend. It is a rare politician who asserts that view against the clamour for harshness.

As a result of these dynamics, British jails are near capacity. Cutting short custodial sentences is the only way to avert chaos in the system. The last Conservative government knew this when they called the 2024 general election. That didn’t stop them lambasting Sir Keir Starmer when he bowed to the inevitable and approved a wave of early releases. Another round was due in September. That has been pushed back a month by Andy Burnham.

It is understandable that a new prime minister doesn’t want to leap into unpopular actions so soon after taking office. Mr Burnham also has a markedly different style to his predecessor, striving for empathy where Sir Keir tried to make a virtue of unsentimental analysis.

In justice policy, the more empathic way means heeding the concerns of victims of crime and their families, who are naturally distressed by the thought of perpetrators getting off prematurely. In particular, Mr Burnham has signalled amenability to averting the earlier release of two men convicted of the manslaughter of Andrew Harper, a police officer. Mr Harper’s widow has campaigned on the issue, and senior serving officers have signed an open letter lobbying to keep the killers in jail.

The prime minister has tasked his justice secretary, Alex Norris, with finding a way to satisfy those requests. It isn’t straightforward without measures that change the terms of release more widely, such as a provision that none convicted of manslaughter is eligible, for example. Ministers cannot and should not customise rules ad hoc, for individual cases, but broader change starts to undermine the basic utility of a policy intended to free up prison places.

Mr Burnham has already said that rapists and those convicted of some child sexual abuse offences cannot be released early. That is a reasonable line to draw. But wherever the boundary falls, there will be cases that look like unmerited leniency. There will be victims of crime who feel short-changed by the justice system, which is the unavoidable outcome when the system is starved of resources.

There are obvious advantages to emotional literacy in political communication. But the prime minister is at risk of becoming trapped in a cycle of concessions, driven by empathy in individual cases, that limit his room for policy manoeuvre on a more strategic level. Mr Burnham would be better off using his talents as a communicator to advance the argument for a reformed justice system that serves the whole of society. There might not be a lot of votes in it, but prime ministers who prioritise the emotional urgency of the moment over practical policy also pay an electoral penalty.

The Guardian view on Japan’s yen: Trump wants to keep the easy-money machine running

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 17:39:46 GMT

A cheap currency helps finance the US tech boom. Washington is intervening because allies matter only when they are useful

Japan’s yen has slid back towards 160 to the dollar, despite last month’s extraordinary US-Japanese intervention. Traders are betting that its role as a cheap funding pipeline for global finance will continue. Earlier this month the Trump administration stepped in to help Tokyo stabilise its currency. “Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor,” Donald Trump explained. More help is likely to be on its way.

But this is less a rescue of the yen than an attempt by Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, to preserve a cash spigot that benefits the US. Japan’s ultra-cheap money has become a global funding utility: bankers borrow yen, sell them for dollars and buy higher-returning US assets, notably tech shares. Rising American stock markets support collateral and investment. Japan’s “carry trade” is one of the reasons Wall Street can lever hundreds of billions into AI. Research suggests AI sucks up more than 1% of US GDP.

Washington wants to keep this tap open, but not at the cost of a collapsing yen or US treasury sales. This column predicted this in April, warning that Tokyo’s monetary choices had bound US markets to the yen trade. What Mr Bessent did was to sell at least $10bn in euros and buy yen to arrest its slide to a 40-year low. Not telling the Europeans said it all: allies matter to Washington only when they are useful.

Traders are probing US resolve. Rising oil prices, driven by US-Iran tensions, stoke Japan’s inflation and weaken the yen. Suppose it slides back to 164 yen to the dollar? Tokyo might respond with aggressive rate rises. This would be unlikely, as it would choke off the investment cycle that Japan is trying to create. It could also trigger a chaotic market unwind: higher rates shrink the gap between investors’ returns and yen borrowing; a stronger yen also makes yen‑denominated debts costlier to repay; investors then sell US assets to buy the yen needed to close their positions. That strengthens the yen further, inflicting bigger losses and forcing more US asset sales. A currency correction could quickly become a Wall Street rout.

If Mr Bessent dislikes that option, he hates the alternative: Japan selling its $1.1tn treasury pile to buy yen. Dumping US debt would drive yields higher – and leave Washington with a costlier interest bill. Instead, Mr Bessent has allowed Japan to borrow dollars against its treasuries and use those dollars to buy yen. He has used a Federal Reserve lending facility to help – and wants its current $60bn daily limit substantially increased. This would give Tokyo room to stabilise the yen without having to choose between abandoning its reflationary programme and selling treasuries.

If Mr Bessent gets his way, the Fed could turn a substantial portion of Japan’s trillion-dollar hoard of US government securities into cash. Argentina showed Mr Bessent would put American firepower behind currencies, spending billions to prop up the peso. Japan is the bigger challenge. He is asking traders: are you sure that you want to return to 164 yen to the dollar? He has form as a currency trader. Mr Bessent made George Soros a billion dollars in 1992 by selling pounds and forcing sterling from the European exchange rate mechanism. In 2013, Mr Bessent helped George Soros make another billion dollars betting against the Japanese currency. Margaret Thatcher famously said that “you can’t buck the market”. Mr Bessent is saying you can – as long you rewrite its rules.

Politicians among mourners at funeral service for Ann Widdecombe

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 17:21:06 GMT

Family, friends and colleagues attend service at Buckfast Abbey, which former MP described as her ‘safe haven’

About 100 family, friends and colleagues of Ann Widdecombe have attended a funeral service for the former Conservative minister, who was killed in her home in Devon last month.

Politicians and broadcasters were among the mourners at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh, a Catholic abbey in Devon where Widdecombe regularly worshipped and which she described as her “safe haven”.

A 90-minute requiem mass – where prayers are offered for the soul of the dead – was held for the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson.

Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs could be seen searching the grounds.

Widdecombe died on 8 July, aged 78, after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor. Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder on 20 July.

It is understood that Reform leader, Nigel Farage, did not attend the funeral because he did not wish to be a distraction. He is expected to attend a public memorial planned for later this year.

Those slated to attend included the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, the former Conservative justice minister Crispin Blunt and the broadcaster Iain Dale.

The private mass featured a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, the abbot of Buckfast. He said: “In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this abbey church, which Ann called her safe haven.”

An earlier statement from the abbey said: “Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics. Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant.”

The order of service showed tributes would be paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe’s nephew, and Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

Donations made in her memory will be divided between the Leprosy Mission and Abound, supporting the projects of the Christian Endeavour Hostel in India.

Widdecombe was first elected as a Conservative MP for Maidstone in 1987 and became a prisons minister in the 1990s. She later became a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party. At the time of her death she was a spokesperson on immigration and justice for Reform UK. She had also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing and Celebrity Big Brother.

How the Other Half Loves review – Alan Ayckbourn’s ingenious farce brings the houses down

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 17:00:34 GMT

The Old Vic, London The suburban romp of envy and infidelity in two different homes comes bouncing back to life with a fizzing cast led by Roger Allam

Early in a career that reaches 92 plays with The Trial of Romeo Oscar at his Scarborough home base next month, Alan Ayckbourn often spins titles from expressions: Absurd Person Singular, Relatively Speaking, Joking Apart and How the Other Half Loves, his ninth play.

In How the Other Half Loves (1969), the pun is doubled. Two couples – the Phillipses and Featherstones – envy how the well-to-do Fosters, boss Frank and wife Fiona, live. But structurally, the Phillipses and Fosters occupy half the set each, actors blanking out characters in the other house even while making phone calls to each other side by side. In the second scene, when the Featherstones – unwittingly used as adultery alibis by Mr Phillips and Mrs Foster – simultaneously attend dinner parties on consecutive nights with the other couples, the two actors in both scenes swivel their heads at tables laid across each other.

Tying with the middle act of Michael Frayn’s Noises Off as the most ingeniously crafted and reliably hilarious half hour in English farce, it started Ayckbourn’s experiments in theatrical time and space, leading to audiences seeing a cross-section of three apartments in The Things We Do for Love (1997), and House & Garden (1999) occupying two theatres simultaneously.

While the geometric cleverness in How the Other Half Loves remains fresh, other aspects date: men can’t make their own breakfast, have their clothes laid out for them by (further wordplay) “the other half” and offices were completely male. The domestic honorific “dear” has been cut. However, Ayckbourn’s policy of allowing every actor a big moment gives the wives more agency than much 1970s comedy. Even Mrs Featherstone, nicknamed “Mouse”, finally roars.

Director Philip Breen sensibly treats it as a period drama, with 1969 hits including The Boxer and Where Do You Go to My Lovely? covering scene changes. Rob Howell’s sets and costumes delight in an era where transistor radios, Trimphones and egg nog were exotic novelties, as time again has made them.

The cast of six, though, is more than half the joy, their verbal and physical humour stopping the show as surely as big numbers in musicals. Roger Allam’s Frank, managerial pomposity concealing kindness, has a magnificent scene as a hapless marital Poirot, wildly mis-summarising who was in which room with whom when. Laura Elsworthy’s Mary wins a big laugh via a feat of backstage athleticism. Ayesha Antoine’s Teresa shows how spirited acting can update an older play’s social attitudes. Ayckbourn followed this with (so far) 83 more plays but his early work can still deliver two great halves and, this London summer, a tempting sex farce double bill with Florian Zeller’s The Truth.

At the Old Vic, London, until 19 September

Breakfast, lunch and natmad in Denmark – Scandinavian mealtimes explained

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:28:56 GMT

Gary Calder on the differences in names for mealtimes in Scandinavia. Plus Dr Paul Brown on the class division in dinnertimes on the Titanic

Confusion over the names of mealtimes (Letters, 2 August) also reigns in Scandinavia. Breakfast in Norway/Sweden is frokost/frukost, but morgenmad (morning food) in Denmark. Lunch in Norway/Sweden is lunsj/lunch, but frokost in Denmark. At least they can all agree on the main meal of the day, which is middag (midday/noon) but served in the early evening.

If attending a wedding party or function in Denmark, don’t be surprised to be served natmad (night food) around midnight. It is used as a friendly indication that the event has come to an end, hence its colloquial name of skrub af mad (fuck-off food). Gary CalderChandler’s Ford, Hampshire

On the Titanic, dinner for first- and second-class passengers was the meal served in the evening. For third-class passengers the meal called dinner was served in the middle of the day; later in the day they had tea and supper. Interestingly, there was no iceberg lettuce on the menus. Dr Paul BrownWest Bridgford, Nottinghamshire

Jason Arday and the lack of oversight and quality control of academics

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:28:41 GMT

An Oxford academic says teaching and teamwork matter just as much as a CV full of impressive research output

The Jason Arday case is in danger of becoming a red herring when it comes to quality control of university appointments. An anonymous letter-writer (7 August) commented that Arday “is well known for the kindness he promotes” – a rare exception within a slew of commentary that has had nothing to say about Arday’s actual job performance. As an academic at Oxford University, I would say that underqualified appointees are significantly less common or problematic than those whose research output is excellent but who, nonetheless, devote little energy to teaching, are administratively indolent, and/or lack a collegiate sensibility.

There are two main reasons for this. One is that appointment panels are excessively preoccupied by impressive publication records, and pay too little attention to applicants’ willingness to put time and energy into teaching, and to engage empathetically and constructively with both colleagues and institutional systems. Too often bad appointments occur because of, not despite, the “rigour” of our processes.

Second, oversight and quality control of academics once they have been appointed is often almost nonexistent. “Dead weight” appointees get worked around, not challenged; and performance reviews at the end of probationary periods are routinely conducted without meaningful consultation with the colleagues and students that they work with. Sometimes this occurs because senior management are too far removed from the day-to-day realities of academic life, or it stems from a misguided view that research productivity is difficult, whereas the bread-and-butter of teaching and teamwork is easy.

Of course, serious consequences must follow from exaggerating one’s credentials in order to gain promotion. However, although I do not know Jason Arday, it’s a good bet that, from a teaching and teamwork perspective, his (and my) university have made far worse appointments in recent years that have entirely escaped both internal scrutiny and external headlines. From a Gavin and Stacey star to Dani Dyer’s return: every Strictly Come Dancing 2026 contestant rated

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:16:13 GMT

The wait is over. From soap stars to athletes and Kim Kardashian’s hairdresser, we’ve rated this year’s celebrity hoofers in terms of likely glitterball success

No Tessbot. No Clauditorium. Three new presenters, five new professionals and a new-look “vodcast” It Takes Two sister show. Yes, the fast-approaching 24th series represents Strictly Come Dancing’s biggest ever shake-up. This has become a make-or-break year for the BBC’s ballroom behemoth.

Lineup announcements have been strung out over two months, like a boring byelection, but the Strictly class of 2026 is finally complete. There are the usual grumbles about a lack of household names, with theories that the casting department prioritised social media followings over mainstream fame. My personal feeling is they have smashed it with the women, who comfortably overshadow the far weaker lineup of men. This raises the pleasing possibility of the first back-to-back female champions since Abbey Clancy and Caroline Flack more than a decade ago.

So who will be getting double-dipped in orange emulsion and rolled in glitter on autumnal Saturday nights? Whose mantelpiece could be graced by the glitterball trophy? And who’ll be sent home before we’ve even bothered to learn their name? We’ve rated this year’s celebrity hoofers from worst to best in terms of likely sparkly success. Staaaaaart ranking …

He’s a “football influencer”, apparently. A job I didn’t know existed until I started typing this. It says here that the YouTuber is “one of Britain’s biggest sports content creators” with a whopping 20 million followers across social media. The Northern Irishman has never danced before, so should be choreographic cannon fodder. Shame it wasn’t John Nettles. He could’ve foxtrotted to the Bergerac and Midsomer Murders theme tunes.

Will he perform a pekingese waltz, a King Charleston spaniel or a chihuahua cha-cha? Will he be terrier-ble or could he make it to Blackpoodle? Going from house training to dance training is canine cult hero Graeme “the Dogfather” Hall, presenter of Channel 5’s Dog’s Behaving (Very) Badly. Not the most glamorous piece of casting, perhaps, but at least it allows all manner of hound-based hilarity. Let him off the leash and go for rumba walkies. Good boy.

What’s the betting they tried his dad, Ian Wright, first? Strictly got its first ever footballing winner last year in Karen Carney, but former England winger Wright-Phillips will do well to make the away fixture at Blackpool. He’s a pint-sized 5ft 5in, so expect short king Shauny to be paired with one of the pocket rocket female pros, such as Jowita Przystał. Shame Tess is no longer around to say “look at their little faces”.

“Kim Kardashian’s hairdresser” is stretching the definition of “celebrity” to snapping point. Who next? Jane McDonald’s chiropodist? Olly Murs’ dental hygienist? The bloke who does Christopher Biggins’ gutters? The Leicester-born coiffure-wrangler’s other clients include Ariana Grande, Katy Perry and J-Lo. A factor in his casting is surely the hope of seeing a Kardashian in the studio audience. We imagine he’ll be pretty good. And possibly give his pro partner a glow-up. Going anywhere nice on your holidays, hun?

What’s occurrin’? Stopping off at Elstree en route to Billericay will be the actor best known as Gwen from Gavin & Stacey. The Barry-based matriarch is constantly making omelettes in the Anglo-Welsh romcom. That extra protein could come in handy on long training days. At 64, she’s the oldest contestant in the field, but Walters teaches pilates, so is fit and flexible. Stacey’s mum has got it going on. Just ask Dave Coaches. Hey, maybe we’ll finally find out what happened between Uncle Bryn and his nephew Jason on that fateful fishing trip. Lush and tidy indeed.

His Big Brother co-host AJ Odudu reached the final five years ago. Can Will Best follow in her twinkle-toed footsteps? He recently won Celebrity Mastermind with the specialist subject of Danny Dyer, so will be embarrassingly excited to dance alongside Dyer’s daughter. He’s fit, funny and annoyingly multitalented, so could prove a surprise package. He also hosted a flop ITV talent show called Dance Dance Dance, which feels like an omen of … something?

She swims! She cycles! But can she samba? Dame Sarah Storey began her sporting career in the pool, before switching to the velodrome. Her 30 medals, including 19 golds, make her Team GB’s most decorated Paralympian of all time. Having hung up her Lycra onesie this summer, she becomes the first Dame to hit the ballroom floor and the sixth Paralympian. None reached the final but the ever-competitive Storey will have the podium in her sights. What’s the Storey? Glitterball glory?

The field’s other decorated athlete is Team GB skeleton racer Stoecker, who won gold at the recent Winter Olympics in Milano Cortina. She’s clearly a teacher’s pet at the BBC because she’ll also join the next series of Gladiators as “Goldstar”. A former gymnast and circus performer, Stoecker should hit the dancefloor running. Prepare for lifts, tricks and a sled-themed VT with her terrified pro partner.

Goodrem played Nina Tucker in Neighbours before joining the long line of Ramsay Street residents who changed lanes to pop. Erinsborough alumni have mixed fortunes on Strictly. Jason Donovan reached the final, but Stefan Dennis, the flamin’ galah, got an early Qantas flight home last year (other long-haul airlines are available). Non-Brits never win, but Delta could dance into December.

Emmer-males have tasted Strictly success in recent years. Kelvin Fletcher lifted the glitterball trophy in 2019 and Lewis Cope was a quarter-finalist last year. Waltzing out of the Woolpack in their welly-booted footsteps is Glaswegian actor Robb, AKA Mackenzie “Mack” Boyd, part of the Dales soap’s Dingle dynasty. He’s stage school-trained with West End experience, so there could be ringer rumblings. All the Dingle ladies, put your hands up.

Swapping Westeros for Borehamwood is Lady Baela Targaryen from GoT prequel House of the Dragon. Expect sword props, castle themes and gags about the judges being dragons. Antonia has been acting professionally since age 14, went to stage school and is starring in West End musical Hadestown, so we suspect she’ll be a helluva hoofer. Winter is coming and she’ll go far. Surprising precisely nobody, last year’s pre-series injury dropout is back for another go. Dyer Jr married West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen last year, so expect footbantz™ from new host Josh Widdicombe. Like last year, we predict a waltz to Hammers anthem I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles, while her soppy dad gets weepy in the front row. Jog on, you melt.

Get outta my pub! Get into my ballroom! Actor Jamie, daughter of Ray Winstone, is probably best known for her acclaimed portrayal of blond-beehived whirlwind Barbara Windsor in BBC biopic Babs. She later stepped into Windsor’s high heels to play the young Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders flashbacks. Dot, Dr Legg and Ethel’s little Willy would be proud.

WhatsApp ‘drops’, price hikes and queues: scramble for solar eclipse specs

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 16:05:37 GMT

Amid doubling prices and fraying tempers, shoppers hunt for elusive eyewear to prepare for rare eclipse of sun

Europe solar eclipse – latest updates

A secretive WhatsApp group was pinging with notifications throughout Wednesday, letting its members know where in London the latest “drop” would take place.

The group’s focus, rather than being for an illicit substance, was for the much-coveted eclipse glasses, which have prompted a frantic rush on shops before the celestial event.

A near-total solar eclipse will be witnessed by tens of millions of people across western Europe on Wednesday for the first time in more than 25 years, but viewing the phenomenon without special glasses that filter visible, ultraviolet and infrared light can damage the retina.

Queues formed outside corner shops in London in the early hours as hopeful customers waited to get their hands on dwindling supplies of the glasses.

In the weeks leading up to the eclipse, the glasses were selling for about £5, but many corner shops in London that had managed to get hold of last-minute stock were charging double that, making a tidy profit.

Many entrepreneurial people have attempted to cash in. Outside Whitechapel tube station, there was a makeshift stall selling the glasses for £10 a pop. Another person posted on a Reddit thread that they would be outside Camden Town station with a fistful of glasses, at £20 a pair, until they had sold out.

The scramble to buy the glasses caused some tempers to boil over. One corner shop owner appealed to members of a pop-up WhatsApp group to behave themselves.

“We are hearing very bad things about customers and how they are treating the employees and the stores, threatening with bad reviews. Do not drive across the country and then blame the store if they don’t have them.”

Ali Raza, the owner of the AM2PM convenience store in Whitechapel, said he had had to turn people away all day. “On Sunday we had people coming from Surrey, Southend-on-Sea. Yesterday night a lady came from Southampton, and loads of people have come from Birmingham as well. We’re too busy.”

He said he had “already sold 6,000 pairs” on Wednesday. “At 2.30am we had a delivery from Spain and by 9.30am we sold out [of] everything,” he added.

The Royal Greenwich Observatory said it had sold more than 15,000 pairs of glasses in the past month and had now sold out of them.

Exmoor national park had also run out of the glasses. A spokesperson said: “We got to a point where we couldn’t get any more from our supplier in time and we don’t need them again, not until 2081.”

Branches of Sunglass Hut were forced to erect signs saying they did not sell eclipse glasses after being inundated with people searching for them.

Looking at the eclipse without eye protection can permanently damage your eyes. While it is not medically more dangerous to look at the solar eclipse than the sun under normal conditions, the risk is greater because it’s easier to look at the sun when it’s mostly obscured.

Panayiotis Maghsoudlou, a clinical lecturer in ophthalmology at the University of Bristol, said: “Under normal conditions the eye’s protective responses do the work: painful glare, reflex aversion within a second or so, blepharospasm, tearing, and a constricted pupil. Almost nobody can hold fixation on the full disc long enough to reach the photochemical damage threshold.

“During an eclipse, the sky darkens, your pupils widen, and the glare drops enough that staring feels comfortable, so people gaze at the exposed sliver of sun for minutes with a wide-open pupil and no warning discomfort. That’s why eye injuries cluster around eclipses even though the sun itself is unchanged.”

You also may not immediately realise the damage. “The retina does not contain pain receptors. Symptoms generally appear later, as blurred or reduced central vision, a blind spot, distortion of straight lines and altered colour perception,” he said.

After the 1999 eclipse, there were 70 reported cases of visual loss, half of which were reported within two days of the eclipse. Moorfields Eye hospital received 1,600 calls to its eclipse helpline and treated 220 people in its emergency department, while Birmingham Eye hospital received about 300 calls and treated 64 people at its special eclipse clinics.

There have also been concerns about counterfeit glasses, through which it could be dangerous to watch the eclipse.

Kyla Black, Boots Opticians’ director of optical practice, said: “It isn’t worth taking the risk with your eyesight. There are several safe ways to enjoy the eclipse such as wearing certified eclipse glasses that meet the international ISO 12312-2 safety standard.”

Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:46:46 GMT

The body is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light billions of light years from Earth

Astronomers claim to have discovered a new kind of cosmic object, a black hole “star”, which is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light.

The international team made the breakthrough after focusing their attention on a mysterious red spot in images of the early solar system captured by Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.

The object was lurking in the constellation of Cetus, the Whale, billions of light years from Earth. It is thought to have formed 660m years after the big bang, astronomers’ leading theory as to how the universe began.

Measurements of the exotic body found that while it resembles an immense star, it releases 100bn times more energy than any known star can produce. The energy output is far closer to that observed from black holes than stars.

“We have found a new type of astrophysical object, a black hole star,” said Dr Rohan Naidu at the Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, part of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

It “shines with the energy typically associated with black holes, but at the same time bears signatures classically associated with stars”, he added.

The scientists were using the James Webb space telescope to find the most distant galaxies in the known universe. After succeeding with a galaxy named Mom-z14, which formed a mere 280m years after the big bang, they turned their attention to other cosmic objects.

Writing in Nature, the astronomers describe how they focused on an extremely bright red spot known as MoM-BH*-1, the reddest object in the telescope’s image archive.

“The way its light is almost entirely red, and abruptly disappears below a certain wavelength, is so dramatic that there is no comparison among any known class of objects,” Naidu said.

Computer simulations showed that rather than being an enormous star powered by nuclear fusion, the object is a black hole so swaddled in shrouds of dense gas that it radiates like a star.

If the astronomers are correct, it suggests that scores of other mysterious Little Red Dots, or LRDs, that appear in nearly every deep space image from the James Webb space telescope are also black hole stars.

Naidu suspects that black hole stars play a major role in the evolution of galaxies. They might be the seeds of present-day supermassive black holes, such as the one at the centre of the Milky Way.

“For decades we have anticipated something spectacular must be afoot in the very early universe. Black hole stars may be the ‘something spectacular’. They may be the nascent, swaddled phase that marks the beginning of almost every supermassive black hole’s journey,” he said.

Supermassive black holes are found at the centres of almost all galaxies such as the Milky Way and are thought to shape the fate of those galaxies.

“They may govern when stars are able to form and when they cease forming, setting the course for everything that follows from star formation: the birth of planets, the rise of life, the emergence of species that may one day piece together this entire history,” Naidu said.

Military families and Congress members are sounding the alarm about an intensifying mental health crisis onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, as its 5,000 sailors and marines endure a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran.

Two leading specialist military papers, the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, are reporting that there have been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard as poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach the breaking point. The crew is in its ninth month at sea, and has spent 250 days consecutively without making land – a record for an aircraft carrier in modern times.

Worried families vented their anxieties about loved ones onboard the Lincoln at an emotional town hall meeting with navy leaders in San Diego last Thursday, Stars and Stripes reported. One spouse among the 200 or so family members said that her husband had texted her that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”.

The families’ worries were expressed directly to navy leadership, represented at the town hall by the acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, and other top officials.

A woman at the meeting told Cao that the navy had “broken trust between us and the leadership”, the paper reported.

The Navy Times gave details of thwarted suicide attempts onboard the aircraft carrier during the current deployment. Annabelle Loma told the outlet that her husband had tried to jump overboard after his spell at sea kept being extended.

“He’s scared. He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out his 13-year career is ruined, just like that,” she said.

The paper quoted another sailor’s wife whose husband was involved in a separate incident onboard the Lincoln in which he prevented a fellow crew member from jumping, grabbing them and bringing them back on deck.

Mike Levin, a Democratic member of Congress from California, has sounded the alarm over conditions onboard the warship, which is in its fifth month of combat operations against Iran. He described the lot of the crew on X as “moldy showers, broken toilets, laundry down for weeks, long stretches with no hot water, a meal that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas. No soap, deodorant, or toothpaste.”

Jason Crow, a Democratic Congress member from Colorado who is a former army ranger having served in Afghanistan and Iraq, has warned that the strain on service members and their families on the Lincoln is “building week by week”.

The current crunch has been months in the making. The warship left San Diego on 21 November and was originally intended for the Pacific but was redirected to the Middle East once the US-Israel war with Iran began.

Since then, MS Now revealed, the 5,000-plus crew has had only two days on land, in Guam in December and Oman in July. The deployment was scheduled to end in May but has been extended a couple of times amid the ongoing war.

In April, there was a flurry of public criticism about dire conditions onboard the carrier. Photos emerged of poor-quality and rationed food, and there were reports of water shortages, moldy showers and broken laundry machines.

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed the accounts as “more fake news”.

Levin responded to Hegseth’s remark this week. He said: “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”

The Guardian contacted the US navy for its response to reports of attempts to jump overboard. After this article was published, a navy official responded, saying that they were aware that “extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make”.

The official said that the health and wellbeing of every Lincoln sailor was a priority: “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship.”

Religious, medical and mental health professionals were available as part of a “comprehensive support network” that included “onboard deployment-resilience counselors and chaplains”. The official recognised that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but added that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC and healthy meal options”.

The mental health challenges faced by active-duty US navy personnel are well known. A study from last year looked at the unique stress factors faced by sailors on deployments and found the most common included loud noises, lack of rest, and inadequate mental and physical healthcare.

The researchers conducted a survey of deployed sailors and found that almost half complained that they were not receiving adequate help in coping with stress at sea. The study concluded that “given the high rates of military suicide, including within the navy, efforts to improve healthcare access on ships are urgently needed”.

‘Whole and meaningful’: Red Roses coach John Mitchell becomes British citizen

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:26:57 GMT

England ready for revamped WXV tournament

England women’s World Cup-winning coach, John Mitchell, has revealed he became a UK citizen in July after a six-year process. He said it would make representing the country on a sporting stage “very whole and meaningful”. Mitchell, who is from New Zealand and coached the All Blacks at the 2003 men’s World Cup, said he “belted out” the national anthem in his final citizenship test and that his time in English rugby was a motivation in his decision.

“I am very happy to be a British citizen,” he said. “More importantly, I am very happy to be an English citizen because rugby isn’t who I am, it’s what I do, but it does play a big part in my life.

“I think I have had more Tests with England than any other sporting team so that is quite special to me. To be able to represent your country and also be a citizen is meaningful and very whole.”

Mitchell, who joked he would be good in a pub quiz after swotting up on his history for the exam, was a forwards coach for England’s men’s team from 1997-2000 and defence coach under Eddie Jones between 2018 and 2021. He was named in his role with the Red Roses in 2023.

The 62-year-old will lead England in the revamped WXV tournament in September and October. The team will play three games at home against Australia, Canada and New Zealand and travel to Canada and the US.

For Mitchell, this gives England a chance to prepare for the next Rugby World Cup. “We can be very patient around how we go about things,” he said. “Ultimately, you are auditioning for Australia in 2029 because we are definitely going to be travelling some distance. In many ways we are trying to mirror that and understand how important our connections are and play exciting rugby. But it is going to be our connections that are first and foremost the most important thing, before playing exciting rugby.”

Aside from no trophy being up for grabs and more games, the WXV tournament will have a ball trial in force. Players usually compete with a size five ball, but teams will be using a 4.5 ball. The trial comes after World Rugby used the ball at a women’s sevens competition last November.

The England fly-half Zoe Harrison has criticised the decision and Mitchell said: “If we have younger players and we want to keep them in the game and we want to build confidence then I am all for that. It is too early for me to say it is going to help our offloading game or it’s going to help out with passing.

“I am sure there will be consequences as well, there might be more contestable kicking, which is something we probably want to keep away from our game because it is a point of difference between our game and the men’s game. Will passes drop away? Will kicks go as far? All of those things need to be answered.

Burnham to consider ban on disposable barbecues as wildfires rage in UK

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:13:45 GMT

PM to look at imposing restriction on devices in public spaces, though campaigners fear it does not go far enough

The government will look at banning disposable barbecues as wildfires continue to rage across the UK, Andy Burnham has said.

Disposable barbecues have been the cause of a number of serious fires over the last few years, but campaigners were critical of the prime minister’s failure to link those fires more broadly to the climate crisis.

In July this year, firefighters called to Cannock Chase found an area the size of a football field blazing in the summer heat. The heathland in Sherbrook Valley, part of a special area of conservation, was home to adders, toads and other wildlife, which were thought to have suffered severe damage, though no people were harmed. The cause of the fire was identified as a disposable barbecue.

This was one of two fires in the area that were particularly concerning, Staffordshire council officials said, because Cannock Chase is home to protected wildlife, including ground-nesting nightjars. Fires can destroy nests, chicks and vital heathland habitat, causing damage that can take many years to recover from.

Disposable barbecues, which can be carried into public areas, present a number of problems: they remain hot, sometimes for hours, after they are used, making them extremely difficult to dispose of safely, and when they cannot be carried away, people are forced to leave them or place them into bins where they carry on smouldering.

Burying the barbecues, as some try to do, will not stop the danger as these trays of charcoal can reach 450C and will carry on burning underground, where they can still ignite fires long after use. On beaches, the buried coals and metal grills are also a hazard for walkers, and in fields for farm animals.

Over the last few years they have been identified as the cause of a number of serious fires including:

Macclesfield, Cheshire, July 2026: a large woodland fire that was tackled by dozens of firefighters. Cheshire fire and rescue service said a discarded barbecue was the probable cause

Three separate fires in one day around London, July 2026: in Feltham, 6 hectares of heathland close to houses were damaged. The London fire brigade urged people not to use disposable barbecues and to properly extinguish cigarettes after crews tackled three grass fires.

The Trossachs, Scotland, May 2025: covered 2 hectares in the Glen Finglas region of the national park. Glen Finglas is the biggest Woodland Trust site in the UK. The barbecue understood to have sparked that fire was found with a burger still on the grill.

The National Farmers’ Union is now calling for a ban. Although Burnham has said he may consider a ban, government ministers have been set against such measures.

Jon Pearce, the Labour MP for High Peak in Derbyshire, 50 miles from Cannock Chase, has been working on ways to bring forward a partial restriction on the devices in legislation, which would avoid some of the problems of a blanket ban.

He said: “It is hugely welcome that the prime minister has said he will consider imposing a ban on disposable barbecues. He is right that the message needs to go out loud and clear that people should not be using disposable barbecues in public places at this time.

“But we need to be in a better place next summer. Last year was the worst on record for wildfires. This year will surpass it. We need to accept our climate has changed and put in place measures to adapt, and one of those is banning the use of disposable barbecues in public places.”

Portable barbecues could be exempt, he said, as they were taken away after use. “The irony of ‘disposable barbecues’ is that they are actually very difficult to dispose of. They can cause bin fires, and unless you stay around for a long time until it has totally cooled down, there is still a fire risk.”

Other igniters for fire include lightning strikes, carelessly tossed cigarettes, campfires, rubbish and bottles. But it is clear that disposable barbecues pose particular problems. Research for the government published last year found more than 1,600 fires were caused by barbecues in England from 2020 to 2024, though it did not specify whether those barbecues were disposable, and the cause of a majority of the nearly 4,500 fires listed was put down as unknown.

The Greenpeace political campaigner Angharad Hopkinson said: “To truly protect the public, the government must also address the fossil-fuelled elephant in the room that is driving extreme temperatures. The climate crisis is staring us in the face, threatening our national security and straining our resilience to breaking point.

“Burnham has acknowledged the dangers of these conditions by convening Cobra; now he must match that urgency with a real long-term plan to end our reliance on fossil fuels – the ultimate driver of climate change – once and for all.”

‘Always cracking jokes’: questions raised over Jason Arday’s claim he was non-verbal as a child

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 15:00:33 GMT

Fellow pupils at his primary school have challenged Cambridge academic’s story, though others support it

The story of Jason Arday’s extraordinary rise to becoming the youngest black professor in the history of the University of Cambridge is all the more remarkable for one claim: that he did not learn to speak until just shy of his 12th birthday.

This claim was mentioned in a letter announcing his resignation last week, which came amid mounting questions about his academic work and statements he had made about his past.

Arday wrote that becoming a professor at Cambridge was something he “could scarcely have imagined” as an autistic child who was “unable to speak until I was 11 years old”.

His memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, was published by Simon & Schuster in the US on Tuesday and is due to be published in the UK on 27 August. It tells the story of how he joined Cambridge aged 37 despite having been non-verbal throughout his childhood and only learning to read and write aged 18.

But interviews with former schoolmates have produced conflicting accounts of his childhood. Two remember him speaking at primary school, describing a chatty child who loved making jokes, while two others say they did not hear him speak until he reached secondary school.

Jonathan Stewart, 40, told the Guardian he remembered Arday from when they were children growing up in south London. He described him as a good mimic who entertained other pupils by putting on accents and singing songs.

Stewart, a YouTuber who says he was in the year below Arday at Heathbrook primary school in Nine Elms, south-west London, said the academic was known as the class clown. “He was always cracking jokes. He was the comedian guy, he would even put on voices,” claimed Stewart, who said he regularly attended church with Arday.

Stewart said that in the Sunday school minibus that would pick them up, Arday would entertain his peers by singing the jingle from the 90s advert for Baby All Gone dolls. He said Arday, a talented goalkeeper, would bring in his own pair of gloves and dive to save shots, even on the school’s concrete playground.

Another man, 40, who was also in the year below Arday at Heathbrook and asked not to be named, said: “I don’t remember too much about him but I certainly recollect him being able to speak.” Both this man and Stewart said they were in touch with people who had been in Arday’s class.

Arday writes in his memoir that as he approached the age of 12 the local council was on the verge of pulling his speech therapy support because he had made so little progress.

“But miraculously, just a few days shy of my 12th birthday, I spoke. It was at the start of one of my sessions, and Katrina [his speech therapist] had just said: ‘Hello, Jason.’ At that moment, I was fiddling with my hearing aid, which was bothering me, and then I took it out of my ear and said hello back to her.”

Arday said his mother was present to witness the moment, and that beforehand he had “said bits of words and made various noises out of context” but never replied with the correct phrase or at the right time.

Arday denied the accounts provided by Stewart and the second man and organised for the Guardian to be sent statements by two school friends, Nick Clark and Mike Freeman, who said the account in his memoir accurately reflected the boy they remembered at school.

Clark said: “As a boy, I remember Jason not speaking and being regularly removed from class for additional support throughout his time at Heathbrook. I was not in his secondary school, but we joined the same football team at 13, when we became great friends, playing football together ever since.”

Clark’s mother, Caroline Russell-Clark, also sent a statement saying she helped out at Heathbrook for a couple of years when Arday was very young.

“When my son, Nick Clark, was in nursery at Heathbrook, I was asked to help three-year-old Jason, who had serious learning difficulties … I helped him listen to stories and read to him on many occasions,” she said.

“He moved up to reception [class] and the deputy headteacher … asked me in to help support him, and another child. She gave me reading tasks to do with him and also asked me to explain various activities. Jason never spoke to me but he was well behaved and an engaging child.”

Russell-Clark said Arday remained in the same class as her son throughout primary school. “I do not remember him speaking until he was playing in the same football team as my son aged 14/15.”

Freeman said: “I remember him not speaking during our time at Heathbrook primary school. He was regularly taken out of class for his educational needs. His severe special needs didn’t stop him playing football and games with me and others as he was still friendly and could communicate through play and actions.”

Arday resigned from Cambridge last week after being accused of plagiarism in his academic work. Questions were also raised about a long line of claims about his backstory, from endurance running, football exploits and charity fundraising to academic positions, qualifications and authorship. Arday said the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.

Stewart said: “It took someone so long to get in the position that he got into and it’s tarnished. It’s gone and [the black community is] going to be scrutinised more than ever now. I can’t tell my sons: ‘Go look at him as somebody to look up to.’”

Arday claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days, run 600 miles in six days and raised £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions, he revised some of those claims and instead said he was part of a fundraising group that he was unable to name for legal reasons.

He also told the Guardian he had been the target of threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home. Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.

Simon & Schuster, which bought Arday’s memoir for a seven-figure sum, according to the academic, is pressing on with its publication and launch in the UK. The publisher did not respond to requests for comment.

‘Houses with long histories are magical’: David Olusoga on the home history show that’s gripped the UK

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:59:58 GMT

At first, I worried that only historians would find A House Through Time compelling. But its appeal is so enduring that fans of the show stop me in the street to ask when they can watch more

Why is that some TV programmes find an audience, catch people’s imaginations and become not just watched but loved? Most of course do not. Having been making TV since my late 20s and been involved in a number of “first” series that ended up being the only series, I am painfully aware of that. If producers knew in advance which shows would be hits, there would be no flops, as the industry cliche goes.

Producers and presenters are lucky if, during our careers, we get to be involved in a single show that makes that rare transition from being part of the schedule to part of people’s lives. Almost a decade ago, while we were filming the first series of A House Through Time for BBC Two, I was not at all convinced that this was a show that had the potential to break through.

Having studied urban history for my master’s, I always loved the central premise: that we could explore the histories of Britain’s great cities through the people who had lived in a single house, from the very first resident right up to the current owners. Likewise, I was, from the start, enamoured of the astonishing array of human stories which the brilliant teams that worked on the series managed to unearth.

I liked the way the history of the house in that first series, 62 Falkner Street in Liverpool’s Georgian Quarter, perfectly followed the broader history of Liverpool: the city’s rapid rise to wealth and power as the great port of empire, its devastation in the blitz, then a precipitous postwar decline that saw 62 Falkner Street become a warren of slum apartments seemingly doomed for demolition only to be reprieved by the gentrification of the early 21st century.

However, I was concerned that audiences would struggle to understand why we had locked ourselves into the straitjacket of a single house. Why were we viewing the past through such a tiny aperture? What were we missing by being so tightly focused? At times during the scripting and the filming of that first series, I worried that perhaps I was too close to the subject and that only historians of the city would find the show compelling. I was, it turned out, doing what TV producers are infamous for doing. I was underestimating the audience.

This month, almost 10 years after the first series was commissioned, series six of A House Through Time goes to air. We have now made 24 hour-long episodes that have explored the hidden histories of houses in Liverpool, Newcastle, Bristol, Leeds, London, Berlin and now Edinburgh.

Like everyone who presents TV shows, I am regularly stopped on the street by people who recognise me from their screen. Most often what they want to talk about is A House Through Time. Amazingly, that remains the case even after I appeared on the great TV juggernaut of our time: The Celebrity Traitors. The first question I am asked by the fans of A House Through Time is almost always the same: when is the next series coming out? So I am left to wonder why a show about which I had doubts has been such a hit. What had I not appreciated 10 years ago?

What I didn’t get back then, above all, is what old houses mean to the people who live in them. Houses with long histories are magical places. Anyone who has ever lived in such a house has, on a sleepless night or perhaps after too many glasses of wine, found themselves wondering who else had lived out their life in those same rooms. Whose hands once gripped the same banisters; who, like you, knew where the creaky floorboard was and which windows would start rattling on a windy night?

A House Through Time reveals – in incredible detail – the sorts of human stories that would tumble out of our own home if only we had the time to go looking. It reminds us that houses have longer lives than we do. That no matter how many years or decades we live in them, our time there represents a single chapter in their far longer story.

After making 24 hours of A House Through Time, and with the TV industry in a less healthy state than it was a decade ago, I also now appreciate, more than ever, that it is one of those shows that only TV could make.

Only TV – and let’s be more specific, only public service TV – would invest the time and money needed to uncover history at this level of granularity. Only TV would believe that the stories of ordinary people – not kings or presidents or movie stars – could grip audiences of millions. And only TV is capable of assembling teams of specialist researchers, assistant producers, producer/directors, series producers and executive producers with the skills needed to track down the thousands of documents that become the jigsaw pieces that make up the bigger historical puzzle.

In every series, breakthroughs have arrived at the last minute, often in the last weeks of filming, all because an assistant producer or a researcher, digging in the archives and working far beyond the call of duty, has located a missing link or noticed a tiny detail that answers a nagging question or confirms a long-held suspicion.

This new series follows the same pattern but in a new nation. I have long wanted to take A House Through Time to Scotland, and series six is set in an 18th-century house up on Calton Hill in Edinburgh. The Scottish capital was hard to resist. Edinburgh is one of the handful of cities that are not just architecturally but also topographically breathtaking. Built around a castle that sits on top of an extinct volcano, with other volcanic features looming on the horizon, Edinburgh is up there with Cape Town, Hong Kong and Rio de Janeiro when it comes to the sheer drama of its setting.

The architecture of Edinburgh is similarly special. Encircled by city walls, Edinburgh had a scarcity of space that meant the only direction in which to build was up. The result was a vertical city of stone tenements, some rising to 10 or more floors. Edinburgh has been described as a medieval Manhattan. When it comes to urban density and vertical living, it has more in common with Prague and Stockholm than it does with most English cities. Our house, up on Calton Hill, is one of Edinburgh’s smaller tenements – a stolid stone structure built over five floors.

As with the previous series, the life stories of the people who lived in those rooms are diverse and idiosyncratic. Among the earliest tenants was a man at the centre of one of the strangest trials in Edinburgh’s history, having committed a crime so bizarre and infamous that it was depicted in engravings that were sold on the city streets. Another resident took up arms, joining a volunteer regiment during the fraught and divided years after the French revolution, when the elite and the middle classes saw the spectre of revolution in every darkened corner.

One of our Victorian residents was a woman who, more than any of the figures from the past who have appeared in any of the previous series, successfully eluded the efforts of the production team to pin down her story. Why was she so elusive? Perhaps because she converted the house into what Edinburgh police records rather delicately describe as “a house of ill-fame”. Another of our 19th-century residents was a sculptor who created monuments that are still peppered across the Edinburgh cityscape, statues I have been walking past since I was brought to the city as a child in the 1970s.

If there is another reason to explain why A House Through Time has caught on it is that the series plays a small part in a bigger story: the expansion of history. History has for decades been getting bigger and more inclusive. History is no longer just about “great men”. The emergence of social history, working-class history, women’s history and imperial history has uncovered the lives of people once deemed of little interest. The genealogy revolution has made millions of people into amateur historians. Today our ancestors – all of them, no matter how humble their lives – are deemed worthy of study and remembrance.

A House Through Time is on BBC Two on Thursday 13 August at 9pm

From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:34:26 GMT

Rejecting North Sea drilling licences and protecting nature are just some measures Andy Burnham must implement to ready country

From record-smashing temperatures, wildfires, hosepipe bans and thousands of premature deaths, the climate crisis has left its mark across the summer of 2026.

Tackling the root cause – the burning of fossil fuels – and ending the crisis will take years. So will fixing the UK government’s calamitous failure to protect lives and livelihoods against the long-predicted affects of global heating.

But the climate emergency is right here, right now, and here are 10 policies that Andy Burnham’s government should consider announcing urgently.

This would be a vital and confidence-boosting sign that the UK is committed to putting a rocket-booster under the clean, green and very fast-growing economy of the 21st century, not the fossil-fuelled one of the last. It would also give diplomatic weight to the UK as it works internationally to cut emissions and end the climate crisis.

The supposed benefits of approving the North Sea oil and gasfields are mostly fantasy. They will have no impact on UK energy prices – oil and gas are commodities whose price is set by international markets. As the UK Energy Research Council says: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.”

As for jobs, the licences would support very few – again, unlike the growing green economy. Some also argue North Sea production is less carbon intensive than imports, but that ignores the far cleaner record of our main gas importer, Norway, as well as the methane emissions from LNG, and in any case the differences are small compared with CO2 savings of using renewable energy and storage instead of gas.

When people say money is tight, remember the eight biggest oil companies made a staggering $93bn in the three months to the end of June – almost double their profits from the same period last year. At the same time, carbon emissions from the oil and gas these companies produce are driving the escalating climate crisis, and bills for ordinary consumers continue to rise. An increased windfall tax on these excess profits could raise huge sums for government coffers and help pay for emergency adaptation measures.

The UK is predicted to face a shortfall of 5bn litres of water a day – that’s 2,000 Olympic-sized pools of water – by 2055. Grey water recycling or reuse captures water from sinks, showers, baths, washing machines and other “wash water” sources – not toilets – for use in homes. Rainwater capture is another way to make homes more water efficient and reduce the demand for drinking water. Grey water is not safe to drink but reusing it for other activities, such as toilet flushing, can reduce an individual’s water consumption by 50%.

In some water-stressed areas, developers must demonstrate no net increase in water use. But there is no mandate for grey water systems within the government’s future homes standard. The Drinking Water Inspectorate is now moving towards removing these legislative barriers.

The privatised water system has overseen record sewage pollution levels in rivers and seas and presided over a system which critics argue prioritises shareholder dividends, big salaries and bonuses over investing in and maintaining a vital public infrastructure. More than £85bn has gone to shareholders, while the industry has failed to upgrade infrastructure to make it resilient to climate change by building reservoirs, upgrading pipes to stop leaking – a fifth of water running through pipes is lost to leakage – and making sure wastewater treatment plants have capacity for sewage treatment.

With debts of more than £60bn, the industry in many cases is unable to provide the service it is legally bound to – treat wastewater and provide drinking water. Campaigners such as Surfers Against Sewage argue a publicly controlled water industry will remove short-term profit motives, allow access to lower-cost public borrowing for massive capital investments, and enforce a 25- to 50-year resilience strategy across regional catchments rather than the fragmented corporate boundaries that exist now.

Fire brigades in Britain are short of the equipment needed to fight large, unpredictable wildfires. While, for example, Spanish emergency services and the military extensively use specialised amphibious planes and helicopters to scoop up water and dump it on wildfires, the UK does not own any dedicated water-bombing planes. Instead, British fire services rely on ground crews, with occasional military support for heavy lifting, and privately chartered commercial helicopters equipped with suspended buckets to drop water on large wildfires.

During June’s heatwaves, temperatures in some workplaces became unbearable – and dangerous. Teachers reported classrooms reaching well over 40C with children and staff struggling to cope, while bus drivers spoke about the “horrendous” working conditions with temperatures again in excess of 40C in their cabs.
