after newsletter promotion

The Trades Union Congress (TUC) wants a maximum working temperature, a demand recently backed by the government’s advisers on the Climate Change Committee. They want rules to ensure employers take steps to reduce workplace temperatures if they get above 24C and the right for workers to stop work if they reach 30C, or 27C for those doing strenuous jobs.

As heatwaves intensify – and become more dangerous for younger, older and more vulnerable people – having free access to a nearby space that is cool, well-ventilated and comfortable will become increasingly important. Experts say that school halls, libraries or leisure centres are among the buildings that could be reassigned when extreme heat hits. Barcelona has been a pioneer of these climate shelters and now has more than 400 across the city. The idea has now spread across Europe and experts say this summer’s heat shows it is time the UK caught up.

Homes in the UK are among the draughtiest and least energy-efficient in Europe. This means they are often too hot in summer and too cold in winter, leading to high bills and spiralling carbon emissions.

Efforts to persuade the private sector to take on the challenge of making homes fit for the changing climate have failed. But a report earlier this year suggested councils could take the lead on a retrofitting programme backed by national government. Under the plan, councils would train and employ their own retrofitting workforce and, starting with key public services such as hospitals and care homes, then work through council and social housing before moving on to privately owned homes. The report said it would not only make the country’s homes and public services more climate resilient, but it would also tackle the cost of living, create secure jobs and stimulate growth. They added it would also be a more efficient way of spending the public funds already allocated for insulation.

As well as absorbing atmospheric carbon and locking it up for centuries, planting more trees creates shade that can reduce the urban heat island effect. Neighbourhoods with more than 20% urban tree canopy have been found to experience a net cooling effect.

More than four in five homes and workplaces across 25 European cities have less nearby tree canopy than what is needed for meaningful cooling, according to RMIT University. While planting trees today can create cooling in the future, the researchers said a newly planted tree would not shade a building for 15 or 20 years and so conserving our existing trees was essential.

“Every mature tree lost now is irreplaceable on the timeline that matters for current heatwaves,” said lead author, Dr Thami Croeser.

Regenerative farming is an approach to farming that allows the land, soil, water, nutrients and natural assets to regenerate themselves, as opposed to conventional approaches to farming that can deplete these natural resources.

This approach can help crops become more resilient to drought and dry weather. In one study, regenerative management of the soil led to a 23% increase in soil moisture content, and it has been shown to increase yields.

Alastair Chisholm, water, policy, regulation and governance lead at consultancy firm Arup, said current agricultural policies were not driving widespread regenerative approaches, but that changing this would be an easy win to boost food security.

Joe Root has abolished the midnight curfew for his England Test side, telling his players to “be adults” after a string of late-night incidents.

A curfew was imposed on the ­England men’s teams after their Ashes defeat in the winter, when the on-field action was overshadowed by players’ behaviour off it. Most ­notably, there was Harry Brook’s altercation with a nightclub bouncer on the eve of a one-day international in Wellington, with the batter admitting he was fortunate to keep his position as white-ball captain.

Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were suspended for the second Test against New Zealand in June after breaking the curfew while celebrating victory in the series opener. Stokes returned for the series closer before announcing his retirement from international cricket, prompting the return of Root as Test captain.

The Yorkshireman will lead next week against Pakistan, and is embarking on a new era with Stephen Fleming as red-ball head coach. The 35-year-old told the Sky Sports Cricket podcast that the ­curfew has been abolished, arguing: “I don’t think they work.” It is understood the relaxing of rules also applies to the white-ball sides.

“There’s not going to be a curfew,” Root said. “I don’t think this needs to be a big deal. I don’t think they work and if you want guys to take responsibility on the field they’ve got to feel like they can be grown adults off it and make good, strong decisions.

“That’s for us as a team to manage well, and self-police well, for me and [Fleming]. Ultimately, you’re grown adults. You know what it takes to play for England. You know what your responsibilities are off the field.

“ We should be known for how we play our cricket and what we do on the field. We should be on the back page of papers.

“Look after yourselves, look after each other, create a good, strong ­culture where you know when the right time is to celebrate and enjoy a win or to have a sensible beer, and remember you’re playing for England.

Lionel Messi has hinted that the end of his career may be near after ­admitting to “quite a few doubts” about his football future following the death of his father.

Jorge Messi died last week at the age of 68 in Rosario, Argentina, after a long illness, with his health during this summer’s World Cup appearing to take a toll on Argentina’s 39-year-old captain.

In a tribute on Instagram on Wednesday, Messi wrote: “I don’t know what I’m going to do without you. I don’t know how ​to move forward. I only played football and now I have quite a few doubts about whether I’m going to keep doing it for much longer.

“You were by my side from the beginning; there was so little left until the end. Why couldn’t you hold on just a little longer so we could finish it together?”

Messi ​spent time with his ‌father after the tournament, where Argentina were beaten in the final by Spain, before rejoining his club side, Inter Miami, making his Major League Soccer return against Columbus at the start of this month.

Jorge had been a constant presence during his son’s career from his earliest days at Barcelona, with the World Cup the first time he had been absent from a major tournament. Messi revealed that his father, despite his deteriorating condition, had urged him to play for La Albiceleste in their ultimately unsuccessful attempt to defend their title.

“You always asked me to play in the last World Cup and a few days before it started was when you got worse,” he wrote. “It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament … Every time a match ended, I would ‌wait and hope for your message. That’s when I realised how real the situation was.”

After tearfully celebrating the opening goal of his hat-trick against Algeria in the group stage, Messi had explained he was going through “a few difficult, complicated days” because of “something unrelated to football”. he said he ran out of energy in final.

“My legs couldn’t go on any more,” he wrote. “This time I tried to push myself beyond my ​physical limits, but I couldn’t. ​I never felt well … We weren’t champions, ​but you don’t know how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were ​right: I had to ‌be there and play ​it.”

Messi has earned 207 caps for Argentina since making his debut for his country in August 2005. He captained the side to World Cup glory in 2022, matching the achievement of Diego Maradona in 1986, though like Maradona he fell at the final hurdle when attempting to win back-to-back titles.

Too many holes! Why badgers are digging up Britain’s lovingly maintained golf courses

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:04:38 GMT

Thanks to the drought, these black-and-white beauties are struggling to catch worms in the rock-hard earth. But there’s still good foraging on well-watered fairways and greens

Name: Badgers.

Age: European badgers live for five to eight years in the wild. They have been in the UK, where this story is set, for half to three-quarters of a million years.

Appearance: Black and white mustelid anarcho-syndicalists.

Hardly. Badgers are quite posh, aren’t they? Well, perhaps. But everyone has their breaking point, and now I must inform you that badgers have become embroiled in an aggressive form of anti-capitalist class warfare.

What turned them? The cost of living? The rise of the billionaire class? Close, but no. It was the drought.

How so? This has been a historically hot summer in the UK. England and Wales endured the driest July since records began (1836). All the grass is brown and dead. There are wildfires everywhere and 26 million people are living with a hosepipe ban.

It’s awful. Yes, especially for the badgers. Most of their food lives underground, and it’s much harder to get to it when the earth has been baked dry by the sun.

So what’s the solution? That’s easy: turn over a few golf courses.

Are they really into clubhouse sandwiches? Not when there are nice wet lawns to tear up.

Why do golf courses have wet lawns during a drought? The Water Use (Temporary Bans) Order 2010 permits exemptions for watering sports turf. That means that while you are carefully sharing your bathwater, your local golf course is hosing its lush greens.

Yes, but the badgers. Oh, right. Well, if you’re a badger and you need to dig up some worms, and all the ground is hard except for golf courses, where do you think you’re going to get your worms?

From golf courses? That’s right! Jim Croxton, chief executive of the British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association, says: “Badgers generally dig turf to find food and August is the beginning of the period when chafer grubs are generally present.”

Is it a widespread problem? Golf courses from Suffolk to Staffordshire to Worcestershire have reported greens being torn up by badgers, according to the Telegraph.

This sounds like a victimless crime. You would think so, but the golf courses are very upset about it.

How upset? A video of one ripped-up course posted to Facebook prompted the furious comment: “They’re a f*ckin pest, I’ve had countless ornamental lawns wrecked by these f*ckers.”

Quite right. Will nobody think of the ornamental lawns? Exactly. It’s clear that there needs to be an urgent change to the law.

To what? Well, it obviously isn’t fair that golf courses are exempt from the hosepipe ban in a time of national crisis.

But then the badgers would have nowhere to eat, and they would die. No they wouldn’t. Badgers are enterprising creatures. They’d find a way.

Do say: “The badgers have absolutely massacred hole nine.”

Don’t say: “Four legs good, golf clubs bad.”

Why we’re going back to the games of our youth

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 14:00:30 GMT

As millennials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

As much as some people more or less cease to listen to new music in their 30s, I have noticed a retreat to safe, familiar gaming territory among some of my fellow millennial gamers.

Retro collections are started, or resumed; jewel-cases of PS1 classics or cardboard boxes with SNES or Mega Drive games have started to colonise the living-room shelves. People are replaying things from their university days, or sticking to comfort games such as Stardew Valley. Many of the friends I used to game with never bothered to pick up a PlayStation 5 at its launch, and now that current-generation consoles are becoming prohibitively expensive, they see no need. With thousands of great older games, why bother playing something new?

My job, and an insatiable desire for novelty, has kept me in constant contact with new games, but nonetheless, I have been spending a lot of time lately with the titles I played in my youth because people keep remaking them. Lylat Wars (N64, 1997) and Halo: Combat Evolved (Xbox, 2001) have both had summer 2026 glow-ups, in the form of Star Fox on Switch 2 and Halo: Campaign Evolved on the other consoles and PC. These are games I played for many, many hours back in the day, and I remembered them beat for beat (or so I thought – it turns out I did not remember how to navigate the deadly lava planet that ended my first Star Fox run).

I was not enormously enthused by the prospect of either remake, because I’d rather play an original game in either of these series than rehash my rose-tinted recollections from 25 years ago (let’s just gloss over how old that makes us feel, shall we?). But, it turns out all those years have given me a fresh perspective. Both of these remakes are very good. And not just because I played them at the time and remember them fondly, but because each of them does things that new video games don’t. They feel novel, because in 2026, they are.

When was the last time you played an arcadey on-rails space shooter? When was the last time you enjoyed an atmospheric single-player FPS with intelligent computer-controlled enemies? These genres have fallen out of fashion – space games are now wide-open exploreathons such as No Man’s Sky (which celebrates its 10th anniversary this week), and multiplayer shooters have crowded single-player ones out almost entirely. In this context, Star Fox and Halo feel fresh. They’re not awkward transplants from another time.

Neither game really needed all that much massaging. Velan Studios in New York, entrusted with a characterful if visually basic Nintendo 64 shooter, has changed almost nothing about it: we fly through the same webbed map of planets, with the same enemies and bosses, firing off the same simple yet effective lasers and bombs and flight manoeuvres. A Star Fox playthrough takes maybe 60 to 90 minutes and you can play it over and over, like a generous arcade cabinet. In reconstructing the game, Velan has made it look very beautiful, spliced in some new cutscenes and dialogue, and added multiplayer and challenge modes that give some structure to your replays, but quite miraculously, it barely feels different. And it’s great.

Halo: Campaign Evolved deviates more from Bungie’s original space opera. It’s been rebuilt in Unreal Engine 5 with different vehicle handling and more overwrought cutscenes. But the essentials remain: high drama, perfect weaponry, and intelligent enemies that react interestingly to how you play, diving out of the way of fire or ordering a change of tactics. I never minded dying, because each firefight would be different on every playthrough. I still hate the Flood – the mindless zombies that infect the game from the midway point onwards – but despite their unwelcome incursion, I had a blast playing through this game again with my partner. I haven’t played a better co-op multiplayer game than the original Halo in all the years since, which is honestly quite sad.

I have no desire for things to return to the way they were in the late 90s and early 00s; despite its expansion and consequent unwelcome corporatisation as a business, gaming as an art form is far broader and more interesting now than it was then. But these remakes show there are things to be learned from the games of the past, and a lot that is enviable about their design philosophy. Old games don’t necessarily need to be fixed to be appreciated anew. Refreshing them is often enough.

I truly thought I was done with Pokémon Pokopia, having spent 40 hours with it back in March. When I downloaded the new expansion – an underwater area called Bubbly Basin, which turns out to be the ruins of Cerulean City, home to Misty from Pokémon Red/Blue – I did not expect to be consumed by it yet again. The rhythm and purpose of this game is just so comforting: explore, restore, revive. I have enjoyed it so much that I went back to the rest of the game with new enthusiasm for attracting new Pokémon and rebuilding the ruined planet that humans left behind for them.

Available on: Nintendo Switch 2 Estimated playtime: 10+ hours

Rockstar Games will finally show off more of Grand Theft Auto VI on 27 August … via a broadcast on Netflix. Well, that’s new. I can only imagine the £££ exchanged for the few hours of exclusivity that the streaming giant will enjoy.

The Washington Post’s Gene Park spent some time with The Weeknd, who has been documenting his gaming habits on an Instagram alt account – even meeting developers. He wants everyone to know about the horror fishing game he’s currently obsessed with.

Metroid turned 40 at the end of last week – and so did Samus Aran, one of the earliest female protagonists in video games. Maddy Myers writes about her personal heroine.

This week’s question comes from reader Leo:

“My wife and I are big gamers – and we’re having our first kid in September. What should my partner and I play as new parents? Is it even possible?”

I mean, anything is possible if you put your mind to it – my partner played quite a bit of Death Stranding while bouncing around the living room with our second baby strapped to him, in an unlikely case of life imitating art. But it is reasonable to downgrade your expectations for how much time, attention and energy you will have for video games when you have a new baby in the house. When my nine-year-old son was a baby, I wrote this article about how to play games when you’re an exhausted new parent, and though the specific game recommendations are a little out of date, I reckon the advice remains sound. For instance: “Anything even slightly stressful, emotional or difficult might make you cry, so leave the competitive shooters and Dark Souls runs for a while.”

Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 13:16:21 GMT

When I moved to the town in 2022 I loved the beach walks, cheap drinks and panoramic coastal views. Now it feels like a never-ending circus

Clacton town centre is bustling, the beaches are packed and the pier’s raking in cash. We can credit the weather, but no doubt press coverage and Count Binface’s promotional videos have got us on radars too. The tourists look like they’re having a lovely time.

I moved to Clacton in 2022 and the first year was brilliant. It started with beach walks, cheap drinks and decorating a flat with panoramic sea views, and ended fat and happy from chips and ice-cream, a newborn baby in tow. Privileged with my health and stable income, albeit strained by a Truss-era mortgage, it was a place I loved, and was proud of.

Then Nigel Farage targeted us, and shit hit the fan.

With the general election in 2024, the world’s press descended, and then came thousands of social media comments that left me embarrassed, sad and fuming. You’re all thick, racist, gullible, hateful, toothless, jobless old fools, we were told. You deserve him. The worst of the snobbery was, sadly, on my lefty social media platform of choice, Bluesky.

Farage was elected with 46% of a 58% turnout. Fine, some people actually are gullible fools. But the other parties rolled over and failed to bother, treating us with contempt. I didn’t support, but I understood, why 46% voted as they did. I still loved Clacton, but it got harder to defend. Then things died down and we were forgotten again by everyone, including our new MP.

The gag about Farage not knowing where we are isn’t exactly true – he pops by for photo opportunities like a ceremonial mayor – but he seems less keen on surgeries, or representing Clacton in the Commons. Snaps for the local newspaper’s Facebook make fans think he’s doing great things for businesses and charities. It’s smoke and mirrors. Check Hansard for “Clacton” and see how many times he’s raised a Clacton issue in parliament (six times). Then do “Colchester” for Pam Cox and “Ipswich” for Jack Abbott. Compare and contrast.

We wanted him to actually be an MP. To notice the homeless people, freezing all winter in closed bank doorways, and now lining the coastal paths in tents. To notice how we’ve been priced off the railways – the commuter trains are empty. The worsening health, declining life expectancy. The low employment rates and lack of affordable homes. We don’t have an A&E. We don’t have maternity care after 5pm. It would have been nice too, if he’d spent more time doing what he said he would, and what Binface has achieved instead – promoting our towns and villages’ positives. There are many, I promise.

Nobody wanted a byelection. For the many people struggling here, there is little energy for another awful circus. Clacton didn’t need yet more focus on Farage, Farage, Farage, while the area’s entrenched and complex problems continue to be ignored by him and by the government.

This summer, the media presence has been even bigger than in 2024. Content creators and reporters continually vox pop outside Wetherspoons, cherrypicking quotes about how great Nigel is, how persecuted Nigel is. Well, we’re being swarmed with migrants, aren’t we? Getting put up in hotels while we struggle. It’s not like it used to be round here. The Turks, they’re taking over with the barber shops. Or, I don’t really do politics. They’re all the same as each other. A welcome few, it has been pleasing to see, have started to notice the slipperiness, the back of fag packet policies and his absence.

The “Migrants Out” leaflets were pushed into our homes, a turquoise Reform bus did the rounds and sad men with silly hats and placards yelled things in the town square. I’ve seen anti-racism campaigners told to F off, and can’t leave my flat without the smug face of a British Democratic party candidate leering down at me from giant poster boards. It has all felt surreal, hostile, dividing. Generally bad vibes.

The nasty, stereotyping, hurtful comments about us continue. With some exceptions – like Tim Burrows’ thoughtful portrait of Clacton – we’re a human zoo, and the butt of a joke. Farage used us as a pawn, and the media treats us as clickbait.

Yet in shops, the gym, pubs, on the beach, in the street, at the park, at nursery drop off, I’ve not overheard a single conversation about any of it, unless it was between a reporter and a local. Not one. The leaflets started getting left in the hallway, unread. Few of my family or neighbours plan to vote. We’re angry at him, but we are also bored, and exhausted.

My prediction: It’ll be a low turnout, Farage way ahead, with Binface second but the only real winner. I’ll read about how we wasted the chance for a hilarious outcome, you idiots. You gullible, racist fools. You deserve him. And so on. Then it’ll die down again, briefly, and we can get back to what’s left of the summer, the lives Farage has no clue about or interest in and keep talking about the things that really matter in Clacton: litter, landlords, potholes, parking and whether there’ll be a second series of Secret Lives of Gypsy Wives.

Bridget Phillipson condemns Richard Tice’s ‘chilling attempt to silence free press’

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 12:40:23 GMT

Labour chair says Reform deputy leader is trying to harass journalists over reporting on his financial affairs

UK politics live – latest updates

Richard Tice has been accused by Labour’s Bridget Phillipson of mounting a “deeply chilling attempt to silence the free press” after he sent a legal threat to the Guardian over its reporting on his financial affairs.

Lawyers for Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, singled out a Guardian correspondent for her journalism about a series of Tice’s financial transactions that were referred to the National Crime Agency.

Tice is now suing the NCA, claiming that the information could only have come from an officer within the agency.

In a separate letter to the Guardian, Tice’s lawyers made clear they would be seeking disclosure of documents that they believe could reveal the details of sources.

In response, Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said it was an attempt to silence journalism. She said: “Rather than answer serious allegations, Richard Tice is now trying to harass those who have exposed them. The Reform deputy leader should drop this lawsuit [against the NCA] and come clean.

“Trumped-up legal letters targeting honest journalism are very revealing. Reform have zero regard for the cornerstones of British democracy: they’re unpatriotic and pathetic.”

The move was also criticised by the Liberal Democrats, anti-corruption and press freedom campaigners. The Lib Dem Cabinet Office spokesperson, Lisa Smart, said: “Weaponising the legal system to hunt down journalists’ sources is a desperate, bullying tactic. Tice has revealed what we all always knew to be true – Reform’s agenda is completely incompatible with a free and open democracy. They have proven once again that they are entirely unfit for public office.”

Susan Hawley, the director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Using legal threats to strong-arm journalists into disclosing their sources amounts to a deeply concerning attack on press freedom.”

Hawley said Tice would be better served being open about the legitimate questions being asked of him and Reform UK, rather than “trying to discredit those who have reported on them”. “Democracy depends on an independent press, and the government must get serious about introducing safeguards against abusive legal tactics.”

Phil Brickell, the Labour MP and chair of the all-party group on anti-corruption, said Tice had “questions to answer as to how money donated to Reform was reportedly routed through his companies”.

“What we now see is a contemptible campaign by Tice to detract from those public interest questions by threatening hard-working journalists and seeking to uncover their sources. It shows once again that the government must act to ensure that those seeking to expose wrongdoing are protected from the rich and powerful seeking to silence them.”

Tice and Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage, have been under intense scrutiny in recent months because of a continuing investigation by the Guardian into their financial affairs.

Separately, the Sunday Times has also published a series of stories about Reform’s funding.

The Guardian revealed in a series of detailed reports that Reform UK received a secret £1m donation via a fundraising vehicle run by Tice and that Farage received a secret £5m gift shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election.

The Guardian also revealed that these and other transactions were reported by bankers to the NCA over fears they could involve laundered money.

A “suspicious activity report” is not proof of wrongdoing, rather it is an invitation for the agency to examine the transaction to decide whether there are grounds to investigate it further. It is not the same as a crime report.

Farage and Tice have denied any wrongdoing.

Throughout its reports the Guardian has referred to financial industry sources.

Tice has suggested in a document filed at the high court that the Guardian’s award-winning City editor, Anna Isaac, could not have had sources at multiple banks.

In legal correspondence sent directly to Isaac, Tice’s lawyers suggested he was seeking to unmask sources based on his own assessment of the reporter’s work.

Farage has also issued proceedings against the NCA.

Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of the Index on Censorship, said it had the “appearance of an attempt to force a journalist to break the golden rule: that sources must be protected”.

“This has been vital public interest reporting by the Guardian. The sources of such journalism are sacred. If the facts are incorrect, then they can be challenged, but the sources should not be chased down. This appears to be a tactic designed to not only silence journalists but those who talk to them. It is a nasty tactic and we should all be concerned.”

Theo Bamber, the chief executive at the News Media Association, said: “Robust protection for journalists’ sources is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that reporters can scrutinise authority and hold the powerful to account on behalf of the people impacted by their actions and decisions.

“The use of legal threats by an individual or organisation trying to force journalists to disclose their confidential sources is an attack on this important principle, and one that must be resisted at every turn.”

A Guardian News and Media (GNM) spokesperson said: “Richard Tice’s legal threat against the Guardian appears to be a calculated attempt to deflect attention away from legitimate questions about his financial affairs and the funding of Reform UK.

“Instead of providing answers to those questions, he seems intent on intimidating journalists and seeking to expose sources. The Guardian will oppose these attacks on the freedom of the press and will not be deterred from public interest-driven investigations into politicians and the parties they represent.”

Tice and his partner, Isabel Oakeshott, used social media posts on Tuesday night to criticise the Guardian. Tice said: “Lefty journos now bleating as they don’t like tables being turned on them … These lefty journos want war. They’ve got war.”

Last week it emerged that the prominent Reform UK member and Brexit campaigner Arron Banks set private investigators on a Sunday Times journalist after he broke a series of stories about Farage.

Top chefs find grouse in short supply as wildfires add to heat over shoots

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 12:19:57 GMT

As London restaurants say wild birds are smaller and fewer this year, experts say countryside should not be ‘playground for bloodsports’

Every year on 12 August, fans of traditional British cuisine flock to plush restaurants in Mayfair to dine on grouse served with bread sauce and game chips. But those hoping to find the small wild birds, sourced from the UK’s moorlands, may be disappointed.

Wildfires have been raging on moors across the UK, burning habitats and incinerating wildlife, after record-breaking heat turned the landscape into a tinderbox.

The intensive management of grouse moors involves the draining of peatland and the burning of the vegetation that grows on it. Environmental experts argue that doing this creates the conditions for wildfires as dry peat acts as fuel and smoulders for extended periods, making fires almost impossible to extinguish.

Because of this, the Green party in Scotland, where there are a large number of grouse shoots, has called for the Glorious Twelfth – the traditional start of the grouse shooting season, before which time the birds cannot legally be hunted – to be banned. The UK government recently banned the burning of vegetation on deep peat in order to preserve these habitats.

The climate crisis, caused by pollution from burning fossil fuels, makes every heatwave more likely and intense. The heatwave at the end of June was the most severe ever recorded in Europe and would not have been possible without human-caused global heating.

The chef Richard Corrigan, who owns Corrigan’s and Bentley’s in Mayfair, has always served grouse during his multi-decade career running kitchens. But this year they are in short supply.

He said: “I was hoping to get something on the 12th; it’s looking like it’s running a week and a half late. They will be smaller and fewer, which is fine and it is a treat. We should treat them with the respect they deserve. The hot weather hasn’t helped everything this year, that’s for sure.”

Corrigan will be finding it more difficult than some chefs to get birds for the table because he has become more particular about who he buys grouse from. “We now insist [birds] come from small estates rather than the large shoots, where dozens are shot at a time. I am not too sure I agree with the large shoots. I would rather people shoot wild animals for the table rather than shoot for the sake of having a day out.”

He also refuses to buy grouse from any moor that has been associated with raptor persecution – the shooting or poisoning of birds of prey to artificially boost grouse numbers. “Something that has really annoyed me is the killing of raptor birds on the estates. They are being poisoned by people on these estates. I would never buy grouse from those estates. We all know who they are,” Corrigan said.

The chef, who grew up in County Meath, Ireland, said the management of the moors had led to them being more susceptible to wildfires. “I was brought up in moorland, I am very aware of the heather and the turf, they need the wetlands to be restored to keep the moors in good shape. Some estates have taken it all a bit too far and have turned it into factory grouse shooting operations.”

While some will be serving their grouse with bread sauce and game chips, which are deep-fried, thin slices of potato, Corrigan is going to dish out a lighter option. “They will be on the menu barbecued with peaches and jalapeño. There is nothing better to eat than peaches from Provence and little spatchcocked grouse.”

Henry Harris, the chef-owner of Bouchon Racine in Farringdon, London, said he was keeping his fingers crossed that he would receive grouse this week from his supplier. “I will know today whether there’s been a problem,’ he said. “If they fly, they will be shot. If it is too hot, they will not fly. If the weather really is too hot, they tend to struggle to drive them up into the air, which will mean there are less birds out there.”

He added that he was concerned about the wildfires and their impact on moorland wildlife, including grouse. “People do expect us to serve it, it is very popular,” he said. “We had a queue for them last year.”

Unlike Corrigan’s untraditional peach and jalapeño recipe, Harris said he would be “serving it very traditionally with a slight Gallic twist, on a lovely piece of sourdough toast with a bit of paté, armagnac sauce, bread sauce and game chips”.

Ariane Burgess, the rural affairs spokesperson for the Scottish Greens, will not be joining the queue. She said the countryside should not be “managed as a playground for bloodsports”, and the moors of Scotland were “intensively managed so that grouse can be killed for entertainment”.

She said: “Scotland’s land is one of our greatest assets. It should be supporting thriving rural communities, restoring nature and tackling the climate crisis, rather than serving as a private playground for the wealthy few.

“The real glorious future for Scotland’s moors would be seeing wildlife flourish on them, peatlands restored and rural jobs created through the recovery of our natural environment.”

Heard about the ‘luteal uglies’? Women know more about our hormones than ever – and that’s beautiful

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 10:29:33 GMT

When I was younger, female biology was seen as something to be overcome. Now we can talk about the reality of living in our bodies

Have you got the “luteal uglies”? I’m not trying to insult you, merely deploying the latest hormonal buzz phrase on social media, which refers to the phase in a woman’s cycle, two or so weeks between ovulation and menstruation, when she apparently feels at her lowest and most unattractive due to a drop in oestrogen levels.

Women’s hormones have become trending topics and, as someone who only found out what a “luteal phase” is when she Googled it, mid-fertility panic, in her late 20s, I am somewhat in awe of the expertise with which younger women discuss their menstrual cycles now. They’re just so incredibly literate.

Beyond being taught at school about periods and my mum explaining PMT, the impact of hormones on our emotional lives wasn’t discussed much when I was younger. In the “post-feminist” 1990s and early 2000s, female biology was seen as something to be suppressed and overcome, and the emphasis of most sex education was preventing teenage pregnancy. Being on the pill from 14 didn’t exactly put you in touch with the natural rhythms of your cycle, either, though of course it had other benefits (such as preventing the aforementioned teenage pregnancy).

You can understand the rationale, which was that female biology should never hold you back. Yet sometimes that felt like pretending your reproductive system didn’t really exist, or that you should simply push through the more difficult, painful aspects. “My period always comes as a surprise to me,” a friend said recently. She’s not the only one.

There were always girls who diligently marked the days in their diaries, but a large proportion of us barely kept track, unless of course your period arrived very late (prompting an urgent trip to the school nurse). By contrast, today’s young women have access to a plethora of period tracker apps and products, not to mention an avalanche of content pertaining to menstruation, ovulation, the luteal phase and how our hormones can impact everything from our psychological states to our body image to our sex lives. This also applies to postpartum and older women, with topics such as matrescence, perimenopause and menopause being discussed far more widely.

Despite the proliferation of psychobabble and therapy-speak, there’s also some good science. I can’t help but be impressed. Knowledge is, after all, power. I’m glad I was taught that biology doesn’t have to be destiny, but it shouldn’t have meant needing to play catch-up on educating myself about my own reproductive system. Knowing what’s going on in your body and having the language to describe it can have all sorts of psychological benefits. It’s comforting that the negative body image and the tiredness, bloating and other symptoms that come with the luteal phase can be fleeting. There’s a reason you feel this way, so maybe you don’t need Botox, you just need a rest.

And maybe, actually, you don’t want to have an affair, you’re just ovulating, which can increase your libido (or, to quote another friend, cause you to “go a bit feral”) and make you appear extra attractive to members of the opposite sex.

For me, it has been important to understand that a monthly desire to explode my life is probably a mild form of premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Knowing this not only helps me warn my loved ones in a “here be dragons” sort of way, but also prompts me to try to take better care of myself instead of deciding to get divorced and move to Crete to become a ceramicist. I don’t think my symptoms are serious enough to warrant treatment, but the increase in online discussion about these issues has helped equip many with the language needed to access diagnosis. Misinformation can be an issue, though, which is why the curriculum needs to catch up.

The fact is, hormones can shape our lives in profound ways. It’s something I explore in my fiction. That is not to say that we should always let them. We must, too, be vigilant. We have seen, especially in the US, how women’s cycles can be co-opted to forward patriarchal, authoritarian agendas, as in the period tracker data scandal, and Maga’s attempts to put women off taking birth control. I’m less worried about women’s willingness to adopt labels than I am about capitalism’s inevitable response to labels: a “fix”, whether that’s a pill that can “cure” the luteal uglies, an app that “tracks” your cycle and sells the data on, or something even more sinister.

Usually, when the mainstream media talks about this subject, it is almost always in a pro-natalist context of women needing better “fertility education” so that they don’t leave it too late to have babies, despite the fact that the biological clock is one of the few things we are very used to being lectured about. That’s why hearing reproductive education discussed in the context of aiding women’s self-understanding, wellbeing and mental health feels so radical.

The information itself isn’t new – I could have looked it up in a textbook – but the way of talking about it is. It’s emancipatory, in that it encourages women to know and take control of their bodies, but it’s also realistic about the reality of living in those bodies. Women of previous generations have also navigated that balance – they weren’t all sold on the notion of “burying the body” – but never so many, all at once. It’s basically a movement, and I am here for it.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist and the author of Female, Nude

I was enjoying growing vegetables. Then the climate crisis raised its ugly head

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 10:00:26 GMT

My child and I were bonding over our hit-and-miss approach to reaping crops. But with heatwaves pushing more of Britain into drought, it’s starting to feel like a luxury we can’t afford

For the first time in my life, I live in a home that has real outdoor space. What a concept! There are no downsides to a garden. Back in spring, I made grand plans – I watched all the TikToks, I bought seeds and trays and pots and grow bags, I ordered soil, a trowel and a watering can. I knew what I was after: super-tiny-scale subsistence farming with a side of Zen. A little fruit, a little veg, lots of flowers to attract pollinators. And I knew I wanted my elder child to gain an understanding of how things come to be and how to cope if and when they fail.

We love a tomato side salad, so that was the first thing we attempted. The seedlings flourished and then died in the first heatwave of the season. An omen, surely. The dahlias, ranunculus and freesias refused to grow, let alone bloom. My enthusiasm began to wane.

But then: our first harvest! Three (three!) bright-red Tumbling Tom tomatoes. We halved them, then tossed them in olive oil with some salt and pepper. They were gone in the blink of an eye, but we were grinning as we chomped. Ah, the pleasure of growing something small you can eat. We have sown onions, carrots, lettuce and basil and eagerly await miniature crops as the days get shorter.

At the back of my mind, though, is the very real fear of food shortages. Britain is approaching its sixth climate-crisis-induced heatwave of the year. Drought no longer threatens the country – it’s here. Conflicts around the world have inflated food prices. Is everyone aware of this? And are they in a state of low-grade panic, too?

What was supposed to feel like a fun bonding experience with my kid is morphing into something darker. Our garden has been heavy on trial and error, which feels increasingly like a luxury. Fun over – time to get good at this, fast. I know I’m doing too much, but I’ve started considering Kilner jars at TK Maxx and following homesteaders who grow their own produce. My favourite doomscroll these days is planting calendars and seed catalogues. Send tips, please. See you at the garden centre.

Bim Adewunmi is a freelance journalist

If the markets reject OpenAI and Anthropic, the US should nationalize them

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 10:00:26 GMT

From space to telecommunications, the US has a long history of fostering technology for the public good. These AI models could be aligned to democratic values, not corporate profits

OpenAI, and then Anthropic, were each formed by AI developers who feared unrestrained corporate AI development – specifically, that companies like Google and Meta would steer the technology towards deleterious, maybe even catastrophically unsafe, outcomes for society. Their founders proclaimed that their new labs, uniquely, could be trusted to develop the technology in humanity’s best interest. But each, in turn, were themselves co-opted by the same market incentives, themselves becoming corporate behemoths zealously guarding future investor value rather than the public interest.

It was only a few weeks ago, in June, when OpenAI and Anthropic each filed for their IPOs and were met with buzz about trillion-dollar valuations. The hype around their valuations is so extreme that many worry about their potential for concentrating wealth on a global scale. In an effort to leave something for the rest of us, some observers have proposed that the federal government seize a share of these companies’ stock to create a US sovereign wealth fund, or redistribute their revenues to produce a dividend for taxpayers.

Now the headlines are about public backlash to AI datacenters and the AI chip giant Nvidia’s slumping stock. The tech and AI giant SpaceX’s newly minted stock price tanked just weeks after its IPO. There are even questions about whether the leading AI labs will ever be sustainably profitable. All of a sudden, the makers of ChatGPT and Claude face strong headwinds as they seek to generate the massive equity assets that once felt all but assured.

In fact, evidence suggests the market itself could reassess that these companies offer nothing of financial value. In that case, perhaps we can return them both to their original purposes. If these AI companies should fail in the financial markets, the US should nationalize them and convert them into national labs operated under democratic control that preserve their benefit to the public interest.

The economics of the big AI labs hardly guarantee a booming return on investment. Frontier AI models are both expensive to train and depreciate within months, when a newer model appears. This means that the payback window to extract profit from them is very narrow. Meanwhile, enterprise clients are getting smart about minimizing AI token usage. Even worse, the models are basically commodities; the best ones largely perform and behave similarly, which depresses prices. Perhaps most importantly, open-source and Chinese competitors – lagging only a few months behind the leading labs in capability – give away for free the kinds of models Anthropic and OpenAI sell.

Even setting aside the model training costs, it’s not clear whether the unit economics of AI as it’s currently conceived will ever be sustainably profitable. Many of these free and open-source models can be run locally: the large ones on private clouds and high-end servers, the smaller ones on anyone’s laptop or even cellphone, putting to question the companies’ exorbitant capital investment in datacenters.

It’s not that OpenAI and Anthropic are not valuable as organizations. They have remarkably talented AI scientists and engineers that are continuously producing innovations driving a global mania for their offerings. These leading labs might not ever be profitable, but their products are doing a lot of good in the world. You may or may not be a user of or believer in their technology, but their staggering, ongoing usage growth suggests that an awful lot of people would be disappointed if the companies simply disappeared.

The problem isn’t the people or the products, it’s the system. As constituted, OpenAI and Anthropic may not be valuable as market equities. If the market assesses they are not capable of producing a growing financial return on investment for shareholders, the companies will collapse.

Maybe private, for-profit is just not the right economic model under which to develop AI. Perhaps OpenAI should be returned to its private non-profit roots, the legacy they fought so hard to change and which Anthropic’s founders spurned. Or possibly both could be reorganized as research centers at universities, returning to academia the scores of high-profile research faculty they have poached.

But a better outcome for society would be to establish public ownership and operation of their product-oriented capabilities. Turn OpenAI and Anthropic into US government agencies producing AI as a public good.

Transitioning the big AI labs into public agencies would require some restructuring. We can separate these companies into two pieces: product innovation and compute operations. The innovation function can be publicly managed, akin to national labs. Congress could provide more rigorous oversight than the kind of unfettered venture capital these labs have recently had access to. The US has a long, successful history of these kinds of institutions, which have produced world-shaping innovations in spaceflight, telecommunications, nuclear power and more. Congress currently manages a $200bn R&D portfolio, within which frontier AI development is, arguably, a glaring gap.

AI operations could be managed as a commodity resource, like public electrical or water utilities: local or regional ownership, nationwide distribution and strict regulation on how they balance fee extraction from ratepayers with raising capital for infrastructure investment. Although AI datacenters are not the same as power or water treatment plants, the US also has a long history of managing national, regional and state supercomputing centers.

Other countries, including Switzerland, Spain and Singapore, are already operating public AI labs. They also have national supercomputing centers already providing public access for running AI models for general use, as do Germany and Australia.

The benefits to the public are clear. Through democratic oversight, the most important AI models could become open, transparent and responsive to the demands of the public rather than private shareholders. They could be aligned to democratic values rather than corporate profits, never taking advertiser money to promote certain brands and training on only appropriately licensed data. And they could be set to focus on the realistic and pro-social goal of maximizing the usefulness of AI to society rather than the fanciful and anti-social goal of supplanting humans with artificial general intelligence.

By emphasizing scientific cooperation rather than corporate competition, we could also reduce the overall resource and environmental cost associated with AI. Instead of perpetually dueling training runs of each companies’ models at ever large scales targeted to fuel investor hype, we could limit AI training resources based on cost and benefit to the public.

What’s in it for the companies themselves and their employees, who sacrifice hypothetical billions in equity by ceding to public ownership? A return to their roots and to their core mission of developing AI safely in the public interest, if they are serious about it. Both companies are theoretically bound through their governance structures to prioritize mission over profit anyway (not that anyone really thinks that’s how they currently operate).

To be clear, we’re not advocating for a golden parachute for the executives or investors, or for continuing the outlandish pay rates of the most highly remunerated AI researchers. If the public is footing the bill, these compensation packages should be aligned to the civil service and those employees not satisfied with that can go elsewhere – if the business models of any remaining private labs still support much higher pay.

While we believe that these companies are unsustainable as private firms, the timeline remains unclear. Their primary investor story is that AI is a race to “artificial general intelligence” – the kind of AI you’re used to from science fiction. The bet seems to be that the two companies can convince enough people that this outcome will turn them a profit, go public, and then make their investors and employees rich before the bubble bursts.

But suppose that the bubble bursts. If the US is smart, it will catch the companies as they fall. Regardless of what the markets think, to the public, they’re too valuable to let die.

Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and University of Toronto’s Munk School

Nathan E Sanders is a data scientist affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center of Harvard University and co-author, with Bruce Schneier, of the book Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and Citizenship

Nigel Farage and Count Binface: a visual guide to their electoral careers

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 07:26:45 GMT

Farage was elected to EU parliament five times before becoming Clacton MP, while Binface has been less successful – so far

Nigel Farage has been standing in British elections since 1994, when he narrowly beat Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony party into fourth place in a Commons byelection. He was elected five times to the European parliament before achieving his goal of abolishing his seat.

Finally, after 30 years of trying, he was elected to the Commons as member for Clacton in 2024. He resigned that hard-won seat in July after a parliamentary inquiry was launched into a £5m gift he accepted from a Thailand-based businessman shortly before the general election, but is standing again in the resulting byelection on Thursday. The other major parties are not putting up candidates, so the chief contenders, according to the limited polling, are Farage and Count Binface.

These charts show the respective electoral histories of the two main runners.

Count Binface, or rather, his earthling avatar the comedian and writer Jon Harvey, has had a shorter and, so far, less successful electoral career, although he has stood against four prime ministers. On Thursday, he will face Farage at the ballot box for the first time, alongside his longstanding electoral adversary Laurence Fox, standing for Reclaim.

Over the years, Nigel Farage has stood against dozens of British politicians, including in 2006 a young Labour candidate by the name of Rachel Reeves.

In her capacity as chancellor a few weeks ago, it fell to Reeves to accept Farage’s resignation as MP for Clacton. There was some speculation at the time that she was not obliged to do it, but she accepted the resignation on the basis that “if he [Farage] wants to spend summer arguing with a bin, I won’t stop him.”

Thursday’s contest will, of course, not be the first time that either Farage or Binface has faced a novelty opponent. Riding high in the polls in 2015, Farage was so confident of winning Thanet South in that year’s general election that he pledged to resign as leader of Ukip if he did not take the seat.

This led Al Murray, a comedian whose main persona is the Pub Landlord, a straight-talking conservative patriot, to stand against Farage. Even without the resulting split in the straight-talking conservative patriot vote, Farage would have lost the seat. Ever a man of his word, Farage resigned, and then unresigned three days later.

Voters in Clacton on Thursday can, of course, choose to vote for neither Binface nor Farage. In fact, there are 34 candidates in all, including three from the Monster Raving Loony party.

Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 06:00:22 GMT

The climate crisis is hitting Europe hard in 2026, warming twice as fast as any other continent – and the consequences are deadly

The whole world is getting hotter as carbon pollution from fossil fuel burning traps ever more heat, but Europe is heating up twice as fast as other continents. The consequences are increasingly deadly, with tens of thousands of heatwave deaths so far this summer.

Land requires less heat than the vast and deep oceans to warm up, so all continents are warming more quickly than the seas. But Europe is particularly vulnerable for four reasons: changed weather patterns, its closeness to the Arctic, less snow and less air pollution.

As a result, Europe is now 2.5C hotter than before the mass burning of fossil fuels, almost double the global average 1.4C rise. Temperatures in Europe have risen by 0.56C a decade since the mid-1990s, compared with 0.42C in North America, 0.36C in Africa and 0.27C in South America.

Shifts in how the atmosphere circulates over Europe have led to more frequent and more intense summer heatwaves. This includes the worst ever heatwave, in June 2026, in which a vast area of hot air was trapped under a stationary “heat dome”.

Scientists are still investigating the role of global heating in causing changes in atmospheric circulation, but a link seems increasingly likely.

Dr Samantha Burgess, from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, said: “We see statistically significant changes in surface pressure patterns and other measures of circulation when we look at trends over the last 40 or more years, and on this timescale they are more likely associated with climate change than natural variability.”

The association may be the result of a changing jet stream, a fast high-level wind that has a powerful influence on Europe’s weather and is itself affected by rising temperatures.

The Arctic is the fastest warming region on the planet, despite having no land. This is because the white polar ice cap, which normally reflects the vast majority of sunlight back into space, is melting away fast. As a result, the darker ocean exposed by the melting absorbs much more heat, which then melts more ice, forming a vicious circle. With a significant proportion of Europe relatively close to the Arctic, temperatures are therefore rising faster.

Most of Europe had snowfall in winter in the past. Like the Arctic sea ice, this snow reflected sunlight and kept the continent cooler. But the climate crisis is shrinking snow-covered areas.

In March 2025, Europe’s blanket of snow was about 1.3m km2 below the 1991-2020 average, a 31% drop. That lost area is roughly the area of France, Italy, Germany, Switzerland and Austria combined. It was the third lowest snow cover since records began in 1983.

Air pollution kills millions of people globally every year and so Europe’s record of cutting toxic air levels in recent decades is unequivocally a good thing. However, cleaner air is also unmasking the impact of the rise in carbon dioxide pollution in the atmosphere.

Air pollution particles can reflect the sun’s rays, directly or by seeding the formation of clouds, meaning the heat does not reach the ground. Fewer particles means less reflection and more heat that is trapped by greenhouse gases. Lower pollution might even be connected to the increase in blocking weather patterns.

The short answer is that scientists don’t yet know, but they aim to have an estimate next year.

Burgess said: “What we can say is that the importance of each factor must vary with season, with proximity to the Arctic important in autumn and winter, and circulation changes since the late 1970s of greater statistical significance in summer.”

The drop in air pollution is most marked in winter because of declining coal heating in homes, and snow cover is a winter issue. Winter warming in Europe in recent decades has been strongest in the north, while summer warming has been strongest in the south-east.

The rapid heating is leading to ever more deaths and more intense wildfires and droughts. Storms, intense rainfall and floods are also being supercharged by the extra heat in the climate system. All deeply affect lives and livelihoods across the continent and will continue to worsen until emissions reach net zero. Rapid cuts in CO2 pollution and the rollout of measures to protect citizens are urgently needed.

The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said in late July: “The awful costs of this climate crisis – both human and economic – are now reaching national emergency levels. What needs to be done is clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people.”

Nigel Farage looks trapped and rattled – now the nationalist tide can be turned

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 06:00:22 GMT

There are more votes in tolerance and decency than in toxic division. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to fight back against Reform

Nigel Farage can be confident of victory against a man posing as an ennobled space traveller with a dustbin on his head. At least, in Clacton he can.

The refusal of major parties to contest this week’s byelection sets the bar low. But even if the competition were more serious than Count Binface, the Reform UK leader would be the favourite to win on his chosen turf. He picked the constituency as his safest shot for a parliamentary seat in the 2024 general election for a reason. Now he is betting that the stench of scandal around his personal and party finances, pungent in Westminster, won’t sicken his fans on the Essex coast.

He’s probably right, which is why Labour and the Conservatives sensibly denied him the spectacle he craved – a “people versus the establishment” prize fight. The plan was to put the question of his failure to declare a £5m donation to the electoral court of Clacton. It would be settled not by adjudication of the parliamentary standards authority but with a knockout blow from the fist of Furious Farage.

Unfortunately for the crypto-billionaires’ champion, the investigation hasn’t disappeared and could resume if he wins his pantomime bout with a bin.

If a subsequent decision goes against him, a second byelection could follow. That twist could easily be written into Farage’s script as further proof that the system was rigged against him; that the acclamation of his innocence by his loyal Essex jury was not sufficient and they must vindicate him again, louder.

The shape of the argument is textbook populism. A candidate’s virtue is measured by the volume of clamour he can summon from a crowd. Institutions of established democracy are valued only as ladders aiding his ascent. If they hold him accountable in any way, they are dismissed as tools of the elite that conspires against the will of the people.

It is a sign of vulnerability that Farage’s definition of “the people” has shrunk to whatever portion of Clacton constituents turns out for him on Thursday. When his cause was Brexit, he could wield a national referendum mandate to denigrate dissent. When opinion polls and council ballots showed Reform on course to win a general election, the party leader had a putative prime ministerial swagger in his step. He has slipped.

For now, Reform strategists are not too anxious about losing their headline lead to Labour. Second place, after a period of unusually hostile media coverage, while a new Downing Street regime enjoys a (probably brief) honeymoon is not a calamitous position. It could be proof of resilience as much as weakness. More worrying for Farage are his tanking personal ratings and evidence from recent Greater Manchester byelections (two for parliamentary seats; one for the mayoralty vacated by Andy Burnham) that aversion to Reform is coalescing into an effective tactical bloc vote.

That sentiment is resolute. Farage has been a prominent British public figure for two decades. People who see his multiple, rebranded parties as one metastatic malignancy in the body politic are not open to persuasion that he can be something more benign. He used to curate his brand with feinted moderation. That is harder now that Reform faces competition from Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party in the far-right zone where hostility to immigrants dispenses with non-racist euphemism.

Lowe is more anchor of a social media channel than leader of a party. He harvests clicks in the field of digital paranoia, irrigated by extreme content on Elon Musk’s X platform, where it is axiomatic that “indigenous” Europeans face systematic replacement in their homelands by dark-skinned aliens.

Restore took almost 9% of the vote in the first round of the Manchester mayoral byelection, ahead of the Tories and Liberal Democrats. Lowe, elected to parliament in 2024 as a Reform MP, has offered to form an alliance with his old party, but with conditions attached, including the insistence that Tory defectors be barred from any future role in government.

A less-rattled Farage would heap derision on his former comrade. He might even have exploited the schism to confect a new boundary between “mainstream” and “far” right. He could highlight tonal differences between his and Lowe’s politics and apply them as camouflage of respectability.

That he doesn’t suggests lack of confidence in the loyalty of Reform’s hardcore vote. More disturbingly, it implies openness to the idea that, where immigration is concerned, British politics is not yet maxed-out at the furthest limits of rightward expansion.

The shift is stark enough already. Parliament has passed a new act tightening border control or limiting migrants’ rights every year since 2022. Such assiduous attention to the issue has done nothing to satisfy demands for harsher measures. Nor has it refuted the absurd suggestion that mainstream politics and media, constrained by timorous liberalism, refuse to address a question that has, in reality, dominated the agenda for a generation.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The legislative ratchet is also a rhetorical dial, turning public debate more shrill. The language of invasion, once the metaphorical preserve of extremists, has been normalised. Gangs of masked marauders who go on racist rampages through UK towns are cast as protesters manifesting legitimate concerns. The articulation of their grievance in terms that make foreignness synonymous with parasitic consumption of benefits, criminality and sexual predation goes unchallenged.

Meanwhile, net migration has fallen dramatically from its peak earlier this decade. Instead of welcoming the turning tide, the anti-immigrant right has shifted its focus from resisting new arrivals to undermining the status of legally settled communities, denying their entitlement to public services, blocking paths to naturalisation and building a case for mass deportations. This used to be the stuff of skinhead rallies and crank byelection candidates who lost their deposits. Now resistance depends on the guy with the bin on his head. Or at least, in Clacton it does.

Elsewhere the picture is less bleak. Farage retreated to his coastal haven for an electoral comfort break, getting relief from scrutiny in a place where he can still enjoy unchallenged status as the man of the people. But his people are fewer than they were and never as many as he claims. If he has hit the ceiling of his national support and feels part of his base wobbling beneath him, he will try to consolidate by further radicalisation. That will then give more urgency to the anti-Reform voter coalition.

He is trapped. But only if other parties refuse to follow him a single step further down the road to ethno-nationalism, where immigration policy degenerates into sinister fantasies of demographic engineering, and instead push back.

It isn’t a hard choice. There are many more people in Britain who like to live happily alongside their neighbours, regardless of skin colour and country of origin, than want to burn them out of their homes. It doesn’t take a great leap of political courage to draw a line between rigorous migration control and racist demagoguery.

There were good reasons for major parties to sit out this Thursday’s byelection. But from Friday onwards, the task of fighting Farage can’t be delegated to a man with a bin on his head. Not even in Clacton.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

‘It’s been a revelation’: how heat pumps can cool your home as temperatures soar

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 06:00:21 GMT

It might seem an unlikely way to stop overheating, but many owners have found the tech a lifeline in hot weather

“If it is 35C outdoors, I can get the temperature down to 21C,” says Andrew Ingram of the sanctuary that his living room has provided this summer.

“On the nights I’ve slept in there, you have to put your thick pyjamas on,” jokes Ingram, who lives in Maidenhead, Berkshire, with his wife, Sue.

“When I post on Facebook about it, people say: ‘That’s air conditioning’ and I say: ‘No, it’s the heat pump.’ It’s just working the other way around.”

Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, a heat pump transfers heat energy from one place to another. However, despite the name, heat pumps can be used for cooling, too.

The energy is released through an “emitter” such as a radiator or underfloor heating. The Ingrams have an air source heat pump. It extracts heat from the air outside and uses it to warm the radiators of their three-bedroom house (this is called an air-to-water system).

In 2023, when the Ingrams ripped out their gas boiler, the firm suggested they consider whether they wanted to cool any rooms.

“We thought about it because the sitting room gets really hot, and that’s the room we spend time in,” Ingram says.

“It’s been a revelation. We bought it on the basis that there might be a heatwave, and it’s been an absolute lifeline this year.

“You know those times when you are really feeling exhausted and want to sit somewhere cool. We turn it right down and then let the temperature drift back up again.”

The couple have radiators throughout but the living room also has another “emitter” – called a fan coil unit. This is an appliance that blows air over hot or cold pipes. The whole new home energy system cost roughly £18,600, with the cooling aspect accounting for £1,700 of that.

“If you’re pumping cool water around a property, it’s a bit like putting cool beer in a glass on a warm day,” says Ingram of what is potentially one of the pitfalls of cooling this way.

“You get loads of condensation, so you either have to wrap pipes in quite sophisticated trunking or do what we did, which is have them outside.

“We used the cooling a bit in 2024, and, guess what, in 2025 even more – and in 2026 we’ve been a rather popular place for people to visit.”

The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to assist homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water system (a heat pump that extracts heat from the ground through buried pipes).

Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000.

If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get an interest-free loan or a grant to make your home more energy efficient.

To qualify for funding, the heat pump must be certified through the Microgeneration Certification Scheme, which certifies installers.

Previously heat pumps that also cooled required planning permission, as the permitted development rights rules (legal permissions that allow certain home improvements without a planning application) stated they had to be solely for heating. The PDR has now been updated to allow cooling.

To date, Britons have mostly installed air-to-water systems, and of the UK’s 358,000 heat pumps, approximately 323,000 are this type, according to MCS data.

This could be about to change because the government is to offer £2,500 grants for air conditioning units that can heat and cool. The air-to-air heat pumps move heat using wall-mounted fans and cost about £4,500 to fit in a flat or small house. (Air-to-water heat pumps typically cost in the region of £12,000.)

The run of heatwaves has thrown the spotlight on “heat-trap homes”. A recent report by the Climate Change Committee said that hotter heatwaves could lead to 92% of existing homes overheating by 2050 and they may require air conditioning, as passive measures such as drawing curtains and opening windows are unlikely to be enough.

A recent study conducted in the Energy House 2.0 – a £16m climate-controlled chamber at the University of Salford – found that using a heat pump for cooling can “significantly reduce overheating” in modern homes.

Two new modern houses have been built inside the weather simulation facility so that scientists can test how “real” homes perform under extreme conditions.

The Salford scientists paired a heat pump with fan coils in one of the houses. When the lab weather was 32C, the rooms stayed comfortable – between 19C and 24.9C. With the heat pump running around the clock, the cost was £2.50-£3 a day.

Prof Lubo Jankovic, the scientist leading the research, says the results “demonstrate that reversible heat pumps can play an important role in protecting future homes against overheating”.

But Jankovic says the challenge of designing systems with both heating and cooling in mind “needs to be addressed before cooling this way becomes mainstream”.

With the October price cap predicted to exceed £1,700 a year for a typical dual fuel bill, the big question for many is: will a heat pump save me money?

A recent poll by the consumer group Which? revealed growing consumer interest in heat pumps, but also that they were a “high-stakes gamble” owing to their unfamiliarity, high upfront costs and uncertain impact on bills.

One way to get a better understanding is to look round a home with one and quiz the owner. The charity Nesta runs the “visit a heat pump” scheme, which offers tours of more than 1,200 homes, including the Ingrams’.

When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.

The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits.

Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can save about £330 a year compared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.

The Ingrams have solar panels and a home battery to help keep their bills down. “There’s lots of juice in the batteries from the solar,” Ingram says. “The batteries charge up overnight if they’re not full, but they have been recently. So if you want to run the pump, it is running on free or very cheap electricity.”
