Ceuta showed just how easy it is to divide Europe

The Guardian Wed, 12 Aug 2026 04:00:18 GMT

The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note

Within hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on 30 July, 22 European Union leaders, the Trump administration and Israel had piled on to criticise Madrid.

The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponisation of migrants by non-EU countries.

That Donald Trump and JD Vance should seize the opportunity to accuse socialist Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez of inviting the mass influx by allowing more than 1 million irregular migrants already working in Spain to apply for legal status is hardly surprising, given the US administration’s own relentless drive to detain and expel illegal immigrants.

On the other hand, European leaders who signed a letter to the European Commision, criticising Spain and demanding an emergency meeting of interior ministers, should ask themselves how their behaviour helps the EU implement a coherent response to migratory pressures. Many are open to charges of hypocrisy, since Germany and Italy have, between them, regularised hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrant workers at the request of employers who need their labour as the home workforce dwindles.

There was also a monstrous foreign policy double standard in the initial EU response.

When Poland and Lithuania faced a sudden influx of irregular migrants from Belarus in 2021, the EU rallied behind its eastern members and imposed sanctions on Minsk’s authoritarian regime, which stood accused of weaponising displaced people from the Middle East. The previous year, the EU sent its Frontex border agency to help Greece repel a surge of migrants from Turkey at the countries’ shared border in Thrace, which had apparently been encouraged by Ankara to put pressure on the EU.

Yet this time, EU governments quickly fell into a divisive blame game, terrified by images that recalled the loss of control over borders in south-eastern Europe in 2015, when more than 1 million mostly Syrian refugees entered the bloc. Amid the internal finger-pointing, neither the EU leaders nor the European Commission dared question the role of Morocco, whose border guards apparently stood aside as more than 72,000 Moroccans, mostly young men, risked their lives swimming to Ceuta after seeing viral social media claims that “Spain is open”.

The incident occurred on Morocco’s annual Throne Day when King Mohammed VI, who does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over the territories of Ceuta and Melilla, just happened to be visiting the nearby northern city of Tétouan, once part of the Spanish protectorate. Some commentators have called the stampede to Ceuta a “Blue March”, in reference to the mass Green March that the king’s father, Hassan II, launched in 1975 in an attempt to claim the vast territory of Western Sahara, then a Spanish colony.

“In Morocco, nothing happens by chance,” says Anna Terrón Cusí, a senior fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former Spanish secretary of state for immigration. Even if the stampede to Ceuta started spontaneously with social media posts, she believes “this was a multi-actor, multi-factor event. It was more a geopolitical than a migration crisis.”

Intra-European party politics played a big role. It was not surprising that the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, should lead the assault on Sánchez. She heads up the hard-right Brothers of Italy movement and faces a domestic challenge in elections next year from a new, even further-right party, led by a retired general.

Some Spanish and UK anti-immigration politicians rushed to Ceuta to take selfies, one from Reform UK doing a standup interview on the beach to cash in on the purported alien “invasion”.

It was more bizarre that Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, who heads a centre-left government, should co-initiate with Meloni the letter to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, and say that the EU should consider suspending Spain from the Schengen area of open-border travel.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

A facade of European solidarity was restored after EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged videoconference. By that time, almost all the migrants had left Ceuta and returned to Morocco after realising that they had no chance of reaching Europe. The “invasion” had deflated. In fact, irregular migrant arrivals in Spain fell sharply last year, while across the EU they’re down for the second successive year, and far below the 2015 crisis peak. But the damage was done.

Italy and Spain are now engaging in tit-for-tat passport and nationality controls on each other’s travellers, and Russian president Vladimir Putin, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and King Mohammed himself will have noted how easily Europe panics and turns on its own members at the first sight of migrants on its beaches.

Whether out of misinformation or malice, some EU ministers distorted the nature of the Spanish amnesty for undocumented migrants, labelling it a “pull factor” for mass migration. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, claimed they were being granted Spanish and therefore European citizenship, rather than simply being given a chance to apply for temporary work visas.

Europe faces what in game theory is called the “prisoners’ dilemma”, and in social sciences a “collective action problem” . EU countries have a shared interest in preserving the Schengen zone of free movement, with open internal borders vital to the smooth operation of the economy, well-managed external borders to deter irregular migrants and combat people smugglers, and legal migration routes to permit an inflow of workers needed by businesses as the European population ages and shrinks.

Yet they keep undermining cooperation due to a seemingly irresistible short-term political interest in anti-migration grandstanding.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

To all the betting shops littering our high streets: people power is coming and the odds are against you

The Guardian Tue, 11 Aug 2026 17:01:17 GMT

Too many shops are blighting too many communities. With the rule change I fought for now on the horizon, ordinary people can fight back

How much gambling do you want in your high street? Are you happy with all the betting shops, the problems they cause, the effect on your environment?

It’s worth asking because for years, local councils have been expected to say yes to new gambling venues, even when communities made clear they did not want them. Now, under new rules announced on Monday, that’s about to change. And about time.

Speaking to local residents I hear a clear message time and again: people are fed up with seeing so much gambling where they live, while having little say over whether new venues open.

I knew grappling with this issue would be an uphill battle. The gambling industry is lucrative and deeply embedded in our communities. When I looked into why councils were struggling to stop new betting shops, casinos and adult gaming centres opening, I discovered the problem.

At the heart of it was the outdated “aim to permit” principle in the Gambling Act 2005. It meant councils were effectively working against a presumption that gambling premises should be permitted, leaving them limited ability to say no. This one principle is the root of the crisis on our high streets: it has stripped local people of any real power to shape their own communities, and let the industry expand largely unchecked.

So in 2021 I started my campaign to put power back where it belongs: in the hands of councils and local communities. Today, after years of campaigning, I’m delighted to say that we’ve won.

The government has announced it is scrapping aim to permit, giving councils and communities greater power over what happens on their high streets. This is a huge victory for London, and for communities nationwide. But it took years of pressure and persistence to get here.

I took a minister to Harlesden high street to see the reality for themselves. I launched a petition so Londoners could make their voices heard. I organised a cross-party letter backed by more than 280 MPs, councillors, mayors and gambling reform advocates, including the then mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham. I took the campaign into parliament too, raising it at prime minister’s questions and leading a debate.

During my summer tour last year, I took the campaign into communities across London, listening to what people wanted to see on their high streets, and meeting families affected by gambling harms, such as the campaigner Jackie Olden, who watched her mother’s life spiral out of control thanks to a slot-machine addiction.

It was a shock to discover how much gambling machines generate: B3 (higher-stakes) gambling machines – essentially slot/fruit machine-style games, found in places such as betting shops, adult gaming centres and casinos – generate an average of £35,000 in gross gambling yield per machine each year – more than the roughly £26,400 a year earned by someone aged 21 or over working 40 hours a week on the national living wage. The scale of the problem is clear in Brent, where gambling premises outnumber supermarkets in 17 of Brent’s 22 wards. We have 81 licensed gambling venues across the borough. For my constituents, this is about improving the places they live and raise their families. People want to be proud of their high streets again.

The consequences of gambling-related harm can be devastating. A 2023 report estimated there could be between 117 and 496 gambling-related suicides in England each year. I’ve worked with campaigners and advocates with lived experience of gambling harm, and highlighted organisations such as Gambling with Lives and Gambling Harm UK, whose expertise helped make the case for reform.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I’m grateful to residents who signed my petition, representatives who backed my campaign, councils including Brent council that pushed for this change, and every reform advocate who helped build momentum. I’m also grateful to Andy Burnham, who followed through on his support by committing to make this bold change.

Our high streets should work for local people – not for companies profiting from harm. No longer should residents feel powerless when they see changes on their doorstep. That is why scrapping aim to permit matters: it will make a real, tangible difference to people’s lives.

With the support of Londoners and campaigners across the country, we fought, organised and delivered. So, this is your chance: take back your high streets. Get involved, hold your council to account – use these new powers to demand and shape the neighbourhoods you deserve.

Dawn Butler is the Labour MP for Brent East

A. O. C. Said ‘Woke 1.0 Was Crazy.’ But What Is It?

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a recent interview, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez distanced herself from the 2020 era of progressivism.

By Madison Malone Kircher

“Woke 1.0 was crazy,” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York said in a recent interview.

The congresswoman, speaking on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, seemed to distance herself from the positions of an era of Democratic politics around 2020, shortly after she rose to prominence. Some on the left now see the rhetoric of that time as ineffective and divisive. There has been a widespread retreat on diversity, equity and inclusion efforts among corporations. And some public officials, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, have walked back their calls to defund the police.

If Woke 1.0 is in the past, when did it die? And has Woke 2.0 risen from its ashes?

Ocasio-Cortez said on “This Week” that she was quoting Chi Ossé, a far-left New York City councilman, when she described the so-called Woke 1.0. (Ossé posted about the “crazy” era on X in May. )

That era is sometimes referred to colloquially as peak woke. In May, Yemisi Egbewole, a former Biden White House aide, posted on X praising Texas State Representative James Talarico, who is running for a Senate seat, after he walked back statements from that era.

“I think it’s great that Talarico is calling some of his high-net-woke comments cringe,” Egbewole wrote. “Honestly, more young people running for office are probably going to have to do this. Peak woke got weird. It’s okay to say that!”

Though the word “woke” itself originated in Black slang and had been around for decades in grass roots movements, in recent years it has been used pejoratively by some Republicans and moderate Democrats as a way to describe policies they view as out of touch.

Woke 1.0 retroactively describes the age of the #MeToo movement, and backlash against sexual assault and discrimination, and the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd, which led to widespread protests against police violence and racial injustice, said Spencer Goidel, a political science professor at Auburn University.

“This is what activists are prone to do, they overreach,” said Goidel, adding that the movements had bipartisan support. “They say, ‘This is our moment.’” Goidel published a paper in 2025 about “ordinary Americans’ understandings of wokeness.”

For many survey respondents in his research, Ocasio-Cortez was a symbol of Woke 1.0, he said, as well as groups like Black Lives Matter.

Erik Bleich, the chair of the department of political science at Middlebury College, said some voters were turned off by a shift during the late 2010s to more “symbolic politics,” or debates that appeared to focus on language.

Goidel, the Auburn professor, said that President Trump’s victory in the 2024 election was an important moment in the move away from Woke 1.0. “I think that’s kind of a wake-up call where Democrats then have to self-reflect and go, ‘Oh, we aren’t speaking to the common person,’” he said. “I do think there’s this active effort within the party now to kind of silence a little bit the academic-ese.”

Bleich also pointed to the calls to defund the police as a divisive goal. Years after the large-scale racial justice protests, efforts to cut funding for police departments or get rid of traditional policing proved unpopular and were largely abandoned.

He pointed to President Biden’s call to “fund the police” during his 2022 State of the Union address.

But many in the Democratic Party emphasize that the era, despite some attention-grabbing policies that never gained widespread approval, led to positive change. “The doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place,” Ocasio-Cortez said on ABC, describing the discussions of that era as “fruitful.”

In the ABC interview, Ocasio-Cortez was asked why she had not endorsed Francesca Hong, a Wisconsin state assemblywoman and democratic socialist, who lost the Democratic primary for governor this week despite being ahead in polling.

Hong once called for abolishing the police and said the country should “cancel Thanksgiving,” but has since walked back those statements. (Her opponent in the primary, David Crowley, is a moderate Democrat.)

“I think that what’s important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now,” said Ocasio-Cortez, who has also softened previous stances on the police.

For Bleich, the congresswoman’s comments are emblematic of a shift in the party, saying “Hey, OK, we know that went too far. We know that we progressives essentially wound up demobilizing and neutralizing what could have been and should have been our allies on the left,” he said, “and made an opening for the right to really use that term publicly against the goals that many people on the left share.”

As for when Woke 1.0 officially died? Perhaps it was Ocasio-Cortez’s interview that delivered the fatal blow, Stu Loeser, a longtime Democratic communications strategist, said.

“In politics, like if they’re talking about it on ‘This Week,’ well, you know, then it’s dead.”

Madison Malone Kircher is a Times reporter covering internet culture.

For Trump, Secret Flight Was a Stunning Ruse. For Putin, ‘a Regular Tuesday.’

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump’s Air Force One subterfuge pales in comparison to the secrecy surrounding Russia’s president, whose fixation on security has reached new heights in recent years.

By Anton Troianovski

Anton Troianovski writes about foreign policy in Washington. He was previously the Moscow bureau chief.

President Trump’s Air Force One subterfuge was a stunning episode of official deception.

But it pales in comparison to the secrecy surrounding President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, whose activity is shrouded in so much mystery that journalists have tried to track it by assessing the wilting of his office plants.

That is the method some reporters resorted to this year as they worked to ascertain whether the Russian leader’s televised meetings took place when the Kremlin said they did. The apparent reversal of the leaf decay seen in Mr. Putin’s plants suggested that the meetings actually took place in a different order and on different days.

For Mr. Putin, such deceit is par for the course. The White House, by contrast, has been criticized for not revealing Mr. Trump’s secret plane switch on a Turkish tarmac last month until The Washington Post broke the story this week.

“Compared to Russia,” said Mikhail Rubin, a Russian investigative reporter, “this is child’s play.”

Mr. Rubin and other reporters have found that Mr. Putin has outfitted his residences with nearly identical offices so that video footage of meetings does not reveal his location. His security apparatus has developed a presidential train, along with special railroad spurs and secret stations near at least three of his country residences, according to news reports and satellite images.

Government officials are forced to play along, keeping their meetings with Mr. Putin a secret until they are televised — sometimes weeks later — and then pretending they happened on that day.

In Russia, official falsehoods about the president’s whereabouts “are just a regular Tuesday,” said Farida Rustamova, a Russian journalist who covers the Kremlin from exile. She has reported that Mr. Putin’s interlocutors in his televised meetings sometimes speak of outdated events, in at least one case in clothes and a haircut incongruous with other public appearances.

There is even a term of art for those delayed-release Putin meetings among Russian journalists: konservy, or canned goods.

The Kremlin has previously denied deceiving the public about Mr. Putin’s location and did not respond to a request for comment.

Covering Mr. Putin as a New York Times correspondent based in Moscow, I got a sense of the lengths the Russian president goes to in order to hide his movements when I visited Lake Valdai, where he has a country residence, in 2021. Residents told me about a mysterious new railroad line that had been built toward his compound. Satellite imagery showed a new station, with a helipad, that did not appear on timetables or railway maps.

In 2023, a defector from the Russian version of the Secret Service, the F. S. O., asserted that Mr. Putin was using train travel to avoid being tracked. Leaked documents indicated that a secret armored train outfitted for the office of the president, painted like a regular passenger train but complete with a gym, spa and special communications equipment, was used by Mr. Putin himself.

Mr. Putin’s preoccupation with secrecy and security appeared to increase during the pandemic, when he forced officials to quarantine for two weeks to see him and when his isolation made it easier to hide his whereabouts. And it has reached new heights since his invasion of Ukraine in 2022, especially as that country’s drones flew deeper into Russia, helping precipitate mobile internet shutdowns and reportedly curtailing his travel.

In Moscow, there is now speculation that the enormous motorcades racing down city streets that are presumed to be carrying Mr. Putin are actually sometimes decoys, according to Ms. Rustamova. One of my Kremlin-connected contacts in Moscow told me the same.

Mr. Rubin, the investigative journalist, first reported in 2020 that Mr. Putin worked from identical-looking offices in his residences in the Moscow suburbs and in the Black Sea resort of Sochi, allowing the Kremlin to lie about his location. A report last year by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty uncovered more details about that deception effort, highlighting tiny differences between those otherwise identical offices — like the placement of door handles and wall seams — that indicated they were in different places.

Mr. Rubin, who is now based in North Carolina and is deputy editor of the news outlet Proekt, first got a sense of Mr. Putin’s secrecy when he covered the Kremlin for a Russian business newspaper a decade ago. Mr. Rubin once happened to see members of Mr. Putin’s Security Council arriving for a meeting, but his office only announced the gathering days later, as though it was a new occurrence. He came to realize, he said, “that Putin’s public image is made up, it’s an absolute lie from beginning to end.”

For Mr. Putin, the deception is not only about security, but about projecting an air of constant activity and control. The intensity of U. S. press coverage of the president, on the other hand, would have been unimaginable in Russia even before the Ukraine war and the pandemic.

But the Trump administration’s restrictions on the news media and its misdirection surrounding the president’s flight last month still look familiar in some Russian eyes.

“Putin in this sense is a caricature of a figure who has taken everything happening around him to the point of absurdity,” Mr. Rubin said. “Trump, it seems to me, is only starting to move in this direction.”

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

News analysis

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s sharing of her decision to freeze her eggs, the news that her longtime relationship had ended and talk of a presidential run have intensified the debates that swirl around her.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-CortezCredit... Celeste Sloman for The New York Times

Supported by

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

Since she won her first election in 2018 at 28, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, has been a political obsession for fans to adore and critics to abhor.

Her body, her weight, the clothes she wore in magazine shoots, her lipstick, her endorsements, her ill-fated decision to attend the Met Gala in a “tax the rich” gown, have been parsed and picked apart, in ways she has described as sometimes “dehumanizing” even when that parsing was coming from her supporters.

One area where she was insulated from such scrutiny was her love life: Ms. Ocasio-Cortez arrived on the national political scene with her boyfriend from college, Riley Roberts, by her side. And he stayed there as she became one of the most consequential women in American politics, a burly redhead who stood mostly outside the frame of Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s public life. In 2022, her team announced in a fund-raising email that the couple was engaged.

Four years later, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is at a new juncture. Her relationship with Mr. Roberts quietly ended some time ago and her decision to livestream her egg-freezing journey has forced to the forefront an uncomfortable topic for a lawmaker who is both unusually open and incredibly private: a breakup that she had never broadcast, despite giving her followers a sense that they are often along with her for the ride.

The new information about Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s private life is coming alongside a spate of speculation that she’s preparing to run for president. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who has said she hasn’t ruled out a presidential run or a run for Senate, could now be navigating a possible national or statewide campaign as a young, world-famous, single woman, a profile that would only intensify the ideological and cultural debates that swirl around her.

The reality of that new level of exposure became apparent on Tuesday night after a reporter for Puck and TMZ reported that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had split with Mr. Roberts, which was confirmed to The New York Times by multiple people knowledgeable about her personal life. Her relationship status was not new, but public disclosure of it all but broke the internet.

“All the single left-wing men in this city are about to line up nightly for dinner in her district until she picks one like the suitors in The Odyssey,” Asad Dandia, a Brooklyn-based community organizer, wrote on X.

As early as 2020, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was open about struggling to find a balance between life and work. “I’m sitting here, I’m like, Do I freeze my eggs? Can I afford to do that?” she asked in an interview with Vanity Fair that year. “My orthodontist was telling me about how she was doing I. V. F., and I’m, like, asking her what her experience is like.”

Diana Z. O’Brien, chair of women, gender and sexuality studies at Washington University in St. Louis, said that as a 36-year-old progressive lightning rod with political ambitions outside of the House, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had no real choice but to make public her decision to freeze her eggs — and then, by association, her breakup.

“If she says nothing, then people will infer that she’s making a decision to de-prioritize family,” Ms. O’Brien said.

Ms. O’Brien said it was inevitable that with that disclosure came the less comfortable one, about her relationship status.

“It came up for Senator Cory Booker before he was married, so it will definitely come up for a woman,” she said. “This allows her to say, ‘yes, I’m single right now, but that doesn’t mean I intend to be child-free or single forever.’ It counterbalances a narrative that would try to portray her as a very particular type of leftist single woman who hates men.”

David Axelrod, the former top adviser to President Barack Obama, said that being an unmarried woman “probably adds a degree of difficulty” to any run she might make to become the first woman elected president, although he noted that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez operates in her own orbit and according to her own rules because of her “unique ability to take people along for the ride in a way that is personally connecting.”

He added: “The bigger question to me is whether this is a ride she wants or needs to take at this stage because it would require an absolute surrender of so much of her life.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has not publicly addressed the end of her relationship, but that has not stopped anyone from weighing in on it. Conservatives piled on to criticize her for putting her political ambitions above her relationship. And group chats lit up with ideas for who Ms. Ocasio-Cortez might date without their politics being picked apart: A chef? A musician? A Knick?

On Capitol Hill, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s colleagues have long known she was no longer engaged. And she has not exactly hidden it. For one thing, she doesn’t wear an engagement ring. But she has also not gone public about her relationship status or whether she is dating again.

When a reporter asked her on Sunday what her fiancé thought of her decision to freeze her eggs, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez sidestepped the question, noting only that “all of my loved ones have been very supportive.” Her chief of staff, Mike Casca, did not respond to a request for comment for this piece.

But the reality is that being a prominent young, single woman lawmaker draws attention and poses challenges that men with a similar profile might not encounter, including reproductive choices.

Representative Yassamin Ansari, the 34-year-old Democrat from Arizona, said dating can be difficult when she feels like she is never in one place for long.

“I have my Arizona life and I have my D. C. life and I never feel like I’m rooted somewhere,” she said in an interview. Ms. Ansari said she was in a relationship when she was first elected in 2024, but that it ended in part because “it was super difficult for me to prioritize that on top of everything else going on.” As for dating, she said she prefers meeting people in real life and that “the apps do make me nervous. The job responsibilities make everything more challenging.”

She added: “I will probably freeze my eggs, too.”

For Ms. Ocasio-Cortez the scrutiny exists at another level. Over the years, she has given her followers a sense of shared intimacy by allowing them to watch her make black bean soup and assemble IKEA furniture on social media while talking about policy and answering questions about her daily routines. She participated in an emotional livestream after the Jan. 6 mob attack on the Capitol, describing in detail the trauma she felt from the day.

But being vulnerable and prominent has not been without cost, or easy.

“I miss being able to go outside in sweats,” she told Time magazine in 2019, just after she was elected. “I can’t go anywhere in public and just be a person without a lot of people watching everything I do.”

After she was criticized for attending the Met Gala, despite her Democratic Socialist politics, she wrote online: “I and my body have been so heavily and relentlessly policed from all corners politically since the moment I won my election.”

Jessica Valenti, the feminist writer who publishes the popular newsletter, “Abortion, Every Day,” said that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was so triggering to the right because she represents a direct affront to their well-funded message that women should get married young and have children young.

“Here, you have this very beautiful, very powerful woman, who is creating the life that she wants and appears to be very happy,” she said. “A very big part of the conservative Republican agenda right now is targeting young women. The last thing they need is a young woman modeling what a life could look like that they are so desperate to stop.”

Ms. Valenti said that “to a certain group of people, there is nothing A. O. C. could ever do, nothing would be OK with them” and that will likely carry into her personal life. “Regardless of who she dates,” she said, “how public she is or how private she is, someone is going to have an issue with it.”

Indeed, Allie Beth Stuckey, a conservative commentator, wrote online that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was “glamorizing the lie that women can have it all. You can’t. Biology is real and how you order your life makes or breaks your future.” Ms. Stuckey’s criticism was emblematic of the view from the Christian right on reproductive rights like egg-freezing and I. V. F., which remains culturally contested ground when it comes to judging the personal choices of a young lawmaker.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has long been self-aware about the strangeness of growing up in a political petri dish. In her livestream on Sunday, she told her followers that the downside of being elected as a young person is “you have to then grow up in the public eye in a time that most people get to grow more privately.”

She added: “when you get elected later in life, you’ve made all of your mistakes in private. When you get elected when you’re young, you have to do all of that in public.”

As she prepared to inject her exposed belly with a fertility shot, she warned viewers, “don’t be weird about this,” no doubt knowing full well that they almost certainly would be.

An earlier version of this article misstated the year Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona was first elected. It was 2024, not 2021.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

A Space Expert Hoped to Use the Eclipse as Science Class. The D. J. s Had Other Plans.

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Europe’s Total Solar Eclipse

Advertisement

Supported by

Mar Carretero-Castrillo, an astrophysicist, returned to her remote village in Spain to be in the path of totality. Hundreds of partygoers came too.

By Jason Horowitz

Reporting from Castrillo de la Reina, Spain, in the path of totality

The day before the first total solar eclipse on the Spanish mainland in more than a century, Mar Carretero-Castrillo, a 28-year-old astrophysicist, climbed the hill in the tiny and remote northern Spanish village where she spent her childhood summers staring up at the starry night sky.

Ms. Carretero-Castrillo had returned home from her job overseas for the big celestial event, she said, with the “beautiful idea” of gathering a small watch party on the same hill to quietly experience the eclipse with snacks, scientific discussions and educational games played with kitchen colanders.

“But we have this fiesta,” she said, looking down to the normally isolated village of Castrillo de la Reina, which on Wednesday is playing host to “Eclipse-fest,” a party for hundreds of outsiders. The event will be free to the village’s 160 full-time residents as well as the more than three times as many people who spend the summer there. Ms. Carretero-Castrillo wondered if her planned hillside gathering would be overshadowed by the party’s water-gun fight, laser light-show, musicians, and D. J. s playing electronic, punk and reggaeton music until 6:30 a. m. It was possible, she acknowledged, that the fiesta “will interfere,” noting that many people seemed to “prefer partying.”

The largely uninhabited and arid land around the village — known as a setting for the film “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly,” dinosaur fossils and purple-tinted cured beef — is in the path of totality.

As such, it has drawn legions of astronomy enthusiasts from around Spain and the world, looking to experience the eclipse from what would usually be a place of solitude. Yet it has also been pulled into the orbit of the big eclipse-night party, leading Ms. Carretero-Castrillo to worry that a once-in-a-lifetime chance to instill villagers with a love of science was being eclipsed by Eclipse-fest.

“Sometimes, it’s difficult to put a value on science,” she said, wearing a blue T-shirt branded with the logo of the observatory she works for in Chile.

Ms. Carretero-Castrillo was raised in the Canary Islands but spent her summers in the village. Her career as an astrophysicist has since brought her to Barcelona, where she earned a doctorate, and won her acclaim for helping to identify 175 “massive runaway stars,” or stars that move at unusually high speeds across space.

In the days and hours leading up to totality, she did her best to put the emphasis on the heavens, giving presentations and holding eclipse workshops in the area.

She was joined by her family, who wore “Mar’s Stars” T-shirts, and her partner, Martí Roset, 30, a mathematician who killed time by working out number theory equations in his notebook. (“He’s my boyfriend,” she said with a knowing nod to their shared passions.)

On Tuesday morning, she stood between a “Solar Eclipse 2026 in Rural Spain” slide show and a few dozen older residents, many in wheelchairs. This would be the first eclipse on the Spanish mainland since 1905, she said.

“Was anyone here born in 1905?” she said. “Almost?”

Afterward, she sat with them around tables and helped with eclipse-themed crosswords (among the answers: “moon” and “glasses”) and card games in which she helped a 101-year-old woman put the stages of the eclipse in order.

In the back of the room, her father, Juan José Carretero, 60, marveled at his daughter’s commitment to spreading the scientific gospel. Still, his interests were somewhat divided. He’d watch the eclipse up on the hill with her, he said, but he also wanted to check out the party.

“It reminds me a bit of the raves they hold in Spain — raves where people come from various countries,” Mr. Carretero said.

She had originally, she said, hoped to give a scientific talk at the village hall on the day of the eclipse. But the mayor told her “we have many people for the party, I don’t know if we will have the space,” she recalled.

They finally agreed that she could hold it the day before, and it seemed the entire town showed up.

“We have a space problem,” she ebulliently told the standing-room-only crowd. “I’m going to tell you everything you need to know about the eclipse.”

She repeated the presentation she gave the group of older residents, stressing that she was a local girl and encouraging them to join her gathering on Wednesday evening for hilltop colander experiments. At the talk’s conclusion, a 12-year-old boy came up to her and asked what he could do to follow in her footsteps. She told him to keep asking questions.

“The eclipses we had in 1905 really pushed astronomy in Spain,” she said. “This is another opportunity.”

Yet even as she spoke, her competition was already setting up.

During her talk, a black van parked in the square and workers began setting up the D. J. booth and stage. The mayor, Galo Contreras Sanz, sped onto the square, dashed into his office and retrieved eclipse glasses to hand out to the departing townspeople.

Mr. Contreras Sanz said that while only locals came to hear the astronomer’s talk, the party would draw people from all over. (He himself, he said, would watch the eclipse from up in the church bell tower. “The view is going to be amazing,” he said.)

He greeted Ms. Carretero-Castrillo and they spoke politely, but guardedly, about the eclipse and the party. As she left to join her family, friends and dozens of other locals in the town’s watering hole, she and her boyfriend watched tests of the laser lights on the church’s stone tower. The party, her boyfriend said, looked like it was “going to be fun.”

On Wednesday afternoon, as Ms. Carretero-Castrillo gave another packed talk in a nearby town, partygoers started putting up tents and filing into the town hall to collect their orange ribbon wrist bands and Eclipse-Fest hats.

Nacho Donoso, 50, an out-of-towner from Madrid, said the promoter’s parties were always top notch, and for many, “it doesn’t matter that there’s going to be an eclipse.”

But the party’s organizer, Jorge Barrero, who handed out eclipse glasses, picnic-spot recommendations and hats and bracelets, said the eclipse would still be the star of the show.

“The eclipse gives you the right here, the right now,” said Mr. Barrero, 51, a chemist by training and former science ministry employee.

He said there would be no music for the minute or so of total eclipse, “out of respect.” The D. J. s would start playing at 10 p. m., he added, and go until a breakfast of churros and chocolate more than eight hours later.

About a half an hour before the eclipse began, Ms. Carretero-Castrillo and her family arrived up on the hill. People asked for cues about when to put on and take off the protective glasses.

“Just do what I do,” she told them.

Moments before the total eclipse, as the D. J. down in the square played the theme from “2001: A Space Odyssey,” the hill remained quiet.

Then, the sun vanished.

Ms. Carretero-Castrillo shouted, “now, now, now,” and everyone took off their glasses. Day turned dark and she kissed her boyfriend and looked around with wonder.

For nearly the next hour, she answered lingering scientific questions. When the eclipsed sun had set and most everyone had left, she, too, descended the hill, exhausted but satisfied with how much everyone had learned.

As she arrived at the square, and the D. J. set was about to begin, she said she would join the party. If the music moved her, she said, “I will go until the churros.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting.

Jason Horowitz is the Madrid bureau chief for The Times, covering Spain, Portugal and the way people live throughout Europe.

Israeli Settlers Are Out of Control. Could an Election Change That?

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Nicholas Kristof

By Nicholas Kristof

Opinion Columnist, who visited West Bank villages that have faced settler attacks.

Benjamin Netanyahu is the longest-serving prime minister Israel has had, as well as its most disastrous for Jews and Palestinians alike.

Gaza has faded somewhat from global consciousness but remains in desperate shape with no clear path forward, while the West Bank endures brutal attacks by settlers that create a widening chasm between Israel and the rest of the world. All this is Netanyahu’s legacy.

Finally, polls suggest a chance that his malignant reign may come to an end with October’s election in Israel.

The question hanging over the region is whether, if he is ousted, what follows will be better. The answer I hear from experts is: Yes, maybe to a degree. Don’t expect a Palestinian state or a transformation. But the worst excesses and brutality might be reined in.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief, seems the most likely to lead Israel if Netanyahu proves politically mortal, and Eisenkot is by no means a dove. He is well known for helping to formulate the Dahiya doctrine: Respond to attacks with overwhelming, disproportionate destruction to create deterrence. It is named after the Beirut suburb where Israel applied it two decades ago, and it’s sometimes seen as a forerunner of Netanyahu’s demolition of Gaza.

But Eisenkot also withdrew from Netanyahu’s war cabinet because of disagreements over the direction of the Gaza war (in which he lost a son, which has made him a particularly sympathetic figure in Israeli politics). His comments suggest that he would try to move Israel in a more moderate direction and control the violent settlers in the West Bank who have been committing terror attacks against Palestinians.

“Eisenkot would make a substantial difference in terms of calming the waters on the one hand and cracking down on lawlessness,” said Daniel Kurtzer, a former American ambassador to Israel who now teaches at Princeton.

Most settlers are not violent, and some live in settlements (which are generally regarded as illegal under international law) not for ideological reasons but because it is cheap. But it is also true that settler attacks causing damage or injury are at the highest level in two decades, with an average of five a day last year. That rose to six a day in the first half of this year, according to United Nations figures.

About 1,100 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli soldiers or settlers since the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attack on Israel, the United Nations says. The circumstances are often disputed, but the total includes at least 243 children.

Under Netanyahu, the Israeli Army increasingly takes the side of settlers, even when they are engaging in illegal or violent behavior, according to Palestinians, Israeli human rights groups, news accounts and others. “The army routinely accompanies settlers in attacks,” a U. N. commission reported.

What all this means in practice is misery for people like Abdel-Majeed Hassan, a Palestinian farmer in his 70s whom I’ve visited periodically for many years. He is a soft-spoken shepherd in the village of Qusra, deeply proud that all 12 of his children attended university.

“My sheep sent my children to university,” he told me during an April visit as he herded his flock.

Over the years, settlers have shot Hassan in the leg, he said, partly burned his home (twice), stolen his sheep, invaded his home, blocked his access to his olive trees, tried to burn his sheep alive, prevented him from accessing the spring where he drew water for his animals, threatened his grandchildren, destroyed five of his vehicles and hurled rocks at him more times than he can count, according to accounts by him, fellow villagers and human rights monitors.

“It’s getting worse,” he told me. Before, the Israel Defense Forces would sometimes restrain the settlers, he said, but now they often protect them. As we spoke, one of his sons called to warn that 20 or more settlers were approaching. “They will start throwing stones, and if they see a car, they will burn it,” Hassan told me resignedly.

One development that makes a clampdown on extremist settlers more possible is that growing numbers of prominent Israelis are acknowledging the savagery of the attacks and demanding that the government crack down.

Two former prime ministers and other former senior figures signed a joint letter this summer calling on Netanyahu to “immediately take all measures necessary to terminate the Jewish terror that has been widespread” in the West Bank.

Tamir Pardo, a former head of the Mossad security agency, told Israeli television after touring West Bank villages: “My mother was a Holocaust survivor, and what I saw reminded me of the events that happened against Jews in the last century.”

Jonatan Shimshoni, a retired Israeli brigadier general, put it this way: “Israel is now using its power to start ridding the West Bank of Palestinians.” Even Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned settler attacks as “a wave of terrible violence that is being carried out by an anarchist mob.”

Terrorism is doing its job, instilling fear and leaving entire families wondering whether to flee.

“We think about leaving a lot,” Shifa Abuaram, 54, told me when I visited the remote Palestinian hamlet of Halawa, under regular attack by settlers. “I worry a lot about my children. I have young daughters, teenagers, and I fear the settlers might rape them.”

Settlers have invaded homes in Halawa, handcuffed and beaten the men, burned one home to the ground, cut water pipes, uprooted olive and pomegranate trees, destroyed solar panels and water tanks and pounded on latrines with women inside, multiple villagers told me. Sometimes the settlers are armed with American assault rifles, they said.

Perhaps scariest of all for parents, the settlers rammed the vehicle that takes children to their school, the parents and children told me.

“I got scared when they attacked our car,” one girl who was inside, Kawther, 9, told me.

When I was leaving Halawa, a group of settlers blocked our vehicle. I spoke to the settlers in English, asking to interview them for The New York Times; they declined and retreated.

The Trump administration is notably soft on this kind of terrorism, even when Palestinian Americans are injured or killed. That happened in February: Settlers killed a 19-year-old American citizen in the West Bank.

But in the United States, West Bank attacks by settlers are further draining Israel and Netanyahu of support. An Economist/YouGov survey last month found that Americans by a 22-percentage-point margin favor arresting Netanyahu for alleged war crimes in Gaza. And attitude shifts are evident not just among Democrats: An Emerson poll found that two-thirds of independent voters believe America gives too much aid to Israel.

The brutality of settler attacks should rouse American officials as well. Because of U. S. support for Israel’s security apparatus, we Americans are enabling some of this terrorism.

My colleague Thomas L. Friedman has aptly called Netanyahu not just the worst leader in Israel’s history but also “maybe in all of Jewish history.” And that’s a lot of history. What I know personally from my reporting on the ground in the West Bank and Gaza for many years is that countless lives have been destroyed to serve Netanyahu’s political career, and that at least until recently we Americans haven’t reflected adequately on our own complicity.

I’m hoping that Netanyahu’s political end is coming, and that someone like Eisenkot will dial back the repression. But even if that happens, let’s be honest: Gazans will still suffer unconscionably, and the West Bank will remain oppressed and unequal.

“Even if a new government wanted to rein in violent settlers, it would be difficult,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel. “Settlers have been given weapons and vehicles by the government, they’re emboldened, and the Israeli Zionist left and center has never rushed to use violence or other strong measures against Israeli Jews. This genie might not fit neatly back into its bottle.”

It's easy for Americans to point fingers at others, but I wrote this in part because I wanted to call attention to what I see as American complicity in the settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. The U. S. has provided some of the weapons that end up used by settlers in these assaults, we've helped underwrite the security establishment and I think we've been too slow to speak up. Don't we bear some responsibility as well?

Suit Challenges Plan to Sell Early Access to Trump’s Truth Social Posts

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The lawsuit filed in federal court said President Trump “stands to gain financially by giving ‘market-moving’ government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company.”

By Matthew Goldstein

A lawsuit filed Wednesday in federal court in New York challenges a plan to sell early access to President Trump’s posts on Truth Social for up to $100,000 a month, arguing the First Amendment “guarantees equal access to the President’s public announcements.”

The lawsuit also charged Mr. Trump “stands to gain financially by giving ‘market-moving’ government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company.” The complaint was filed by Freedom of The Press Foundation and The Intercept.

The lawsuit noted that since Mr. Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he has published thousands of posts on Truth Social that were not followed up by any official announcement from the White House. “In other words, President Trump’s posts are the only way to get official government news,” the lawsuit said.

In the complaint, lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that the First Amendment requires any restriction on equal access to public information to “serve a legitimate governmental purpose.” Selling early access to Mr. Trump’s posts to private buyers does not meet that constitutional test, they said.

In a statement, a company spokesman said “left wing activists are trying to wrongly weaponize the courts to censor” Mr. Trump and to harm the company’s shareholders.

Mr. Trump is the largest shareholder in Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns Truth Social. His eldest son Donald Jr. is a board member and oversees a trust that controls his father’s stake. The suit names Mr. Trump and other White House officials as defendants, but does not name Trump Media.

The lawsuit comes after weeks of criticism from some Congressional Democrats, who said the fast-feed service would give an unfair market advantage to some traders. Some have also said Trump Media is attempting to boost its sagging stock price by improperly monetizing Mr. Trump’s posts.

The company, which has lost money ever since it went public in 2024, said in a conference call with investors on Monday that the criticism of the new product is misplaced. During the call, Kevin McGurn, the company’s interim chief executive, said, “Our customers will get published and publicly available posts fractionally faster” than everyone else. He added that this is a “well-established business practice.”

The company said that more than 10 customers — mostly trading firms — have signed up for the service. The company also said several news organizations have inquired about buying the product.

Trading firms that rely on algorithmic programs can use the new Truth Social product to make lightning-fast trades tied to Mr. Trump’s policy announcements that contain potential market-moving information. For these high-frequency trading firms, being able to trade faster than the competition can mean substantial profits.

Trump Media has not disclosed the names of its customers. It also has said the new product will give customers early access to other high-profile posters on Truth Social.

Ever since its debut in 2022, the main draw on Truth Social has been Mr. Trump, but the platform has lagged well behind X, Threads and Bluesky in getting new users. And lately traffic to Truth Social has dropped dramatically. In July, the overall number of monthly visitors to Truth Social was down about 36 percent from a year ago, according to estimates by the online tracking firm Similarweb. Monthly visitors to the site also fell in June as well.

The falloff in Truth Social traffic comes as Trump Media continues to lose money and struggles to generate revenue. In the second quarter ended June 30, the company posted a net loss of $238.1 million, largely driven by the decline in value of a substantial investment Trump Media made in Bitcoin last year. The company took in $1.7 million in revenue in the same period, most of that tied to advertising on Truth Social.

Matthew Goldstein is a Times reporter who covers Wall Street and white-collar crime and housing issues.

Should the M. M. R. Vaccine Be Split Into Three Separate Shots?

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump is calling for immunizations for measles, mumps and rubella to be given in individual jabs in three different appointments instead of the standard combination shot.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

President Trump issued an executive order this week calling for immunizations for measles, mumps and rubella, a mainstay of vaccination programs worldwide, to be offered as three individual jabs given at separate times, instead of in one combination shot.

In an Oval Office signing ceremony, the president made a frightening and unsubstantiated claim about the combination shot. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal.”

Researchers have not linked the combination M. M. R. shot to a risk of death, and there is no evidence that it is dangerous or that splitting it into its three components is any safer or more effective, vaccine experts said. Combination shots for the diseases have been used in the United States since 1971, and were introduced only after careful comparison against individual shots. They have been given to hundreds of millions of children.

What’s more, separate vaccines for measles, mumps or rubella have not been available in the United States for many years. Vaccine manufacturers said it would take a minimum of five to 10 years for them to be tested and made available.

“We don’t have any way to implement what he’s suggesting,” said Dr. Kathryn Edwards, a retired vaccinologist and professor emerita at Vanderbilt University who studied individual and combination vaccines.

“It’s just simply more confusion for the poor parents,” Dr. Edwards said. “And it’s just showing the world that our health system and our H. H. S. and our president are totally uninformed,” she said, referring to the Department of Health and Human Services.

Mr. Trump’s executive order does not carry legal weight and does not affect the availability of the current combination vaccines or their reimbursement by insurance companies. States set requirements for which shots children should get, and vaccine mandates across Republican and Democratic states have been remarkably similar over decades.

If some states opt to follow Mr. Trump’s executive order and require the shots to be given individually, parents would need to bring their children to three separate appointments. And the children would receive even more needle pricks than they currently do. (Mr. Trump and Mr. Kennedy have repeatedly said American children receive too many shots — although the numbers they give are vastly inaccurate. Children in the United States may receive 35 shots by age 5, including a seasonal flu shot, not 72 as the officials have repeatedly said.)

Combination shots were developed in part to address parents’ worries that their children were becoming “pin cushions” for vaccines, said Dr. Frank DeStefano, who led the vaccine safety office at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 2009 to 2021. No safety concerns emerged in the years of clinical trials that compared the two approaches.

“It’s never been demonstrated that separating the vaccines is any safer than combined vaccines,” he said.

Mr. Trump said his executive order was based primarily on unsubstantiated theories that childhood vaccines can cause autism. Those concerns have been thoroughly researched and debunked since a 1998 study, which was later retracted and exposed as fraud, floated the idea that the measles vaccine caused autism. But Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have nevertheless fueled the theory for years, at times pointing to the combination M. M. R. vaccine, the hepatitis B vaccine or the entire childhood vaccination schedule as possible culprits.

“These ideas never die,” Dr. DeStefano said. “They’re zombie ideas. They keep popping up.”

The combined M. M. R. vaccine is associated with a very small risk of seizures if a child develops a fever, but that type of seizure — which can occur after any high fever, including one that may develop after receiving a single shot — does not cause long-term harm, according to the C. D. C.

“Most people who get M. M. R. vaccine do not have any serious problems with it,” the agency’s website says. “Getting M. M. R. vaccine is much safer than getting measles, mumps or rubella.”

Requiring parents to bring their children in for three separate visits to receive that protection may deter some from getting the required shots and decrease immunization rates, or at least delay protection for vulnerable young children. In studies that compared timing of shots, parents who had to bring their children in more often ended up dropping out because of the inconvenience, Dr. Edwards said.

Japan offers a cautionary tale for countries that rescind combination shots. In 1993, the country paused use of an M. M. R. vaccine containing the Urabe mumps virus — which is different from the one used in the United States and Europe — because it caused aseptic meningitis in 0.05 percent of the recipients.

That type of meningitis resolves on its own and does not cause long-term damage. Still, responding to parents’ concerns, Japan switched to recommending individual shots for measles and rubella, and made the stand-alone mumps shot voluntary. Use of the mumps shot quickly “dropped to almost nothing,” said Dr. Margie Andreae, a pediatrician at the University of Michigan who studied the events.

Cases of mumps soared, and caused aseptic meningitis in 1.24 percent of the children, as well as more harmful types of meningitis, brain damage and hearing loss.

And vaccination for measles and rubella also plummeted, leading to surges in those illnesses. “There’s strong evidence that splitting multicomponent vaccines into single components leads to decrease in immunization coverage rates,” Dr. Andreae said.

If immunization rates for measles in the United States drop to a similar level, according to one modeling study, the country may see 11.1 million cases of measles over 25 years. This year, a much smaller drop in the vaccination rate has already led to the highest number of measles cases observed in more than 25 years.

The M. M. R. vaccine relies on weakened live viruses, which change over time, so companies cannot simply resurrect the individual shots, which were phased out in 2009.

“Essentially, these would be considered three investigational vaccines and would require full clinical trial testing and regulatory review for each new product to be licensed,” said Dr. Paula Annunziato, who heads vaccine clinical research at the pharmaceutical company Merck, which manufactures one of the two M. M. R. shots available in the United States.

Alison Hunt, a spokeswoman for the pharmaceutical company GSK, which makes the other one, said, “We stand by the safety and effectiveness of our combination vaccines, which are backed by decades of global use and robust scientific evidence.”

Combination shots support public health by “reducing missed doses, improving immunization coverage and minimizing the burden on families and health care systems,” she said.

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

ICE Agent Points Gun at Woman in Car in Virginia, Videos Show

The New York Times August 12, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The agent accused the woman of trying to run him over with her vehicle, a claim she denied. It was the latest tense encounter between a federal agent and a driver.

By Madaleine Rubin

A federal agent on Monday brandished a gun at a Virginia woman who had shouted at him, according to videos of the encounter, the latest in a string of clashes between immigration agents and drivers.

The woman, Carolina Molina, 36, said in an interview that around 3 p. m. on Monday, several Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents surrounded her car in a shopping center in Falls Church, Va., after she had yelled at them as they detained people on a sidewalk nearby.

Ms. Molina had pulled into a parking spot and backed out and was driving through the center when agents encircled her, blocking her vehicle by parking cars behind and in front of her, a dashboard video shows.

The agents repeatedly accused her of trying to run them over with her car and threatened to arrest her. But in videos captured from several angles, there is no indication that Ms. Molina had tried to harm the agents.

During the roughly one-minute interaction, Ms. Molina’s car does not move, according to the videos, which she recorded on her cellphone and the car’s dashboard camera and then shared on social media.

As one masked agent approached her car, he pulled his gun from its holster and held it up to the car window at an angle, pointing it at Ms. Molina as he shouted at her. Ms. Molina warned him that she was videotaping.

“This is the one that tried to run us over,” the agent who pulled the gun told a colleague as the masked agents crowded around her. “I will arrest you. Keep it up,” he shouted at Ms. Molina.

But then, the agents left, according to Ms. Molina, a mother of two. She said she had never used her car as a weapon while she drove through the shopping center or before.

“There is no way I would put myself at risk knowing I have two girls to go home to, to go and chase after ICE agents,” said Ms. Molina, a licensed counselor who works with undocumented people.

Representative Don Beyer, a Democrat whose district includes Falls Church, said that his staff had spoken to Ms. Molina and “will be demanding answers and consequences.”

The Department of Homeland Security said in an unsigned statement late Tuesday that the agents had been trying to detain undocumented migrants who had committed crimes when they were approached by Ms. Molina, whom the agency called an “anti-ICE agitator.”

The D. H. S. said she had driven circles around the officers and tried to harm them with her vehicle to help the migrants get away. The agents were afraid, the department said, when they stopped Ms. Molina in the shopping center.

The agency did not provide any videos of the encounter or events leading up to it. Ms. Molina, whose videos do not capture events outside the shopping center, was not detained and has not been criminally charged.

The confrontation was just the latest involving federal agents and drivers amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Since last year, more than 20 people in their cars have been shot at by federal agents, some fatally. In July, two men were killed in their vehicles during encounters with ICE agents, in Houston and Maine. In January, federal agents shot Renee Good, a U. S. citizen, in Minneapolis. The killing set off weeks of protests nationally.

In many cases, federal officials have defended the agents’ actions, saying they were justified acts of self-defense. The department reiterated that defense on Tuesday, saying that “when faced with dangerous circumstances, D. H. S. law enforcement used their training to protect themselves, their fellow officers and the public.”

After huge immigration operations in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis that roiled entire cities, federal authorities are using lower-profile tactics. They are reinvigorating the president’s crackdown after a spring slowdown; daily arrests of immigrants doubled in the last week of June and have continued to increase.

Ms. Molina, a mental health therapist in Loudoun County, Va., is a first-generation American whose parents emigrated from El Salvador. She conducts psychological evaluations for clients in immigration cases and was in Falls Church on Monday to distribute business cards at the offices of several immigration lawyers, she said.

Ms. Molina said she had been driving through Falls Church when she witnessed federal agents apprehending two men. She said that she rolled down her window and shouted at the agents. She said she saw them in the shopping center minutes later and shouted again, profanely.

“You almost ran us over,” an agent says to Ms. Molina in the video, after asking if she had followed his vehicle. He kept his gun pointed at her during the exchange.

Ms. Molina, who remained in her car, denied the agent’s accusation and said that she had not been following his vehicle.

“I’m a legal citizen,” she told him.

“I don’t care,” one agent replied, threatening to arrest Ms. Molina.

“Doesn’t matter,” another said.

Mr. Beyer, the lawmaker, said in his statement that “the habitual dishonesty and dangerous and unjustified escalation seen in this video matches what we have seen from ICE agents across the country.”

He added that “this kind of misconduct and threat of force against members of our communities cannot be tolerated.”

How the Polls Got it So Wrong in Wisconsin

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Francesca Hong, the democratic socialist running in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor, had a double-digit lead in polls as recently as last week. Then she lost. What happened?

By Bayliss Wagner and Ruth Igielnik

For months, polls indicated that Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, was far and away the front-runner in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin.

Then David Crowley, a moderate and the chief executive of Milwaukee County, won the race, albeit narrowly.

The result comes just one week after Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, significantly underperformed polls to eke out a narrow victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary.

Why were the polls so wrong?

Possible explanations range from a genuine, last-minute change in voter sentiment — Ms. Hong, a state representative, faced significant negative publicity in the closing days of the race — to miscalculations by pollsters about the makeup of the primary electorate.

The disparity between polls and results in Wisconsin and Michigan prompted Frank Luntz, a Republican pollster and consultant, to jokingly call for “a total and complete shutdown of primary polling in the Midwestern United States until we can figure out what the hell is going on” in an early-morning X post on Wednesday.

The Wisconsin primary drew a crowded field of candidates after Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, announced last summer that he would not seek re-election. Here’s what experts, pollsters and the data say about the results of the Democratic primary to replace him:

The Wisconsin governor’s race was tumultuous. Mr. Crowley had suspended his campaign just over a month ago after polls indicated he had failed to gain traction. Then he re-entered the contest and won.

“The polls were made out of date very quickly” as a result, said Celinda Lake, a Democratic pollster from Michigan.

In a survey taken by Marquette Law School just after Mr. Crowley re-entered the race in mid-July, 38 percent of respondents said they favored Ms. Hong. Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor, was in second place at 16 percent, and Mr. Crowley had just 7 percent of the vote.

But almost as large as Ms. Hong’s vote share was the percentage of undecided survey respondents: 34 percent.

Mr. Barnes dropped out after that poll was released.

In the weeks that followed, surveys continued to show voter support was fractured among Ms. Hong’s numerous opponents.

As recently as last week, a poll conducted by Mr. Crowley’s campaign found him trailing Ms. Hong by 18 percentage points. He trailed Ms. Hong by 22 points in another poll from State Navigate, which surveys in state-level elections.

Polls failed to predict the outcome of Tuesday’s election, but they did not significantly overestimate Ms. Hong’s portion of the vote. Most surveys estimated she would win about 40 percent of the vote, and she ended up winning 39 percent.

What changed was Mr. Crowley’s support. In a ballot-counting marathon that stretched into the wee hours of Wednesday morning, he over-performed the Marquette poll’s estimate by more than 30 points.

In the end, Mr. Crowley was less than half of a percentage point — or just under 4,000 votes — ahead of Ms. Hong on Wednesday morning, with more than 95 percent of ballots counted.

Mr. Crowley may owe much of his success to the support of previously undecided voters.

In primaries, news coverage and campaign advertising tend to increase in the last weeks of the race. And voters may not research candidates until minutes before they walk into the voting booth. In some Wisconsin polls, as many as one-third of voters said they were undecided heading into Election Day.

“It is well known that voters in Wisconsin tend to make up their minds, tend to start paying attention to primary elections pretty late in the game,” said Anthony Chergosky, an associate professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse.

Ms. Hong faced a barrage of negative press in the election’s final days, after six-year-old social media posts surfaced in which she called to defund and abolish the police and “cancel Thanksgiving.”

Mr. Crowley was not as well-known to voters before he re-entered the race in July. Mr. Evers campaigned energetically for him, and a super PAC supporting him also spent heavily on ads disparaging Ms. Hong in recent weeks.

The governor’s late endorsement made the race unusual, said Charles Franklin, who conducts the Marquette University Law School poll.

“In our final poll, 36 percent of Democratic primary voters said that endorsement made them more likely to support Crowley,” said Mr. Franklin. “Evers’s job approval with Democrats was also over 85 percent.”

Mr. Crowley may also have consolidated support from moderates after the early establishment-backed candidate, Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, and Mr. Barnes ended their campaigns last month.

Even after an internal poll found that Mr. Crowley was trailing Ms. Hong last week, his campaign manager predicted that polls would not reflect the primary results.

In a memo to supporters on Aug. 5 obtained by The New York Times, the campaign manager, Garren Randolph, argued that Wisconsin surveys overrepresented voters between the ages of 18 and 45. In some cases, polls expected twice as many young voters as actually showed up to vote in 2018 and 2022. Ms. Hong was strongest among young voters, according to the internal poll.

Across elections, primary voters tend to be older, and Wisconsin is no exception. Older voters and moderates were also more likely to remain undecided until close to the end, Mr. Franklin said, based on his polling data.

Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of the firm State Navigate, which conducted polls in Wisconsin, suggested that Ms. Hong’s early and enthusiastic supporters may simply have been more willing to respond to polls, thus skewing the results.

“One candidate’s supporters were just more eager to answer the poll,” Mr. Nuttycombe said.

Pollsters have long grappled with what is known as nonresponse bias, where certain voters may be more likely — or less likely — to respond to a poll.

The same issue may have occurred in Michigan. In a post-mortem of that state’s Democratic Senate primary, Adam Carlson, a Democratic pollster, speculated that the “main driving factor” behind the polling miss was selective responsiveness of voters.

“El-Sayed’s supporters were more fired up and willing to take polls down the stretch, but more enthusiasm does not necessarily equal more votes,” Mr. Carlson, the founding partner of Zenith Research, wrote in a post-mortem analysis on Monday.

Conducting surveys in partisan primaries has long been a challenge for pollsters, requiring them to make assumptions about the partisan composition of who will actually turn out to vote.

That is particularly difficult in states like Wisconsin and Michigan that hold open primaries and where voters are not registered by party.

As pollsters attempt to target likely Democratic primary voters in surveys, they are often unsure about the percentage of Republicans and independents who might vote in a given election.

Mr. Nuttycombe said polls likely underestimated the Republican share of the electorate.

“If Republicans did vote, they went overwhelmingly anti-Hong,” he said.

Mr. Carlson noted that in the Michigan Senate primary his likely voter model — which pollsters use to estimate who will actually vote in an election — probably underrepresented seniors, low-income Michiganders and self-identified Republicans.

Julie Bosman contributed reporting.

For me, one of the biggest takeaways here is that a significant number of Wisconsin voters— more than one-third in this case— remained undecided until the last weeks of the primary. It's a good reminder to pay attention to the "undecided" numbers in polls, rather than just the head-to-head comparisons between candidates, and a lesson about how voters make their decisions.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Ruth Igielnik is a Times polling editor who conducts polls and analyzes and reports on the results.

By Erica L. Green

President Trump said Wednesday that Karoline Leavitt, his press secretary, would step down at the end of the month.

In a post on Truth Social, Mr. Trump said that Ms. Leavitt, who recently returned from maternity leave after giving birth to her second child, would be departing to spend time with her young children and family — a decision he said “I totally understand and respect.”

Ms. Leavitt, the youngest person to assume the role, worked for Mr. Trump in his first term and on his second campaign. She said in a post on social media that serving as press secretary over the past year and a half had “been the honor and adventure of a lifetime.”

“Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least,” Ms. Leavitt continued. “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.”

She added that she would “always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party,” and that she would remain on the front lines of the party’s fight against what she called an “existential threat” by Democrats.

“My fight is entering a new phase,” she added, “but it is far from over.”

Erica L. Green is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

A Bright Spot in Colombia as Rescuers Free Quake Victim

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Sometimes you get lucky.

This is Diana Marcela Troncoso. For almost 30 hours, she was trapped in earthquake debris. She gripped the arm of a Colombian firefighter like a lifeline.

As rescuers worked to free her, a police doctor, Claudia Milanes, monitored Ms. Troncoso’s vital signs, making sure she was hydrated.

At least 181 people died in Colombia after the quake. But not Ms. Troncoso. “Diana! Diana!” the crowd chanted as she was carried out. Some applauded.

In Cali, mountains of debris like this one are now commonplace. Many people are still missing.

Military forces were deployed to help the civil authorities cordon off the hardest-hit cities and to coordinate the search for survivors.

But ordinary citizens pitched in, too. They mobilized to gather supplies, food and hydration for the rescue teams.

Supported by

By The New York Times

Diana Marcela Troncoso, a biomedical engineer, was just one of more than 200 people feared trapped alive on Tuesday in the rubble of Cali, the city perhaps hardest hit by the earthquake that rocked Colombia a day earlier.

As emergency workers labored to find buried victims elsewhere in the city, firefighters from the capital, Bogotá, were able to extricate Ms. Troncoso, who is 31.

To get to her, firefighters had to make their way through a narrow tunnel under over 20 feet of rubble. On the surface, it was over 94 degrees Fahrenheit. In the tunnel, it was even hotter, and electrolyte drinks were kept close at hand.

A crowd of onlookers cheered on the rescuers. They could hear a newly freed Ms. Troncoso cry in pain when she was strapped to a backboard. Then they watched as firefighters carefully navigated the debris field and delivered her to a waiting ambulance.

But with the first 48 hours after a disaster like the quake considered critical, the rescue workers could not afford to linger.

Genevieve Glatsky contributed reporting from Cali, Colombia.
