How Crowley Eked Out a Win in the Wisconsin Governor Primary

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A shifting race and a key endorsement helped the moderate Democrat overcome his progressive challenger, Francesca Hong, voters said.

By Julie Bosman

Reporting from Milwaukee

Miriam Shelef, a physician in Madison, Wis., had a hunch that the polls were off.

Two weekends ago, after researching the candidates in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor, she began canvassing for David Crowley, whose record as the Milwaukee County executive impressed her.

At one house after another in her west side neighborhood, people changed their minds on the spot about supporting other candidates after hearing Dr. Shelef talk about Mr. Crowley’s perceived electability and his work on housing and cutting carbon emissions. One woman gave Dr. Shelef a warm hug, grabbed a Crowley sign and plunked it in her yard.

“I was like, oh my gosh, I think there’s clearly late enthusiasm for him,” Dr. Shelef said. “I was amazed at how popular Crowley was at the doors.”

On Wednesday morning, Wisconsin Democrats woke up to an unexpected result, as Mr. Crowley, a moderate who had briefly dropped out of the race, narrowly beat Francesca Hong, a chef and democratic socialist who had led in the polls for months.

With 95 percent of the votes counted, Mr. Crowley edged out Ms. Hong by fewer than 4,000 votes to the relief of the Wisconsin Democratic establishment, which had feared that Ms. Hong would lose in a November matchup with Representative Tom Tiffany, a Republican endorsed by President Trump.

Mr. Crowley’s 11th-hour surge may have been buoyed by the race’s rapid shifts in its final days, according to interviews with campaign officials, volunteers and voters. Mr. Crowley benefited from Ms. Hong’s missteps on social media and in national TV interviews as she backtracked from comments about hating Thanksgiving and abolishing the police.

He toured the state with Gov. Tony Evers, a popular leader who pulled Mr. Crowley back into the race after he abandoned his campaign last month and endorsed him. Perhaps most crucially, Mr. Crowley captured the notice of a large number of voters who had missed many of the primary’s earlier twists and remained undecided near the end.

In an interview, Mr. Crowley said that traveling with Mr. Evers showed voters that he could “coalesce people across the political spectrum to build the type of coalition needed to win,” he said. “That’s what we’re able to do, and I think that’s how we won this race.”

Election results showed that Mr. Crowley was popular across Wisconsin. He easily beat the other candidates in the Milwaukee region, won a large number of rural counties and even captured 37 percent of the vote to Ms. Hong’s 44 percent in Dane County, a liberal stronghold that was her physical and philosophical home base.

Many voters said they had tuned into the primary only in the last week, missing what had been a bumpy and dramatic campaign throughout the year. When they started paying attention, they said, Mr. Evers’s endorsement helped them decide.

One Crowley voter, Pam McAllister, a 72-year-old retired pharmacist in Verona, Wis., said on Tuesday that she disliked Ms. Hong’s politics. Her second-most important reason for voting for Mr. Crowley: “Because Evers endorsed him.”

“Evers’s endorsement gave Crowley attention and voters the encouragement to give Crowley a look,” said Alex Lasry, a prominent Democrat in Wisconsin who supported Mr. Crowley. “Once they did, they saw Crowley was not only part of the next generation of leaders, but also very experienced and the right person to lead Wisconsin forward.”

After touring the state with Mr. Crowley for days, Mr. Evers appeared last weekend to be either resigned or confident. On Saturday night, he headed to a theater in rural Spring Green for some Shakespeare under the stars.

At one point in a soliloquy during “The Two Gentlemen of Verona,” an actor made a knowing reference to the perfect lover having little to say — and looked directly to the front row at Mr. Evers, who is not known for his loquaciousness. The audience burst into laughter.

On Wednesday morning, after Mr. Tiffany’s overwhelming primary victory, Republicans hinted that they would frame the general election campaign as a battle against leftist extremism despite Mr. Crowley’s moderate credentials.

“Democrats are moving further and further to the left,” Brian Schimming, the chairman of WisGOP, said in a statement. “This election comes down to the difference between common sense and radicalism.”

Mr. Crowley’s first stop on Wednesday was in Milwaukee, where he was mobbed with hugs from supporters and, in his remarks, promised to leave behind the divisive Democratic primary and focus on Mr. Tiffany.

One Crowley supporter in attendance, Stephanie Johnson, said that she had been drawn to his campaign because of his work for low-income people in Milwaukee, especially the homeless. “You hear everybody talk about the working class, but what about the ones at the bottom?” she said.

Mr. Crowley specifically thanked Ms. Hong, saying that her campaign “reminded people across Wisconsin that there are no long shots when it comes to believing in a better future and fighting to expand opportunity for every family.” They later had breakfast with other Democrats in Madison before television cameras, sharing a meal intended to show unity for the campaign ahead.

Julie Bosman is the Chicago bureau chief for The Times, writing and reporting stories from around the Midwest.

The White House aides Natalie Harp and Dan Scavino were among those traveling with the president on a military jet.

By Maggie Haberman

When President Trump sneaked out of Turkey last month in a clandestine operation, he brought a select few with him on the secret flight.

The White House aides Natalie Harp, Dan Scavino and Walt Nauta, as well as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, were all traveling with the president on a military jet, a U. S. official said.

Two cabinet members, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, left the country on the decoy flight, which was an older model of Air Force One, the U. S. official and a second official said. That plane carried other aides who had been attending the NATO summit in Ankara, along with journalists.

Mr. Trump had said he would be taking the older plane “for old time’s sake” for the first leg of the trip home, from Turkey to Britain.

But the reality was that U. S. officials had determined there was a credible threat to Air Force One. So Mr. Trump boarded the decoy Air Force One in front of the cameras, then sneaked out in a catering container elevated on a hydraulic lift.

Joining him on the other plane were Ms. Harp, his ever-present aide; Mr. Nauta, his longtime “body man” who now is the head of Oval Office operations; and Mr. Scavino, a deputy White House chief of staff and head of presidential personnel, who has also handled Mr. Trump’s social media for years.

Those names were reported earlier by CBS News.

Unlike Mr. Trump and the other passengers, Mr. Hegseth was seen publicly boarding the military jet, which apparently was part of the deception plan.

The reporters traveling on the older Air Force One were instructed to lower their window shades, without an explanation given; in hindsight, it kept them from catching a glimpse of Mr. Trump leaving the plane.

In addition to Mr. Rubio and Mr. Bessent, several senior White House and administration officials were on the older, decoy plane, according to one of the U. S. officials.

They included the top policy adviser Stephen Miller; the White House communications director, Steven Cheung; the staff secretary, Will Scharf; the deputy national security adviser, Michael Needham,; the deputy chief of staff Richard Walters; the aide Christopher Ambrosini; and staff members from the White House advance team, the official said.

A White House spokesman did not respond to an email seeking comment and asking for a full accounting of who was on the plane.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Driver Sets Record for Hydrogen-Powered Vehicle at More Than 406 M. P. H.

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Andy Green, a 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot from Britain, was already the only person to break the sound barrier on land. “The ground comes at you very, very quickly,” he said.

By Claire Moses

The fastest driver on Earth has set another record.

Andy Green, 64, the only person to break the sound barrier on land, set a record for the fastest land speed in a hydrogen-fueled internal-combustion vehicle on Tuesday, at 406.320 miles per hour (653.909 kilometers per hour). The record, set at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, was confirmed by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile, the governing body for motorsports.

“The ground comes at you very, very quickly,” Mr. Green, a former pilot for the Royal Air Force, said in a phone interview on Wednesday. “You’re driving five or six times as fast as on the interstate. Everything happens very quickly.”

Mr. Green was driving a JCB Hydromax — which looks more like a rocket on wheels than a car — “ the fastest hydrogen-powered vehicle of any kind in history,” according to JCB, the British machinery company that manufactured it. Beyond setting a land speed record, the company is hoping to use hydrogen engines in the products it builds, Mr. Green said.

No plumes of smoke were produced by this speed record: Hydrogen powers the vehicle and water comes out of the exhaust.

“This is as zero carbon as it gets,” Mr. Green said.

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the F. I. A. president, called the record a “historic milestone” in a statement. The previous land-speed record for a hydrogen combustion vehicle was 185.5 m. p. h., and was set in 2004 by the BMW H2R vehicle, according to F. I. A.

Mr. Green set the record on a 12-mile track on the Bonneville Salt Flats, a 30,000-acre expanse of hard, white salt crust on the Great Salt Lake Basin in Utah.

“You can physically see the curvature of the earth,” Mr. Green said. “This smooth surface is so long.”

How does it feel to be in a vehicle going 400 m. p. h.? Loud, and with heavy vibrations, Mr. Green said. As he accelerated, he looked farther in the distance, and the markers along the course came at him faster and faster, he said. Around him, there was nothing but white salt. The track seemed to get narrower. All of this is happening as he was sandwiched between two roaring engines in a cockpit that was built to fit his 6-foot-3 frame.

It takes about 72 seconds to get from 50 miles per hour to 400, Mr. Green said.

The Bonneville Salt Flats have been the site of speed races since 1912. Once part of a large prehistoric lake that covered a third of the state, the flats are composed mostly of table salt, according to the U. S. Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management.

Mr. Green said on Wednesday that he had considered himself to be retired from speed racing — until JCB called. In October 1997, he broke the sound barrier on land in the Black Rock Desert of Nevada, driving a jet-powered car at an average speed of 763.035 m. p. h. over two runs. That vehicle was powered by two Rolls-Royce engines from a Phantom fighter jet.

That run broke the overall land-speed record set in 1983 by Richard Noble, a British entrepreneur, who traveled at 633.4 m. p. h. with a jet-powered car.

The JCB Hydromax was not built to rival the 1997 record, according to F. I. A., but rather to set a new fastest speed for a hydrogen vehicle. But, the organization said in a statement, “it has laid down an important marker in the world of motor sport and beyond.”

Claire Moses is a Times reporter in London, focused on coverage of breaking and trending news.

Gulf Oil Giants Are Spending Billions to Build Ways Around Strait of Hormuz

The New York Times August 12, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Even if a cease-fire materializes, Gulf exporters recognize that relying strictly on the Strait of Hormuz is a risk they can no longer take.

By Lisa Friedman

Lisa Friedman is the London-based energy correspondent focused on Europe and the Middle East.

Six months ago, exporting oil from the Persian Gulf was fairly straightforward: Produce crude at the cheapest price possible, export it through the fastest route and sell it to the countries that can pay the most.

Those days are over.

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, long the most efficient path for exports, remains greatly curtailed because of the war in Iran. Much of the oil getting through the strait is on tankers navigating a treacherous gantlet of Iranian attack drones, or running dark with their location devices turned off. At least 17 seafarers have been killed in the region.

Gulf countries that have for decades produced much of the world’s oil are now intent on breaking their dependence on the narrow waterway. They are building or expanding pipelines and other infrastructure that can bypass it, and vastly expanding storage capacity in places like Asia.

These endeavors show how the war is changing the oil business in the Persian Gulf. They will cost billions of dollars and take years to complete, but companies and governments consider them essential hedges in an increasingly volatile region. Even if a cease-fire between the United States and Iran materializes, Gulf exporters recognize that relying too heavily on a single transit route is a risk they can no longer afford to take. And the moves, over time, could diminish Iran’s clout in the region.

“A lot of people assume the Strait of Hormuz will never carry the same share of oil exports as it did before the war,” said Ben Cahill, an energy analyst at the University of Texas at Austin. “No country in the world wants to rely as heavily on that transit point again.”

Energy producers, he said, have begun to put greater stock in making their infrastructure secure, even if comes at greater cost and less efficiency.

Before the United States and Israel began conducting military strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, about 20 million barrels of crude a day sailed through the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Gulf of Oman with the Persian Gulf. But overlapping U. S. and Iranian blockades, sea mines, missile strikes and skyrocketing insurance costs have effectively shuttered the strait.

Crude exports through the strait had fallen to about 3.7 million barrels a day as of last week, according to Kpler, a maritime tracking firm. To be sure, more oil than that is being exported from the gulf, partly via vessels that take steps to make them hard to track. Millions of barrels a day are also exiting through existing routes like pipelines not dependent on access to the Strait of Hormuz.

Still, the frenzy of activity for lasting workarounds to the strait is evident throughout the region. For example, in Fujairah, a United Arab Emirates port city facing the Gulf of Oman, construction crews are working around the clock to lay a secondary crude line parallel to an existing pipeline that delivers oil from onshore fields in Abu Dhabi.

The ambitious project aims to double the country’s bypass capacity to 3.6 million barrels per day, allowing nearly all of Abu Dhabi’s onshore crude to reach international tankers without ships having to use the Strait of Hormuz.

In addition, the Emirates’ state-owned energy giant, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, or ADNOC, said this week that it planned to spend $8.2 billion to expand its natural gas business. The company is also considering plans for a liquefied gas export facility on its eastern coast as a way to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, Peter van Driel, ADNOC’s chief financial officer, told Bloomberg Television.

In neighboring Saudi Arabia, the state oil giant, Aramco, is accelerating a multibillion-dollar expansion of its East-West Pipeline.

Designed during the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s, the 1,201-kilometer (746-mile) pipeline crosses the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Aramco’s chairman, Yasir O. Al-Rumayyan, this year called it the kingdom’s economic “lifeline,” successfully rerouting some seven million barrels per day since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz after U. S. and Israeli military strikes.

Saudi officials are working to add another one million to two million barrels a day, and they also are considering a smaller parallel second pipeline for refined oil products.

“In terms of exporting our crude, we are looking at actively increasing optionality right now,” Amin Nasser, the chief executive office of Saudi Aramco, said last week.

The uncertainty in the Strait of Hormuz is also prompting ventures among Gulf producers.

Kuwait is in discussions with Saudi Arabia and other Arab nations to build a pipeline that would connect the country’s oil fields to ports on the Red Sea or Oman. Iraq and Jordan have revived long-delayed plans for a pipeline that could carry up to one million barrels per day to the Port of Aqaba off the Red Sea, according to state television reports in Jordan. And Iraq is speeding up plans to rebuild a damaged oil pipeline to ship crude oil from the Iraqi fields in Kirkuk to Syria’s Mediterranean coast.

Yet many of these solutions come with enormous friction. Rerouting Saudi Arabia’s trade route has shifted the security burden toward the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait — where the Houthi militia group in Yemen has been attacking vessels. On Tuesday, six people were killed when the Houthis hit a ship in the Red Sea.

In addition to new pipelines, Gulf nations are building physical insurance policies thousands of miles away by expanding storage in places like South Korea, Japan and India.

The logic is simple: If the Strait of Hormuz is closed, the oil is already on the other side of the gate.

“Everybody is trying to add additional storage,” Mr. Nasser of Aramco said, adding, “Energy security is becoming a priority now.”

And yet analysts noted that while the war in Iran had exposed Gulf nations’ reliance on the strait, it wouldn’t ever be eliminated entirely.

“They definitely need the Strait of Hormuz because it brings them so many advantages and the infrastructure is there,” said Carole Nakhle, chief executive of Crystol Energy, an advisory firm. But, she said, “it was foolish for them to put their faith in Hormuz entirely.”

Lisa Friedman is a business correspondent covering energy for The New York Times.

Kennedy Stirred Vaccine Fears in Pennsylvania Years Before Measles Outbreak

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

At a speech in Lancaster County, Robert F. Kennedy mocked the threat of measles. Now local officials are racing to contain one of the largest outbreaks in the country.

By Teddy Rosenbluth

Teddy Rosenbluth spoke to local leaders, doctors and members of the plain community in Lancaster County, Pa., as well as those involved in vaccination efforts in the area.

Pressed recently on whether he might accept responsibility for the resurgence of measles in the country, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fended off any suggestion that his history of promoting vaccine skepticism might be partly to blame.

The groups facing these outbreaks were “almost all religious communities that just don’t vaccinate,” he told CNN’s Dana Bash.

“It’s hard to blame that on me,” he added.

But what Mr. Kennedy failed to acknowledge is his own role, and the role of Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group he once led, in stirring distrust in those very communities. That includes in Lancaster County, Pa., which is now at the center of one of the largest measles outbreaks in the country.

The state has reported dozens of hospitalizations and more than 230 cases, a number some local doctors consider to be a vast underestimate given that local Mennonite and Amish communities tend to avoid traditional health care.

Five years ago, Mr. Kennedy stood behind a wooden lectern on a farm in the county and delivered a warning to the local Amish community about the nation’s public health agencies.

“Those agencies are going to do everything in their power to make the Amish vaccinate,” he said. “Because they cannot stand the fact that you are healthy.”

A large crowd — 1,500 people according to a local paper’s account — spilled out from under a white tent at the annual farming fair to hear from Mr. Kennedy, then the leader of Children’s Health Defense. He turned to measles, a disease that was so horrible, he joked, that when he fell ill with it as a child he “had to stay home and watch TV the whole week.” The audience erupted with applause and laughter.

“The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” he added.

Local leaders acknowledged that improving childhood vaccination rates has long been a challenge within the area’s Amish communities, where just a quarter of people have been vaccinated against measles, according to a 2025 estimate.

But they also said the work of anti-vaccine groups, including Mr. Kennedy’s visit with Children’s Health Defense, hadn’t made it any easier.

“All it takes is somebody like that, an anti-vaxxer, to make a personal appearance to a group who already has second thoughts about immunizations,” said Dr. Alan Peterson, a family medicine physician in the county and former medical director of a program that provided free vaccines to children in Lancaster County. “Some of them just say, ‘OK, that’s all I need to know and we’re not going to get our immunizations.’”

Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for the U. S. Department of Health and Human Services, said that under Mr. Kennedy’s leadership, the agency has mounted an aggressive measles outbreak response which has included investing more than $8.5 million to support affected communities and deploying experts to offer assistance.

She added that the department works “to ensure that all communities — including those who choose not to vaccinate — have access to appropriate medical care, including therapeutics.” Children’s Health Defense did not respond to a request for comment.

To those on the front lines of the Pennsylvania outbreak, Mr. Kennedy’s assessment of the current measles situation was off-base on several counts.

For one, area doctors pointed out that the virus wasn’t only spreading through insular religious groups, as he suggested on CNN, but also those in the broader community. The percentage of children vaccinated against measles has declined in the county — falling to 88 percent of kindergartners in 2025, down from 94 percent in 2019 — as it has in the United States overall.

Several local leaders who work with or are part of the area’s so-called plain communities — a group that includes Amish and Mennonite people, who often refrain from using consumer technology, dress modestly and adopt other lifestyle restrictions — also pushed back against the characterization that they simply refuse vaccines.

There are a variety of attitudes toward vaccines within these communities, though it’s true that vaccination rates tend to be lower. That is because of cultural skepticism toward secular authorities and because children often do not attend public schools, which require vaccinations, said Cory Anderson, who studies those groups at Penn State University.

But historically, the groups were more willing to accept vaccines when there were strong relationships with local doctors, community outreach and acceptance of the shots by local Amish leaders, said Dr. Jeffrey Martin, a physician at Penn Medicine Lancaster General Health.

“The Amish are not a group that simply doesn’t vaccinate,” he added.

Allen Hoover, an Old Order Mennonite, spent nearly two decades leading vaccination efforts as the administrator at Parochial Medical Center, a clinic that mainly serves the county’s plain community. Changing attitudes was a slow process that required gentle encouragement and frequent one-on-one conversations about the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, which is highly effective at preventing infection and has an excellent safety record.

Gradually, as families saw children spared from the worst diseases, vaccination rates began to climb, he said. (The Pennsylvania Department of Health does not routinely collect vaccination data broken out by religion.)

“We had gained so much trust,” Mr. Hoover said.

Then the pandemic hit, bringing mask mandates, business closures and restrictions on church gatherings.

“It just really eroded the public trust, particularly in those communities, and really gave a stronger voice to those that were advocating for alternatives to the vaccination,” said Alice Yoder, the executive director of community health at Penn Medicine Lancaster General Health during that time.

Dr. Ken Brown, a retired scientist living in Lancaster County, remembered taking out an ad in 2021 to encourage vaccination in The Pennsylvania Busy Beaver, a publication that goes out to tens of thousands of Amish and Mennonite people in the region. Two trusted figures in the community had received their Covid-19 vaccines, he wrote, and “neither had a problem!”

The next month, Pennsylvania Coalition for Informed Consent — a partner organization of Children’s Health Defense’s Pennsylvania chapter — took out an almost identical advertisement captioned: “Vaccines can have unintended consequences.”

Distrust spread quickly from the Covid-19 vaccine to other routine shots.

“I would guess that we lost almost as much as we had gained in 20 years,” Mr. Hoover said.

Mr. Kennedy’s visit hammered home the message that public health officials — and the vaccines they promote — should not be trusted, said Dr. Peterson, the local doctor.

Dr. Richard Besser, former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, noted that Mr. Kennedy has a history of promoting vaccine skepticism in vulnerable communities.

He and other public health experts point to Mr. Kennedy’s visit to the Pacific island of Samoa in 2019, where he amplified doubts about the safety of the measles vaccine just a few months before an outbreak that killed more than 80 people. In the midst of a 2017 measles outbreak in Minneapolis within a Somali American community — where vaccination rates had fallen because of fears about autism — Mr. Kennedy visited to “discuss vaccine safety concerns,” according to a Children’s Health Defense post.

Even after Mr. Kennedy stepped away from Children’s Health Defense in 2023, the Pennsylvania chapter continued its outreach to the plain community at the same event he had attended.

The group posted a photo of their table at Family Days on the Farm in 2024, which displayed a poster titled “The Secret to Childhood Health Maybe as Simple As Just Saying No,” above graphs purporting to show better outcomes for unvaccinated children. Another poster advertised Mr. Kennedy’s book “Vax-Unvax: Let the Science Speak.”

The group purchased a table at the event again last month, even as measles cases were rapidly increasing.

“That is one of the modus operandi of the anti-vaccine movement,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, a prominent vaccine scientist who wrote a book about the rise of anti-science movements. “They try to take insular groups that may already be distrusting of either the federal government or health care and they’ll exploit that.”

As outbreaks rage on in the United States, Mr. Kennedy has offered stronger endorsements of the M. M. R. vaccine on social media and during TV interviews. But the Amish community in Lancaster — which does not use social media or own televisions — are unlikely to have heard that message.

Mr. Hoover said he thought that if Mr. Kennedy were to reach out directly to strongly encourage measles vaccination, it would “actually make a difference,” because of his influence with some community members.

Ms. Hilliard, the H. H. S. spokeswoman, declined to comment on whether Mr. Kennedy would do so, but said that the department’s measles response has involved reinforcing that “M. M. R. vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent measles.”

Public health experts said they thought a visit to Lancaster County was unlikely, given Mr. Kennedy’s track record as health secretary, which has included minimizing measles outbreaks, promoting unproven treatments for the virus and undermining confidence in childhood vaccines.

“Every now and then, Kennedy will be dragged in front of the camera and begrudgingly make some offhand positive comment about the M. M. R. vaccine,” Dr. Hotez said. “But that’s about the best you’re going to get out of him.”

Teddy Rosenbluth is a Times reporter covering health news, with a special focus on medical misinformation.

I Was Dick Cheney’s Cardiologist. Trump Has Not Looked Well, and We Should Know Why.

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Jonathan Reiner, M. D.

Dr. Reiner is a professor of medicine and surgery at George Washington University.

Dick Cheney’s heart problems were never a national secret.

I was Mr. Cheney’s cardiologist for 27 years, including his two terms as vice president. During his time in the White House, he needed stents, a defibrillator and medical treatment for an arrhythmia and a blood clot in his leg. After the defibrillator was implanted in his chest in 2001, he would frequently show visitors to his West Wing office a sample device provided to him by the manufacturer.

Mr. Cheney’s candor about his health was an anomaly for an American politician. Grover Cleveland underwent secret cancer surgery while he was president (on board a yacht for maximum privacy). Franklin Delano Roosevelt hid his use of a wheelchair from the public. Ahead of his campaign for a fourth term, he struggled with severe hypertension and congestive heart failure, but the public was told that the president’s health was “excellent in all respects.” Joe Biden’s disastrous debate performance raised concerns that the White House had attempted to conceal the president’s decline. For weeks after his hospitalization this summer, Senator Mitch McConnell shared almost no details about why he was absent from office.

In June, President Trump celebrated his 80th birthday, and at the end of this term he will be the oldest person ever to serve as this nation’s leader. After Mr. Trump’s medical evaluation in May, Dr. Sean Barbabella, the physician to the president, wrote that Mr. Trump “remains in excellent health” and that his “demanding daily schedule, including multiple high-level meetings, public engagements and regular physical activity, continues to support his overall well-being.”

Despite reassurances from the White House to the contrary, at times over the past year, the president has not looked well. I am not Mr. Trump’s doctor, and have only reviewed his records that have been made public. But Mr. Trump is probably the most photographed president in American history, and a variety of physical ailments are easy to see. He’s had large bruises on both hands, swelling in his legs and episodes when it appears that he is struggling to stay awake. He’s also had advanced imaging performed for unclear reasons. The public is again left to wonder whether the nation’s leader is OK.

Despite the unparalleled power afforded to the president of the United States, there is no formal requirement for the commander in chief to certify his fitness for duty. That’s a mistake. Members of the military, Secret Service agents, commercial pilots, school bus drivers and air traffic controllers all must periodically demonstrate that they are well enough to perform their work. The current practice of reporting the results of a yearly medical examination for the president began in the Nixon administration, but it’s only a custom, not a formal obligation. And, as history has shown, it can be unreliable.

This does not mean that every detail about a president’s health must be disclosed. It’s appropriate to withhold elements of a medical history that could be exploited by an adversary. In 2007, when we replaced Mr. Cheney’s defibrillator, we didn’t share information about a new wireless feature of the device that I considered a security threat to the vice president. (We ultimately were able to get the manufacturer to disable that capacity.)

The 25th Amendment to the Constitution allows for the best solution to this problem: It permits Congress to establish a panel outside the executive branch to assess the health and fitness of the president. In April of this year, Representative Jamie Raskin introduced a bill to create a congressional commission that would do just that. Ideally, such a panel would be empowered to review data from routine presidential physical examinations, as well as assessments performed when medical concerns emerge.

If such a commission were in place today, these are some of the medical questions it could clarify concerning Mr. Trump’s health. The American public deserves answers to all of them.

1. Dr. Barbabella’s recent report states that the president was evaluated by 22 consultants, an extraordinary number of specialists for even the most extensive executive health evaluation. Why were so many physicians summoned, and what were their specialties?

2. Mr. Trump often shows prominent bruising on his hands, which the White House attributes to frequent handshaking and frequent use of aspirin. Trauma from handshaking has never seemed plausible, and it doesn’t explain why the president’s left hand is often similarly discolored. Also, why would the president take a dose of aspirin four times as high as the dose typically recommended by doctors?

3. Swelling in the president’s legs last summer led to an unscheduled medical evaluation. The president’s physician described the problem as “chronic venous insufficiency,” a condition common in older people, that results from leaky valves in the veins of the legs. It usually develops gradually over a long period. But during Mr. Trump’s comprehensive physical examination just a few months earlier, Dr. Barbabella documented no swelling in the president’s legs. If that’s true, his swelling would be by definition acute, not chronic. Acute leg swelling is a potentially much more consequential finding that can be caused by issues such as heart and kidney disease. What’s the reason for this discrepancy?

4. The president often appears to struggle to stay awake, signs of a condition doctors refer to as excessive daytime somnolence. This problem, which is sometimes evident during Oval Office events, was not addressed in the report after Mr. Trump’s comprehensive physical exam in May. Although the president is a renowned night owl, his sleepiness seems relatively new. There are several possible causes for the president’s symptoms, some of which could have serious complications if left untreated. Has the president’s medical team identified the source of this issue? And how are they addressing it?

5. In October 2025, Mr. Trump underwent advanced imaging of his heart and abdomen at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. The president’s physician offered a vague description of the reason for the tests: “to identify issues early, confirm overall health and ensure he maintains long-term vitality and function.” He said the tests did not reveal any abnormalities. Was there a specific symptom or clinical event that prompted this testing?

6. Past Trump medical reports have disclosed the president’s use of the drug finasteride, which prevents hair loss. The drug was not mentioned in the report after Mr. Trump’s most recent medical examination. In response to a query from The Washington Post about its absence, the White House responded, “The current report reflects all medications deemed clinically relevant to disclose at this time.” It does not matter, in any material way, if the president is or isn’t taking a hair-loss drug. The more important question is, what medications prescribed for Mr. Trump, if any, has the White House decided to withhold from the public?

7. The president has spoken about how well he performs on cognitive testing. However, the exam that Mr. Trump describes, the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, is a brief and basic screening tool, with simple questions (draw a clock, identify a camel), often performed in response to a concern from the patient or a member of the family. Why has the president undergone this test numerous times, and have there been more sophisticated neurocognitive assessments performed?

Some people would argue that these personal medical details are more than the public deserves to know: After all, Buckingham Palace has not revealed many details about King Charles’s cancer or his treatment.

But the United States does not have a king. In a representative democracy, the people must have confidence in the health of their leader, and in the leader’s capacity to guide the nation. We have been kept in the dark too long.

I entirely agree with this essay. As a physician it is extraordinarily important that the public be able to assess the fitness of the president in an objective fashion. I do not believe that requires revelation of every gory detail of the president‘s health, but there must be a process that is fair, non-partisan, evidence based, and will allow the public to have appropriate information about the physical and cognitive fitness of a president.

I'm no Trump fan, but why do we have the right to know the details of these rather garden-variety problems of an old man? He's not wasting away, he doesn't seem to have had a stroke, he's not in a coma. He's a rather typical 80 year old man and the American people elected him, foolish as that was. I think it's intrusive and unrealistic to expect him (or any 80 year old leader) to divulge all their health issues. Not our business. It IS our business to elect younger and more robust and qualified leaders!

Jonathan Reiner is the co-author of the book “Heart: An American Medical Odyssey” alongside Mr. Cheney and Liz Cheney. The book details the former vice president’s struggle with heart disease.

Connections Coach

Paul Theroux traced the British coastline in 1982 for his book “The Kingdom by the Sea.” This year he walked parts of the new King Charles III England Coast Path, a continuous route along the country’s seashore.

Credit...

Supported by

By Paul Theroux

Visuals by Jeremie Souteyrat

Paul Theroux walked about 30 miles along the King Charles III England Coast Path to report this article.

There’s a glorious Latin expression for the benefits of taking a hike — solvitur ambulando: “It is solved by walking.” Is something fuddled in your mind? Searching for an idea? Wishing for clear skies, fresh air and broad sunlit uplands? Then lace your boots, leave the house and set off alone, and chances are you’ll find the answer on the way. This remedy (attributed variously to Diogenes the Cynic and St. Augustine) is one that all true pilgrims know, and in many respects serious hikers are the modern embodiment of medieval pilgrims.

England now has the longest organized coastal footpath in the world for anyone wishing to test this maxim.

The path’s formal origin dates from 1935, when the British Ramblers Association dedicated itself to “removing barriers so everyone can enjoy walking in green spaces.” I was well aware of barriers when I decided in 1982 to travel the entire coast of Britain — on foot, on trains and buses — for my book, “The Kingdom by the Sea.” Long stretches of the coast were then forbidden to hikers; many beaches and shorelines were private; and there were fences, coils of barbed wire and walled-off farmland that prevented access. Now and then, a tetchy resident would wave me away with a forbidding finger. My circumambulation of the kingdom involved detours, improvisations bordering on fancy footwork and, in some cases, covert trespassing. All for the sight that lifts my soul when I’m next to the sea — a glimpse of infinity.

Now, as a coronation gift to the new king, the whole coast of England is open to hikers: 2,689 miles of continuous trails, inaugurated by Charles III himself in March as the King Charles III England Coast Path. Anyone who is physically able can sling on a backpack in the far northeastern town of Berwick-upon-Tweed and, following signposts, walk uninterruptedly south by the sea, rounding the bulge of the Forelands, following the southern coast to Cornwall, then heading north (skipping Wales) to the uppermost limit of the western path, ending close to the Scottish border near Gretna.

Studying the maps on the path’s website, I devised an itinerary that would allow a sampling of three portions of the path: one on the Isle of Wight, a stretch on the Yorkshire coast south from Whitby, and the northern path out of Dover. In other words, downland, meadowy headlands and the White Cliffs, along with towns and villages, and tussocks of grass on one side, and the immensity of sea on the other, treading a narrow trail in the late June sunshine.

After landing at Heathrow Airport, I made my way to the Isle of Wight via buses, ferry and train, arriving in Ventnor, which I had previously visited for my book, in time for lunch. I was staying at a cottage around the corner from the house where Karl Marx enjoyed several bourgeois winters, seeking the fresh air he was denied in befogged London.

To my surprise, Ventnor was mostly unchanged from my last visit 44 years ago. It is a steep layered town, with terraces of houses from cliff to cliff, unusual in England for its mild climate — temperate enough for palm trees and banana groves in the gardens of Victorian and Edwardian villas. My neighbor had spotted a pod of dolphins near shore that morning.

The following day I took a bus west to Freshwater Bay. Alfred, Lord Tennyson, “a compulsive walker,” as he is described on the website for his house, Farringford, visited Freshwater in 1865 out of curiosity and was so bewitched by its beauty he decided to live there for the next 40 years. Julia Margaret Cameron, the pioneering Victorian photographer who portrayed him, also decided to make her home in Freshwater. When she showed Tennyson his portrait (wild hair, rumpled cloak) he called it “The Dirty Monk.”

You can visit Tennyson’s Farringford and Cameron’s house, Dimbola, near the beginning of the footpath. Up a long meadow, past browsing cows, the path led through dense woods, where I came upon Mike Dennis. He was 87 and had lived and hiked on the Isle of Wight since 1963 when he’d left his native South Africa.

“I was against apartheid. I needed to leave,” he said. He expatriated himself and after retirement walked even more.

He was headed to Tennyson Down a mile off — through moorland populated by rabbits and ravens and blurred by blowing fog, which made it very eerie, across wind-flattened grass with the hint of a path. Other walkers emerged, making their way west through the fog — Andrew and Sarah and their teenage daughter June, who’d traveled from Devon in their camper van for the Isle of Wight music festival that was starting in a few days, and Gillian and David, backpackers from Bournemouth, and a heroic old woman hitching herself forward with the use of two trekking poles.

I now had a glimpse through gauzy fog of the cliffs ahead, and after a while, past the hilly meadows, I saw a sheer wall and beyond it the chalk-white Needles, eroded fragments of the bluff, like a row of half-submerged molars extending seaward. In a level area below me the path passed a cluster of gift shops and cafes, accessible by road, visited by busloads of tourists and school children. Serious hikers stopped for a cup of coffee and proceeded onward for a closer look at the Needles.

Paul Philbrow, whom I met near the Needles, was also a bird-watcher who urged me to look for kestrels and sea eagles. He was born on the Isle of Wight — his mother’s family had lived there for generations, he said, “from the mists of time.”

A dedicated hiker, he welcomed the footpath, saying, “The thing about footpaths is they have a degree of legal protection here. Once established as a right of way, they are difficult to do away with. Which is a good thing.”

He agreed that not much had changed on the island. “More people, better restaurants, no fast food.”

Enid, who worked in one of the cafes, said, “No fast food, because local people wouldn’t eat it, would they?”

I said that for my return on the path back to Freshwater Bay, I wanted to be nearer the edge of the cliff.

“The path is just past that upper gate,” Enid said. “It’s wet today and the cliff is steep. Be careful. If you fell to your death, I’d never forgive myself.”

In any event, the visibility was so poor, I stayed clear of the edge, and so did Roger, a man of about 60, not here for the hike but headed inland, and looking as though he’d had a rough passage — wild hair, torn jacket, muddy shoes.

“Because I live in a cave,” he said. “There’s caves all along this coast. People don’t know about them. I could show you some huge ones.”

He laughed and vanished into the fog.

“What you walked is one of the best paths on the island,” said Simon Ayres, my neighbor in Ventnor, who’d showed me Karl Marx’s house. He suggested extending the walk by starting from Blackgang and then hiking via Freshwater to the Needles, 13 miles of cliffs and sea and gull-clawed sky.

It was easy enough to return to the Portsmouth railway station, and London, where I stowed my bag. I simplified my gear to fit into a small backpack — a change of clothes and assorted necessities, all I would need for a four-day hike from Whitby to Scarborough.

From King’s Cross Station, I traveled north, changed trains at Northallerton and Middlesbrough, and took the train to Whitby. In 1982 I feared this branch line would be abandoned, but it was still in use, creeping through the valley of the River Esk, stopping at tiny villages, going past shapely hills, hedgerows and Yorkshire moorland, some of the stops no more than isolated platforms embowered by fuchsias in bloom.

From my hotel room on Whitby’s West Cliff I had a view of the high cliff on the far side of the harbor and Whitby Abbey — in ruins because Henry VIII ordered this Gothic masterpiece demolished in 1539. Skeletal, blackened and hollowed out, it called to mind lines in the Shakespeare sonnet, “Bare ruined choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.”

St. Hilda established the abbey in 657. Captain Cook was born nearby, and J. M. W. Turner made three visits and painted seascapes of Whitby. Billy Bennett, a man of about 60, had been camping up and down the coastal path for the past five years, after he ditched his job at a bank in disgust: “I’m a wanderer now” he said.

Rugged up in heavy clothes, a wool cap and speaking through a dense reddish beard, he said he spent his nights under a “basha” — a simple tarp — and had humped his gear that morning from a campsite on the coastal path.

“What do you do about bathing?”

He smiled. “It gets to the point where it doesn’t matter,” he said, and shared his hiker’s wisdom: “If you go far away you come back a different person.”

John Cross, down from Derby to fish for cod, agreed with that. He was 75, retired from the Rolls-Royce factory, a lifelong climber of cliffs in Derbyshire, El Capitan in Yosemite, and Peril Rouge in France. He was a supporter of the coastal path, too. “People retire and sit in front of the TV all day. That’s not for me,” he said.

In sunshine, I continued seven miles along the cliff path to Robin Hood’s Bay, much of it level, but with declivities so steep that ladderlike stairs had been cut into the valley walls. Young Ben, a techie from Coventry, passed me, a heavy rucksack on his back — he had walked almost 20 miles from Scarborough, and when I marveled at that, he said, “I walk fast.”

“You might see puffins,” Sue Knapton said, seeing me admiring flocks of terns and gulls nested in crevices in the outer cliffs. She had come down from Leeds with her husband, Andrew, who said, “There seems to be something special about walking near to the sea. It appears to lift people’s spirits.”

We walked together, and at one point I mentioned that I saw mainly older people on the coastal path.

“Here’s what I think,” Andrew said. “Older people are tougher” — and his Yorkshire accent was emphatic, toofah — “tougher than the young. They’ve been through a lot. They grew up without the social media that softens people up.”

After a few miles, the tile roofs and brick villas of Robin Hood’s Bay appeared far below at the stony seafront of a deep valley. I’d planned to stay the night and continue on the path to Scarborough the next day, but the few hotels were full. I idled in this lovely former fishing village, then caught a bus, and rode 15 miles to Scarborough.

The next day, a hot Sunday, Scarborough was thick with visitors seeking ice cream, cold beer, fish and chips, and picnics on the beach. A number of swimmers braved the cold water. Scarborough has been an English seaside destination since the 18th century — and though a bit faded now is still vital. Its local playwright Alan Ayckbourn (still active at 87) was to premiere his 92nd play in September at Scarborough’s Stephen Joseph Theater.

The following morning, I took the King Charles III England Coast Path past Scarborough Castle, along the seaside and the elegant Victorian-era Scarborough Spa, onward and upward to Wheatcroft and rural Osgodby, to Cayton Bay and Filey. On my way, I met Brian Hallet, a retired printer from Derby, taking the air.

“This is my 50th visit,” he said. “Scarborough’s a classic Victorian resort.”

“A bit decaying in places, though?”

“That’s part of its charm!”

Welcome to France, I saw on my cellphone — a Verizon message.

But I was on the outskirts of Dover, England — 21 miles across the English Channel from France — as a coda to my other hikes, climbing to the edge of the White Cliffs, following the directions of a woman I’d met who had introduced herself as Twigs Redman — “Twigs is a made-up name,” she said. “I hate my real name. I’ve been Twigs since I was a little girl.”

At Dover Station I took Dame Vera Lynn Way to Marine Parade and up to East Cliff, “There’s all sorts of caves there,” Twigs had told me. “During the war the children who were evacuated came back and lived in those caves. They were known as ‘the Uneducated’ because all the schools were closed.”

At the cliff top, I had lunch at the National Trust Visitor Center Cafe, chatted with Mary and Greg, travelers from Athens, Ga., and set off across the White Cliffs. Through the sea mist, France was a dim shape, so near, migrants cross on small boats, almost a thousand had been intercepted in the Channel that week and brought to Dover for processing.

This was the busiest section of the coastal path I’d taken — hikers from Germany and Canada; Kelvin and Tom from Hong Kong; many young families; about 20 small boys in yarmulkes and their three black-clad teachers from a shul in London. And young Lola sitting on a bench, admiring the jackdaws strafing the cliffs, celebrating her birthday by hiking the path alone, a day off from her work at the National Crime Agency in London. “I wanted to do something special,” she said.

I was with my son, Marcel, who tramped down a precipitous path to the beach at Langdon Hole and reported there was a wrecked ship under the cliff. Then we talked about children, books, favorite movies, food, travel, memories of other walks and certain family issues, aided by solvitur ambulando.

This undemanding round trip to the South Foreland Lighthouse is enhanced by the brilliant whiteness of the chalk cliffs that endows the eight-mile stretch of the coast with almost edible beauty — like traversing a wedge of wedding cake, a chunk of ice cream, or a slab of Stilton cheese, depending on the variations of marine sunlight.

This Dover path can be extended northeast to Deal or west to Folkstone. I had no time for that now, but with several thousand miles untrodden, I promised myself I’d return, to paraphrase the poet Philip Larkin, to swagger the nut-strewn paths.

Paul Theroux’s new travel book, “True North: On the Road in Canada,” will be published in September.

For Blakeman, Trump Could Make and Break His Bid to Lead New York

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bruce Blakeman, who is vying to become the state’s second Republican governor in the last 50 years, pushes President Trump’s agenda even as he avoids mentioning his name.

By Grace Ashford

Reporting from Great Sacandaga Lake in Mayfield, N. Y.

At a lakeside setting in rural New York, it was not difficult for Bruce Blakeman, the Republican hopeful for governor, to read the room.

“When I become governor on Jan. 1, the first executive order I’m going to sign: New York State is no longer a sanctuary state!” Mr. Blakeman said on Sunday, drawing cheers from the crowd and prompting several middle-aged women to throw their arms up in victory.

He criticized what he saw as the state’s unwarranted generosity to immigrants and its failure to uphold heterosexual family values. And he showered the event’s host, Anthony Constantino, a fellow Republican running to succeed Representative Elise Stefanik in the state’s North Country, with Trump-coded praise.

He said he first met Mr. Constantino at Mar-a-Lago sometime last year, referring to President Trump’s home in Palm Beach, Fla.

“Great guy, business leader, patriot, great American,” Mr. Blakeman gushed on about Mr. Constantino, who is favored to win his House race in November.

Mr. Blakeman, who is seeking to become the second Republican governor of New York in the last 50 years, is more of a long shot.

This is the third time that Mr. Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, has run for statewide office. In his latest iteration, Mr. Blakeman, 70, has taken inspiration from Mr. Trump’s playbook — mocking his opponents with A. I.-generated content, barring transgender girls from playing sports with their peers in county facilities and working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to deport people in the state illegally.

His path is tricky. Although he is fiercely loyal to the president, Mr. Blakeman seldom invokes Mr. Trump’s name on the campaign trail, making no mention of him in the TV ad he has been running statewide since May. He was similarly mum at the Sunday event at Great Sacandaga Lake, despite its MAGA vibe.

Mr. Trump’s popularity is spotty at best in New York. In a Siena University poll released on Wednesday, 60 percent of likely voters held an unfavorable opinion of the president; Mr. Blakeman fared better, with 33 percent of respondents holding a favorable opinion and 26 percent unfavorable.

The same poll had Gov. Kathy Hochul, the incumbent Democrat, leading Mr. Blakeman 49 percent to 39 percent among likely voters — a smaller lead than the governor held four years ago at this time against the Republican candidate, Lee Zeldin. (Ms. Hochul would go on to defeat Mr. Zeldin, who now leads the Environmental Protection Agency, by six percentage points.) Forty-six percent of likely voters held a favorable view of her, while 49 percent disapproved.

John Faso, a former Republican congressman who ran for governor in 2006, said that “Democrats want to make the election about Trump, and Republicans need to make the election about state and local issues under Democratic one-party rule in the state.”

Even so, Mr. Blakeman has avoided criticizing the president, or any of his initiatives. When reporters asked him this week whether he disagreed with Mr. Trump on any issues, Mr. Blakeman gestured vaguely toward differences on the economy and guest worker visa programs.

“I’m going to come out in the next couple of weeks and talk about things that I think are important that the administration may not agree upon,” he vowed.

Indeed, it would be easier for Mr. Blakeman if Mr. Trump were to avoid bringing attention to himself. Instead, the president plans to visit Mr. Blakeman in Nassau County on Friday.

Mr. Blakeman said in a statement that he was “grateful” that the president was coming and looking forward to paying tribute with him to the county’s law enforcement officials.

For a few weeks last year, it appeared that Ms. Stefanik would carry Republicans’ hopes of unseating Ms. Hochul. Ms. Stefanik is a longtime ally of Mr. Trump, but so is Mr. Blakeman — dividing the president’s loyalties.

When asked to weigh in on the two candidates, Mr. Trump refused to take a side, saying both were “great people.” Ms. Stefanik dropped out of the race a short time later.

Since then, Mr. Blakeman has defended the president’s deportation agenda and the tactics of ICE agents, even as they have come under increased scrutiny after a handful of interactions have led to the deaths of U. S. citizens.

If Mr. Blakeman hopes to defeat Ms. Hochul, he will need to replicate Mr. Zeldin’s successes on Long Island and Rockland County, where he won a majority of votes, while keeping Ms. Hochul’s margins in New York City largely in check.

But while Mr. Zeldin did well in the rural portions of Western New York and the North Country, the most populous counties upstate, which include Syracuse, Rochester and Buffalo, chose Ms. Hochul by roughly six points — the same margin by which she carried the state.

Ryan Radulovacki, a Hochul campaign spokesman, said that voters will recognize that the governor “has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets at every opportunity, invested billions in public safety, and stood up against Donald Trump’s endless attacks on this state.”

The last Republican to win statewide was Gov. George E. Pataki in 2002, who won Erie, Onondaga and Monroe Counties by double digits.

Mr. Faso said that winning upstate had gotten harder in the past 30 years.

“Many of the Republican constituencies have moved out of state, or they’ve gone to their great reward,” he said, noting the population decline that has accompanied the shrinking of the private sector in Monroe and Onondaga Counties. Today those areas are dominated by educational and medical institutions, whose employees tend to skew more liberal.

“People are voting with their feet, and often the people who are more mobile are people who might be a little more affluent, or might be retirees,” he said.

Ms. Hochul, a Buffalo native, is a stronger competitor upstate than many of her predecessor Democrats. And as an incumbent, she also wields a significant fund-raising advantage, finishing the last reporting period with more than three times as much funds as Mr. Blakeman’s $6.5 million cash on hand.

That shortfall is exacerbated by the decision of one of the state’s largest Republican backers, the cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder, to seemingly step away from politics. But other groups including the Republican Governors Association and a political action committee called Strong and Safe New York, backed by the Knicks owner James L. Dolan, have signaled they intend to bolster Mr. Blakeman.

There was little evidence of a cash crunch at the event on Sunday, where an ice cream cart and truck offering wood-fired pizzas supplemented the pasta and seafood buffet in the center of the room.

The appearance of Mr. Blakeman alongside Mr. Constantino seemed somewhat noteworthy: Like the rest of the Republican establishment, Mr. Blakeman declined to endorse Mr. Constantino, whose provocative style had led to several high-profile spats with state Republican leaders.

Mr. Constantino, who won a decisive victory in his primary, appeared to have no intention of holding a grudge against Mr. Blakeman. A representative for Mr. Constantino noted that the businessman, who was entirely self-funding his congressional campaign, had also covered the Sacandaga event.

“We want to welcome everybody back into New York State,” Mr. Constantino told a group of reporters before the event. “We want people to start coming back here, living here, wanting to stay here, and you know the best way to do that is to elect Bruce Blakeman.”

Grace Ashford covers New York government and politics for The Times.

8 Takeaways From Tuesday’s Primaries

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A moderate won the closely fought Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin, the latest contest between the party’s progressive and moderate wings.

By Patricia Mazzei and Tim Balk

Patricia Mazzei reported from Columbia, S. C.

An agonizingly close race in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin ended with an upset win for the moderate David Crowley early on Wednesday, the latest turn in a rancorous battle between the party’s ascendant left and its old guard that has defined primary season this year.

Mr. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and standard-bearer for moderates in the race, vastly exceeded expectations by defeating State Representative Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who built a supercharged campaign of energized supporters and overwhelmingly led in most public polls.

Other races were called before midnight. Here are eight takeaways from Tuesday’s long night.

For weeks, polls established Ms. Hong, a democratic socialist, as the clear front-runner. But Mr. Crowley outperformed expectations on Tuesday, narrowly edging his left-wing rival.

Soon after polls closed on Tuesday night, it became clear that, for the second consecutive week in a Democratic primary, a progressive candidate was not winning by as big a margin as predicted. Last week in the Democratic Senate race in Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens in a closer-than-expected contest that was not called until the next morning.

But in Wisconsin, the wait was shorter. And the outcome was far different for the progressive movement.

Ms. Hong was the subject of a string of bad headlines in the final days of the campaign, including some over past remarks she made online. Those comments included her derision of Thanksgiving and other holidays, which she walked back.

The negative publicity could have been a bridge too far for some voters, especially if they made their choices in the final days of the campaign. In addition, some of the biggest national names in progressive politics, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, sat out the race.

Ms. Hong spent more time campaigning in rural Wisconsin than any other candidate, and it appeared to pay off, given how well she was doing in those parts of the state. Democratic socialists and other progressives have won a string of races on the strength of their ground games and populist left-wing proposals that are resonating with many voters. The old-fashioned takeaway? Showing up in person to make your case makes a difference.

But in Ms. Hong’s race, that wasn’t enough.

In another Midwestern race in neighboring Minnesota, the progressive lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, won the Democratic nomination for Senate, notching a victory for the party’s left wing. Ms. Flanagan’s victory over Representative Angie Craig, who had far more financial resources, was a triumph for what some saw as a more palatable form of progressivism.

Ms. Flanagan ran on a suite of progressive priorities — calling for universal health care, a higher federal minimum wage and an end to unconditional U. S. aid for Israel. She said she would challenge the Democratic establishment in Washington.

But Ms. Flanagan did not describe herself as a democratic socialist, and she captured support from a broader constellation of Democrats and progressives, including Mr. Sanders and Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Christopher S. Murphy of Connecticut and Tina Smith of Minnesota, whose retirement opened the seat. Ms. Flanagan also did not suffer from a social-media footprint denigrating Thanksgiving. She will face Michele Tafoya, a Republican and former sports broadcaster, in November.

On the Republican side, Senator Darline Graham, a political newcomer and President Trump’s choice to succeed her brother, the late Senator Lindsey Graham, advanced to a runoff alongside Representative Ralph Norman, a hard-line conservative and a leader of the House Freedom Caucus.

Ms. Graham’s triumph over a field of more experienced candidates provided yet another show of the power that Mr. Trump holds over Republicans. The president came around to the idea that Ms. Graham should run for the seat after she was tapped to finish her brother’s term and met with the president in the Oval Office. He made very clear that he admired her poise.

Ms. Graham had been in the Senate 28 days as of Tuesday, exactly one month after Mr. Graham died. In her remarks on election night, she displayed a steady countenance. She talked up Mr. Trump’s domestic agenda while also touting that she passed a bill sanctioning Russia that would have made her hawkish brother proud.

And she let voters in on her grief, saying she has not had a lot of time to process his death.

“I think a lot about what I would say to him, what he would say,” she said. “Right now, I think he would be very proud.”

Mr. Norman, a five-term congressman, had given up his House seat and come in third in the Republican primary for governor in June. His political career appeared to be over.

But running a statewide campaign, even a losing one, gave Mr. Norman the name recognition and organization to jump into the mad dash of a special Senate primary election after Mr. Graham died last month. And that’s what Mr. Norman did, coalescing enough conservative support around South Carolina to advance to the runoff against Ms. Graham.

His advancement also gave Ms. Graham bragging rights as the lone Trump-supported candidate in the race. Although Mr. Norman is seen as a hard-line conservative, his support for Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential contest may have cost him the president’s affections.

Ms. Graham said on Tuesday that she is “hopeful” that Mr. Trump will campaign for her in the runoff, “but we’ll see.”

Representative John Larson, a 78-year-old Democrat seeking a 15th term in office, lost his primary race in Connecticut’s First Congressional District to Luke Bronin, former mayor of Hartford, in the latest example of restive Democratic voters ousting older lawmakers.

Mr. Bronin, a 47-year-old former Navy intelligence officer, campaigned explicitly on generational change. His victory followed wins by younger challengers in congressional contests in New York and Denver.

Those races pitted younger progressives against older moderates, while the Connecticut race was largely centered on age. Mr. Larson suffered a complex partial seizure on the House floor last year.

Remember Mike Lindell? He lost.

Julie Bosman, Lisa Lerer and Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article described Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee from Michigan, as a democratic socialist. Dr. El-Sayed, a progressive, does not identify as a democratic socialist, and he was not endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Patricia Mazzei is a national political correspondent for The Times, based in Miami.

They Spoke English, Wore U. S. Flags and Attacked Fishermen. Who Were They?

The New York Times August 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ecuadorean crews plying the waters of the Pacific have been targeted by a mysterious outfit equipped with drones. Some sailors appear to have lost their lives.

By Maria Abi-HabibRiley MellenJosé María León Cabrera and Christiaan Triebert

Far out in the Pacific Ocean, Ecuadorean fishermen have been attacked by unidentified “gringos” using drones, survivors say, spurring a mystery over whether the American military, the armed forces of another country or private military contractors were behind the strikes.

One fishing boat has been lost at sea since January, the U. N. says, with eight people still missing and presumed dead. The survivors of two other vessels said they came under attack in March by English-speaking assailants wearing matching uniforms with American flag patches, but without any clear insignia to link them to an official government force.

Some of the surviving fishermen said they had been hauled out of the water, questioned and then handed over to El Salvador’s navy before being released. The Pentagon has denied involvement, as has the U. S. Coast Guard.

Survivors have also said that a plane followed and seemingly surveilled them before the strikes.

The New York Times analyzed flight data and found that a maritime patrol plane — based out of a military base in El Salvador — flew in the direction of all three boats in the days before they were attacked. The pilots onboard spoke English with American accents, according to air traffic control communication recordings.

And as the boats moved through the ocean, the plane’s course also shifted to remain pointed at each of them over several days, The Times analysis found. Flight tracking data shows that the plane flew toward the boat that went missing in January, the Fiorella, on four different days, including on the day it disappeared.

Last transmission on Jan. 20

Left port onJan. 13

Note: Flight paths show only outbound routes

Sources: National Directorate of Aquatic Spaces of the Ecuadorian Navy, Flightradar24, Juan Alvia.

Daniel Wood/The New York Times

But the plane does not appear on the Pentagon’s lists of active aircraft. Instead, it was registered last October to a company that lists its address as a private mailbox in a UPS store in Richmond, Va., according to Federal Aviation Administration records.

Since the Pentagon started blowing up boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean last September, accusing them of being used for drug trafficking, dozens of vessels have been attacked, killing at least 221 people.

Washington has not been shy about claiming the strikes, often publishing footage on social media of tiny fishing boats cutting through the water before being obliterated by American munitions.

These attacks, however, have gone unclaimed.

It is certainly possible that the U. S. or some other military has conducted clandestine attacks on boats in the region. But the many lingering questions surrounding the fishing boat attacks have led some experts to wonder whether a private military contractor has been hired by the U. S. government or one of its Latin American allies — possibly El Salvador, where the plane has operated.

“It would be one thing if the U. S. didn’t have an overt maritime strike campaign, but they do, and they’re posting snuff films of boats going up in flames regularly. And that’s what makes this even more squirrelly,” said Brian Finucane, a former State Department lawyer who specializes in the laws of war. He worked in the Obama and Biden administrations, as well as in the first Trump one.

“Who are these people that are operating, and under what authority?” Mr. Finucane asked. “And they are using a UPS store as their company address? Come on.”

Ecuadorean and Salvadoran officials did not respond to requests for comment.

In November, the plane that tracked the courses of the fishing boats was flown from Tennessee to El Salvador and stationed on the military side of an airport there, flight data show. During that time, the Pentagon began increasing its air assets at another nearby airport in El Salvador to support its counternarcotics campaign in Latin America.

Air traffic controllers told the patrol plane to park at the “military apron.” A satellite image from January shows the plane parked near military aircraft, hundreds of yards away from the closest civilian craft, and images taken from the ground show that the plane’s tail is adorned with the flag of El Salvador. Still, it is unclear what role, if any, the plane played in the attacks on the fishing boats.

The Trump administration has made Latin America one of its top foreign policy priorities, to try to stem the flow of migrants and the region’s drug cartels.

Some private military contractors have shifted in kind.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration discussed issuing “letters of marque,” which were used by the U. S. government during the 18th century, before the nation had built up its navy. The letters would allow the U. S. government to contract private security forces with maritime capabilities to protect Washington’s interests at sea and to detain vessel crews.

The letters, according to three people with knowledge of the discussions, were circulated among various agencies for their input in May and were supposed to complement the Pentagon’s boat strike campaign in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

Discussions around letters of marque seemed to stall around June, and the Pentagon would not say whether any have been issued. When asked about the attacks on the fishing boats, it said, “We have no knowledge of, nor were U. S. Southern Command forces involved in, the incidents described.”

Private military contractors have been active in the hemisphere. Erik Prince, whose firm Blackwater was a notorious private military contractor hired by the U. S. government in Iraq, began touring Latin America in the lead-up to the 2024 election. Mr. Prince has met with the leaders of El Salvador and Ecuador to discuss regional security, although details of those conversations are unknown.

One of Mr. Prince’s security firms was contracted by the Haitian government last year to fight the gangs, a deal the State Department authorized. As part of that contract, Mr. Prince’s company offered maritime services to patrol Haiti’s coast, according to an official in Haiti familiar with the contract.

A spokesperson for Mr. Prince said that “neither Erik Prince nor any entities affiliated with him have any relation to these events” involving Ecuadorean fishing boats.

While the Pentagon’s strikes use sophisticated equipment, including attack planes and MQ-9 Reaper drones, the attacks on the Ecuadorean fishing vessels have been carried out by rudimentary drones fitted with explosives and deployed from a vessel manned by “gringos” with American-flag patches who never identified themselves, a lawyer representing some of the fishermen said.

Ever since the Pentagon began striking boats last year, Ecuadorean fishermen say they have been scared to go out onto the water. But the crew members of the Negra Francisca Duarte II had bills to pay and mouths to feed, they said, so they set out to sea in early March.

Satisfied with their catch, they said, they headed back to the mainland, entering Ecuador’s territorial waters in mid-March. That morning they were stopped by the nation’s coast guard, inspected and then cleared for passage, according to interviews with five of the crew.

That afternoon, they said they noticed they were being followed by a blue boat on the horizon. About an hour later, drones flew toward them and then dropped explosive devices onto their ship, injuring several crewmen and engulfing their vessel in flames.

“The boys were there, hurt and scared. Some got a fire extinguisher to try to put out the fire, but there were too many flames,” the captain of the Negra Francisca, Hernán Flores, told The Times.

As the fire grew, some of the crew members dived into the ocean while others jumped into smaller boats attached to the Negra Francisca. They headed toward the blue ship that had been following them, hoping to be saved.

“We were really scared,” Mr. Flores said.

As they approached the blue vessel, the crew members onboard ordered the fishermen to raise their hands, communicating through a translator, the fishermen said. They said they were then bound, hooded and held on deck overnight, receiving no medical attention even though some were badly injured, with open, bleeding wounds.

The men, who were armed, questioned the fishermen, asking whether they were carrying anything illegal. When an injured fisherman replied that they had been inspected by the Ecuadorean Coast Guard shortly before the attack, the men began arguing among each other, seemingly worried, the fishermen said.

The next morning, the fishermen said, they were transferred to the Salvadoran Coast Guard and taken to a naval base in La Unión, in El Salvador, where they were treated well. The Salvadoran authorities told them that when they received the Ecuadorean crew, the armed men described their captives only as shipwrecked fishermen. They were then released to the capital, San Salvador, with no charges, the crew members said.

What struck Mr. Flores was his inability to identify the group of men on the blue boat, he said. For decades, he said, he had interacted with the navies and coast guards of Ecuador, the United States and other nations that patrol the waters around Ecuador, one of the world’s biggest routes for the illicit cocaine trade. They often sailed boats that clearly identified what branch of government they belonged to — like the Navy or the Coast Guard — and wore uniforms with insignia to match, the fishermen said.

But these men wore just the American flag patches, and their vessel did not fly a flag or have other markings on it, the fishermen’s lawyer said.

A U. S. Coast Guard spokesperson said in a statement that the Coast Guard cutter Bertholf, participated in a search for the Negra Francisca, as it was only about 70 miles from the fishermen. It said it had found debris from the boat but no survivors and suspended the search after 12 hours. The Coast Guard and Pentagon denied any knowledge or involvement in the attack.

While it remains unclear who carried out the strikes, they came as the Pentagon stepped up its cooperation with allies across Latin America to combat the drug trade. In May, the Pentagon applied pressure on Guatemala to agree to joint U. S. airstrikes and other military action inside its borders, to target suspected drug groups. Ecuador agreed to a similar deal earlier this year.

Last week, U. S. Southern Command announced Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, setting up the infrastructure for the more ambitious, Latin American-wide expansion of its war against drugs in cooperation with regional allies.

The attacks on the Ecuadorean fishermen should be a wake-up call for Latin American governments, argued Juanita Goebertus, who leads the Americas division at Human Rights Watch, which published its own report on the strikes.

“The U. S. government is prioritizing operations based on weak intelligence and with illegal use of force,” she said.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington, and Gabriel Labrador from Mexico City. Map by Daniel Wood.

Maria Abi-Habib is an investigative correspondent reporting on Latin America and is based in Mexico City.

Riley Mellen is a reporter on The Times’s Visual Investigations team, which combines traditional reporting with advanced digital forensics.

Christiaan Triebert is a Times reporter working on the Visual Investigations team, a group that combines traditional reporting with digital sleuthing and analysis of visual evidence to verify and source facts from around the world.
